# conjectures-research

Deciding what a Rust performance competition gated on Lean proofs should actually
target — and, first, whether such a thing can work at all.

This exists because the previous attempt ([`../conjectures-rust`](../conjectures-rust),
DataFusion's logical optimizer) built a complete and working pipeline around a
target that could not contain a win. The post-mortem is in that repository's
`docs/STATUS.md`; the short version is that the rewrite fragment could see 40% of
a real query plan and found **zero** profitable rewrites in it, while the
wall-clock metric had a ±10% noise floor against a 2% reward bar.

So the order of work here is inverted on purpose: **establish that a win exists
and can be measured before building anything to measure it with.**

The handoff in the other direction — what these results mean for the machinery
that already exists, which parts of it carry over to a target where the *Rust* is
what gets proved, and what is still missing — is
[`../conjectures-rust/docs/RESEARCH.md`](../conjectures-rust/docs/RESEARCH.md).

## What is settled

| question | answer | where |
|---|---|---|
| Can Aeneas translate hot-loop Rust? | **Yes** — 9/12 patterns. Imperative index-based code is in; iterator chains and SIMD are out. | [`docs/AENEAS_REACH.md`](docs/AENEAS_REACH.md) |
| What does one patch proof cost? | **38 lines** for the full `memchr` contract, axioms clean. | [`docs/PROOF_COST.md`](docs/PROOF_COST.md) |
| Which targets are in reach? | Compression, JSON and Arrow kernels are ~0.1% `unsafe`. `memchr` is not (2.4% + SIMD). | [`docs/CANDIDATES.md`](docs/CANDIDATES.md) |
| Can the metric be noise-free? | **Yes** — compressed size is bit-identical across runs. | [`docs/CANDIDATES.md`](docs/CANDIDATES.md) |
| Is there headroom? | **15.2%** compression-ratio gap to zlib at level 1, algorithmic not vectorial. | [`docs/CANDIDATES.md`](docs/CANDIDATES.md) |
| Is the headroom real? | **~6%, not 15%** — vs libdeflate, in optimal parsing. The zlib gap was one mistuned constant. | [`docs/EXP1_HEADROOM.md`](docs/EXP1_HEADROOM.md) |
| Does real code extract? | **The crate: no.** Aeneas crashes and drops `find_match` and `decompress`. One kernel, verbatim: yes. | [`docs/EXP2_REAL_CODE.md`](docs/EXP2_REAL_CODE.md) |
| What does a *permutation* proof cost? | **449 lines per patch, 250 once.** Total correctness about the extracted Rust, axioms clean. | [`docs/EXP3_PERMUTATION.md`](docs/EXP3_PERMUTATION.md) |
| So what should we build? | `miniz_oxide` DEFLATE, ratio under a generous speed floor, miners writing prover-friendly Rust. | [`docs/RECOMMENDATION.md`](docs/RECOMMENDATION.md) |
| Does the thing actually work? | **Yes.** One submission, proved and scored end to end: **0.892x** the incumbent's bytes, axioms clean. | [`docs/MVP.md`](docs/MVP.md) |
| Can a submission change more than a sliver? | **The whole LZ77 parsing stage**, 90–156 lines of Rust, zero hand-written axioms. | [`docs/MVP.md`](docs/MVP.md) |
| What does a *real improvement* cost? | **32 proof lines** for a 10.8% ratio win. Per-patch total 263, against 449 for a radix sort. | [`docs/MVP.md`](docs/MVP.md) |

Four claims of mine turned out to be wrong and are corrected in place rather than
quietly dropped:

* *"Aeneas is useless for hot loops."* No — v1's codec failure was about `&str`
  and closures, not loops.
* *"Mature Rust performance code is pervasively `unsafe`."* True for `memchr`,
  false for compression and JSON.
* *"There is a 15.2% ratio gap to close."* Unfair comparison — that configuration
  was also 46% faster, and the whole zlib gap is one mistuned constant. The real
  gap is ~6% against libdeflate.
* *"Hot-loop Rust extracts cleanly."* Only code written in a particular style.
  Real third-party code uses labeled `continue` and returns `&mut` borrows, and
  Aeneas crashes on the crate.
* *"`radix_sort_symbols` is a cheap first slot because it is small and
  self-contained."* Backwards. Its contract is a permutation over array contents —
  the most global thing a small kernel can ask for — and it is the most expensive
  contract on the ladder, not the least.

Two of the open questions above were closed by building the thing, and the
answers are better than the estimates. `find_match`'s contract cost was projected
at 150–300 lines; the whole parsing stage came in at **263**, and the *marginal*
cost of a real algorithmic improvement at **32**. The lever was the one the
research predicted — the shape of the published contract — used deliberately this
time rather than discovered halfway through.

## What is not settled

**The speed floor.** 8x the incumbent is a guess. The accepted submission used
2.4x of it, but a near-optimal parser will want far more, and a floor loose enough
for that may be loose enough to matter. Raising it eventually puts SIMD back on
the critical path, at which point the target dies. Load-bearing in both
directions, and uncalibrated.

**How hard the competition actually is.** The incumbent is a single-slot hash
head, roughly level-1 quality, so the first win was easy. libdeflate is still
19.7% below it and 10.0% below the accepted submission, and closing that is
genuine work — but nobody has yet tried to close it, so the difficulty curve past
the first slot is unmeasured.

**The entropy layer.** Huffman coding and block splitting sit in the trusted
harness, identical for everyone. Both are worth ratio and both are natural second
slots, each needing its own contract.

Still understood rather than unknown: a full RFC 1951 `inflate` model in Lean, if
the obligation is ever to be stated against the whole format rather than against
its LZ77 layer. The MVP does not need it — that is the point of putting the
entropy coder in the harness — but a competition that opens the entropy layer
would.

## Reproducing

```bash
just verify       # the competition: proof gate, then score
just verify-proof # the proof gate alone
just score        # ratio only, no proof -- what a miner runs while tuning
just slot-cost    # what one submission costs, in lines

just reach        # what Aeneas translates, and what it leaves opaque
just proof        # the memchr proof, with its axioms
just survey       # unsafe/SIMD density across candidates
just headroom     # miniz_oxide vs zlib: speed and ratio
just determinism  # is the metric exact?
just knobs        # experiment 1a: do probe depth and lazy matching close the gap?
just pareto       # experiment 1b: the frontier, against libdeflate
just real-kernel  # experiment 2: the crate fails, one kernel succeeds
just sort-extract # experiment 3a: extract the prover-friendly kernel alone
just sort-proof   # experiment 3b: the sorted-permutation proof, with its axioms
just sort-cost    # experiment 3c: lines paid once vs lines paid per patch
just all
```

Charon and Aeneas come from `../conjectures-rust/scripts/extract.sh`; point
`AENEAS_WORK` elsewhere if they live somewhere else.

## The resume timer

`scripts/keepalive.sh` exists because this work outran a usage limit. It is a cron
entry that fires every 30 minutes, does nothing unless the Claude Code session
transcript has been idle for 30 minutes, and otherwise resumes it with `continue`,
appends the transcript tail to `docs/AUTOLOG.md`, and commits. It stops for good
when `.keepalive/DONE` appears and takes its own cron entry out.

```bash
scripts/keepalive-install.sh          # register it
scripts/keepalive-install.sh remove   # take it out and delete .keepalive/
```

It runs `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions`, scoped to this repository, and
the cron entry is the only thing it leaves outside the tree. Remove it when the
work it was babysitting is done.
# Research: what the v2 target survey settled

**Written 2026-09-02.** The work summarised here was done in the sibling
repository `../conjectures-research`, and every number in it is reproducible —
but by a recipe in *that* repository's `justfile`, not this one. The command is
named beside each claim, and the "Reproducing" section at the bottom has them in
one block.

Nothing in this document has been run in this checkout, and no code here depends
on it. It exists because whoever picks the work up next needs to know what was
measured elsewhere, which of this repository's parts survive it, and what is
still unknown.

## Why this document is in this repository

This repository's *mechanism* is validated and its *target* is exhausted. The
post-mortem is in [`STATUS.md`](STATUS.md): `examples/normalise` proves two real
rewrites, clears every scoring gate on a development set, is worth ~200x on
queries containing the shape it attacks — and fires **zero** times on public
TPC-H, scoring 0.9897x, a reject. The wall-clock metric has a ±10% noise floor
against a 2% reward bar, and two arms running *identical* plans once reported
1.120x.

So the research repository asked the next question — *what should such a
competition target instead?* — and answered it with measurements rather than
argument. The answer implies a v2 that differs from this repository in one
structural way (the extraction gap reopens, see below), which is why the answer
cannot just be filed away in the other repo.

## What is settled

| question | answer | command |
|---|---|---|
| Can Aeneas translate hot-loop Rust? | **Yes, 9 of 12 patterns.** Imperative index-based code is in. Iterator adapters (`fold`, `chunks`), `count_ones`, SIMD and `unsafe` are out. | `just reach` |
| What does one patch proof cost? | **38 lines** for the full `memchr` first-match contract about extracted Rust. Axioms `[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]`. | `just proof` |
| What does a proof over array *contents* cost? | **449 lines per patch plus 250 paid once.** Sorted-permutation, total correctness, about Charon/Aeneas-extracted Rust. Axioms clean. | `just sort-proof`, `just sort-cost` |
| Which crates are inside the provable subset? | `miniz_oxide` 0.8.0: 4 `unsafe` in 5,988 lines (0.07%), no SIMD. `serde_json`, `base64`, Arrow compute likewise. `memchr` is not: 2.36% `unsafe`, 1.76% SIMD. | `just survey` |
| Can the metric be exact? | **Yes.** Compressed size is bit-identical across runs — 370,547 / 264,602 / 263,710 B at levels 1/6/9, five runs each. | `just determinism` |
| Is there headroom? | **~5.9%, and it is durable.** `miniz_oxide`'s best output is 264,602 B; libdeflate reaches 249,742 B, which `miniz_oxide` cannot match *at any speed*. | `just knobs`, `just pareto` |
| Does real third-party code extract? | **The crate: no.** Aeneas crashes on `miniz_oxide` and drops `find_match`, `compress_fast`, `decompress`, `decompress_fast` and `init_tree`. A prover-friendly *rewrite* of one kernel: yes, with zero hand-written axioms. | `just real-kernel`, `just sort-extract` |
| So what should be built? | `miniz_oxide` DEFLATE, scored on **compression ratio under a generous speed floor**, miners submitting prover-friendly Rust against published per-kernel contracts. | that repo's `docs/RECOMMENDATION.md` |

## The four results that change how a v2 would be built here

**1. The metric can be an exact integer, and that is the unlock.** A ratio score
is a number two validators on different hardware compute *identically*. That
deletes the pinned governor, the isolated cores, the variance gate, the trimmed
median, the interleaved arms and — the one that actually matters for a
decentralised subnet — the possibility of two honest validators disagreeing.
Roughly half of `crates/bench`'s complexity and all of the scoring fragility in
[`SCORING.md`](SCORING.md) exist to fight wall-clock noise. In v2 wall clock
returns only as a *coarse floor gate*, where ±10% is harmless.

**2. The extraction gap reopens, and is closed the other way round.** This
repository's premise, stated in [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](ARCHITECTURE.md) and in
`CLAUDE.md`, is that a rewrite rule runs at plan time, so the Lean-compiled rule
*is* the shipping implementation. That does not transfer to a hot loop:
Lean-compiled code would be far too slow. v2 closes the gap from the other
direction — Charon and Aeneas prove **the Rust that ships**.

The consequence for this repository is a change of status, not a change of tool.
`verify/` and `scripts/extract.sh` are a side quest here, held deliberately
outside the trusted boundary because they prove things about a *mirror*. In a v2
that same machinery **is the gate**. Everything that is currently a caveat about
it becomes a trusted-base and governance concern: Aeneas's own Lean library
contains `sorry`, Charon must be rebuilt against a pinned Aeneas and the pair
drifts, and the extracted model can go stale silently. This repository already
records all three; v2 has to *act* on them.

**3. The incumbent does not need to extract.** This is the realisation that
rescues the design from result 7 in the table above. A miner competing on
`find_match` is *replacing* it: they submit a de-labelled, index-based
implementation and prove it against the published contract. Nobody ever proves
the old code. Aeneas crashing on the shipped crate therefore does not matter —
but it makes prover-friendly Rust a **submission requirement** rather than a
preference, with a documented worked example, because a miner who discovers the
rule by failing is a miner who leaves.

**4. The shape of the published contract is the substrate's highest-leverage
task.** Measured, not asserted: stating a counting-sort pass as *"the output is
the concatenation of the buckets"* forces an invariant about list segments under
`List.set` and was abandoned mid-proof; stating it as *"element `j` lands at its
bucket start plus how many earlier elements share its digit"* turns every
obligation into index arithmetic that `omega` closes. Same theorem, roughly **2x
the cost**, before any tactic work.

This is the same lever this repository already pulls — `Slot/Lemmas.lean` is why
`examples/normalise`'s submission site is three lines and no tactics — and it is
the strongest transferable finding of the whole survey.

## What carries over from this repository

* **`verifier/`, nearly unchanged.** Task-commitment and pinned-hash checks, the
  tokenising policy scanner, elaboration, the statement check, the axiom check,
  and above all the ordering — *nothing is timed until the proof is accepted*.
  The axiom check becomes **more** important, not less: Aeneas's `Std/Slice.lean`
  and `Std/StringIter.lean` contain `sorry`, so build success is not the check
  and `#print axioms` is the only thing that distinguishes a real proof from one
  that reached a sorried lemma.
* **`scripts/slotpack.py`, `tasks/…/manifest.json`, and the hash-pinning
  discipline.** Unchanged in shape; what gets pinned becomes the contract library
  and the extracted model instead of the spec library.
* **`scripts/extract.sh`, `verify/`, and `just verify-extract-check`.** These
  become central. One thing must change: in v2 the artifact being proved is
  *generated from the miner's Rust*, so **the verifier must re-extract**, and
  never trust an extraction that arrives in the submission.
* **[`COMPETITION.md`](COMPETITION.md)'s commit–reveal argument.** Unchanged: a
  public pull request cannot carry a scored submission, because it publishes the
  proof term before it is scored.
* **`crates/bench`'s differential check, shrunk.** The round-trip check
  `inflate(deflate'(x)) == x` over the corpus is the empirical half; the proof is
  what generalises it from a corpus to all inputs. Same division of labour as
  [`WIRE.md`](WIRE.md) describes for the codec.
* **The habit of separating "compiles" from "works".** The research repo copied
  it and it caught a bad synthetic corpus; see the traps below.

**What does not carry over**, so that nobody spends time trying: `lean/Slot/`'s
bag semantics of relational algebra and three-valued logic, `lean/SlotHost/`'s
wire codec, `crates/relalg`, `crates/df-bridge`, `crates/df-rule-host`, and the
whole "a Lean process *is* the rule" host protocol. Nor does the **"no Mathlib,
no Batteries"** decision in [`STATUS.md`](STATUS.md)'s *Decided* list: it is
correct for this slot and cannot survive a change of target, because Aeneas
requires Mathlib and pins Lean v4.31.0 where this repository pins v4.27.0. In v2
the prover's toolchain *is* the slot's toolchain, and the ~2 s cold build goes
with it.

## What is still missing

In the order I would do them.

1. **`find_match`'s contract cost. This is the number that decides v2's
   economics and it is not measured.** Every estimate rests on two data points:
   38 lines for a scan loop with a scalar invariant, 449 for a permutation over
   array contents. `find_match`'s contract is *local* — the returned
   `(distance, length)` really does match, within the window — with no counting
   argument and no bijection, so interpolation puts it at **150–300 lines**. That
   is an estimate. It is where the whole ratio win lives, and it is cheaper to
   measure than the permutation proof was.
2. **The Lean RFC 1951 `inflate` specification.** On the critical path, priced in
   *weeks*, and now confirmed unavoidable — `miniz_oxide`'s own `decompress` does
   not translate, so the round-trip theorem cannot be stated against another
   implementation and must be stated against the standard. This is the analogue
   of this repository's spec library, and it is the item most likely to be
   underestimated. The mitigation is already chosen: ship the LZ77-layer property
   (*the token stream reconstructs the input*, no Huffman model needed) as a
   complete smaller gate first. A complete small theorem beats an incomplete
   large one.
3. **A contract library designed on the "where does each element land" principle.**
   Nobody has built one. This is the 2x lever from result 4, and leaving each
   miner to rediscover the right formulation is the difference between a
   competition and a hazing ritual.
4. **The stability decision.** What was proved is sorted-permutation, *not*
   stability. An unstable-but-sorted replacement yields a different-but-valid
   Huffman table: fine under a ratio score, fatal under a bit-exact one. The slot
   definition has to say which, up front — the machinery for stability exists and
   is not free.
5. **A prover-friendly-Rust checker.** The rule (no labelled `break`/`continue`,
   no early return from nested loops, no trait objects, indices rather than
   iterator chains) is measured but not enforced. `verifier/`'s policy scanner is
   the right place, and the slot must ship a worked example.
6. **Corpus governance.** Held out, commit-revealed, mixed text/source/binary,
   with published *shape* statistics but not contents. The v1 lesson applies
   directly: publish the shape report from the start or the generator drifts into
   rewarding overfitting.
7. **The speed-floor constant.** "~8x the shipped level-9 time" is a proposal,
   not a measurement. It is load-bearing in both directions: without a floor the
   degenerate submission is zopfli (unbounded time for a fraction of a percent),
   and with a *tight* floor SIMD returns to the critical path and the target
   dies, because SIMD is outside the provable subset.
8. **Two upstream items, worth doing whatever is decided here.** File the
   ill-typed `core::mem::swap` extraction against Aeneas — it emits a three-tuple
   destructuring for a model that returns a pair, so the verbatim kernel's
   extraction does not typecheck at all. And send `NUM_PROBES[1] = 1 → 4` to
   `miniz_oxide` as a pull request: it makes the crate simultaneously *faster*
   and 6.7% *smaller* than zlib. A one-constant win is a pull request, not a
   competition, and it should be sent as one.
9. **Whether v1 continues in parallel — an open decision, not a settled one.**
   Nothing in the research says this repository must stop. What stands between
   `examples/normalise` and a win is the *fragment* — decimals, `<=`/`>=` as
   primitives — not the proof burden, and that is a bounded amount of work here.
   The research says v1 should not be the flagship; it does not say it is dead.

## Retractions to carry across

These were claims I held confidently and that measurement overturned. They are
recorded because they are exactly the sort of thing that gets rediscovered
expensively.

* *"Aeneas is useless for hot loops."* No. This repository's codec failure was
  about walking a `&str` and passing a function to `Iterator::map` — neither
  characteristic of a hot loop. [`WIRE.md`](WIRE.md)'s limit is real but local.
* *"Mature Rust performance code is pervasively `unsafe` and vectorised."* True
  of `memchr`, false of compression, JSON and Arrow compute.
* *"There is a 15.2% ratio gap to zlib to close."* Unfair comparison — that
  configuration was also 46% faster — and the whole gap is one mistuned constant.
  The real, durable gap is ~5.9% against libdeflate.
* *"Hot-loop Rust extracts cleanly."* Only code written in a particular style.
  Real third-party code uses labelled `continue` and returns `&mut` borrows.
* *"`radix_sort_symbols` is a cheap first slot because it is small and
  self-contained."* Backwards. Its contract is a permutation over array
  contents — the most global thing a small kernel can ask for — making it the
  *most* expensive contract on the ladder, not the least. This one matters for
  ordering the work: starting there means starting with the least-understood
  cost.

## Traps found there, worth knowing here

* **Aeneas's own Lean library contains `sorry`.** Check the axiom list, not the
  build. This repository's habit of printing `#print axioms` on every submission
  is not optional in v2 — it is the whole gate.
* **`Slice` is a `List`, not memory.** The extracted model says what the code
  computes, not how fast. A proof cannot see cache behaviour or allocation, so
  performance stays an empirical claim and "verified performance" would be a lie.
  The proof only says the optimisation did not change the answer. Same division
  of labour this repository already uses; it must be *stated*, because the phrase
  is tempting.
* **A synthetic corpus measures nothing.** A first headroom run on repetitive
  data compressed ~300:1, was dominated by match emission, and reported
  `miniz_oxide` as 6x faster than zlib. The conclusion would have been backwards.
* **Aeneas's `step*` has two sharp edges.** It will not enter a `do` block whose
  first statement is an `if` (both branches must be rewritten into a choice of
  value first), and the extracted `¬ b` is `decide (¬ b = true)` rather than
  `!b`, which needs normalising before any lemma about `!` applies.
* **Charon and Aeneas drift as a pair.** Charon must be rebuilt against a pinned
  Aeneas. This project lost time to exactly that skew once already.
* **Proof cost is not only line count.** The 449-line proof uses Aeneas's WP
  layer, `step*`, `Finset` sums, `Equiv.ofBijective` and
  `Finite.injective_iff_surjective`. Lines understate what it asks of a
  contributor, and it was a *second draft* written by the same person who wrote
  the contract — the friendliest possible case, which a real competition does not
  have.

```bash
cd ../conjectures-research

just headroom     # miniz_oxide vs zlib: speed and ratio
just knobs        # do probe depth and lazy matching close the gap?
just pareto       # the frontier, against libdeflate
just real-kernel  # the crate fails to extract; one rewritten kernel succeeds
just sort-extract # extract the prover-friendly kernel alone
just sort-proof   # the sorted-permutation proof, with its axioms
just sort-cost    # lines paid once vs lines paid per patch
just all
```

Charon and Aeneas are built by *this* repository's `scripts/extract.sh`; the
research repo points `AENEAS_WORK` at them rather than keeping a second copy.

## Where to pick it up

The next four steps, in order, and where they belong:

1. Measure `find_match`'s contract cost. Still a *probe* — it belongs in
   `../conjectures-research/probes/`, not here.
2. Prototype the LZ77 reconstruction property as the first complete gate.
   Also a probe.
3. Design the contract library on the principle from result 4.
4. Only then the substrate: `inflate` in Lean, and composing kernel contracts up
   to `inflate ∘ deflate = id`.

Steps 1 and 2 can still invalidate the recommendation, which is why no harness
work should start before them — that is the mistake v1 made, and the reason this
repository has a complete, working pipeline aimed at a target that could not
contain a win.
# competition/

A working competition: miners submit Rust, a Lean proof gates it, and accepted
submissions are scored against a baseline through a fixed test harness.

The design, the measurements and the honest risks are in
[`../docs/MVP.md`](../docs/MVP.md). How to write a submission is
[`../docs/MINER.md`](../docs/MINER.md). This file is the map.

```
slot/src/parse.rs          THE SLOT — the miner's LZ77 parser. Compilable as its
                           own crate root, because charon takes it as one.

lean/
  Lz77/Spec.lean           what a token stream means (RFC 1951's LZ77 layer)
  Lz77/Lemmas.lean         valid_lit and valid_match — the whole per-patch
                           interface to the contract
  Lz77/Interface.lean      toks, bytes, and `Obligation`: the statement itself
  Slot/                    generated by charon + aeneas; the verifier regenerates
                           it on every submission and never trusts a supplied one
  Proof/Parse.lean         THE MINER'S PROOF
  Proof/Axioms.lean        `#print axioms` — the check that build success is not
  Verify/Obligation.lean   the gate: three lines, written by the verifier

harness/
  src/token.rs             the token encoding — the same function as LZ77.emit
  src/deflate.rs           tokens to DEFLATE bytes. Trusted, fixed, identical for
                           the incumbent and every submission
  src/baseline.rs          the incumbent: a frozen copy of a promoted parse.rs
  src/main.rs              round-trip check, compressed bytes, speed floor

verifier/
  verify.py                the six-stage gate
  extract.sh               charon + aeneas, run by the verifier
  make-corpus.py           the scoring corpus
  PINS.json                hashes of everything a miner may not change

corpus/                    generated; five files, deliberately different in kind
```

## The one-line version of each design decision

**Why the parsing stage and not a kernel.** A slot has to be big enough to contain
a win. Match finding is where compression ratio lives, and it is 90–156 lines of
imperative index-based Rust — which is exactly the shape Aeneas translates.

**Why the token stream and not the bytes.** Huffman coding is a bijection; putting
it in the harness means the score measures parse quality alone, and means the
obligation needs no model of the entropy layer.

**Why `Found`.** It is the firewall between the search and the emission. The
search may be anything; only the bytes it compared are load-bearing. This is what
keeps a submission's proof from growing when its algorithm changes.

**Why the verifier re-extracts.** An extraction supplied by a miner is a claim
about a program made by the person whose program it is.

**Why a type check and not a text check.** `LZ77.Obligation slot.parse` either
typechecks from the miner's theorem or it does not. A weakened statement is a
compile error, not something to be caught by reading.

**Why `#print axioms`.** Aeneas's own Lean library contains `sorry`, so a proof
that reached a sorried lemma would build cleanly.
# What Aeneas can actually translate

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Reproduce:** `just reach` (probes/aeneas-reach/).

The gating question for any competition where miners submit *Rust patches* and pay
for them with a *Lean proof*: which shapes of optimisation code can Charon and
Aeneas translate at all? Code outside the subset cannot be proved, so the subset
is the competition's real scope.

The v1 project left a pessimistic impression here — Aeneas could not translate
`crates/relalg`'s wire codec, and `docs/WIRE.md` records that as a hard limit. That
impression turns out to be **wrong as a general claim**, and it matters that it is
wrong, because it was the reason to believe patch-level verification was infeasible.

The codec failed for two specific reasons: it walked a `&str` (UTF-8, not a slice)
and it handed a named function to `Iterator::map`. Neither is characteristic of hot
loops.

## Twelve patterns, one function each

| # | pattern | representative of | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | indexed `while` over `&[u32]` | every accumulate loop | **translated** |
| 2 | early-return search | `memchr`, `find`, scanning | **translated** |
| 3 | 4-at-a-time unrolling + tail | the classic hand optimisation | **translated** |
| 4 | word bit tricks (`^`, `>>`) | hashes, decoders | translated, but `count_ones` is opaque |
| 5 | `static` table indexed by byte | hex/base64, char classes | **translated**, table and all |
| 6 | write through `&mut [u32]` | in-place transforms | **translated** |
| 7 | insertion sort (nested loops, swap) | the small case of every real sort | **translated** |
| 8 | `Vec::with_capacity` + `push` | any patch that builds output | **translated** |
| 9 | recursion over an enum | positive control (v1's `Rel::width`) | **translated** |
| 10 | `iter().fold(closure)` | idiomatic Rust | closure translated, `fold` opaque |
| 11 | `for c in xs.chunks(4)` | blocked iteration | loops translated, `chunks` opaque |
| 12 | two slices compared in lockstep | `memcmp`, merge steps | **translated** |

Nine of twelve translate outright. The four opaque symbols are
`Iterator::fold` (two forms), `Slice::chunks`, and `u64::count_ones` — that is,
**iterator adapters and one intrinsic**, not control flow, not indexing, not
mutation, not allocation, not nesting.

## The finding

> **Imperative, index-based Rust — precisely the style hot loops are written in —
> is inside the subset. Iterator-chain style is not.**

This is a fortunate alignment rather than a coincidence. Performance-critical Rust
is *already* written imperatively: hoisted bounds checks, manual unrolling,
explicit indices. The style that resists translation is the style used where
performance does not matter.

The generated code is faithful and workable, not a stub. `sum_indexed` becomes a
`loop` combinator over a `ControlFlow` body with `Slice.len`, `Slice.index_usize`
and `wrapping_add`; `insertion_sort`'s nested loops come out as nested `loop`s with
`Slice.update`. Aeneas's Lean library ships `loop.spec` (invariant plus a
well-founded measure) and `loop.spec_decr_nat`, so there is a standard route to
reasoning about them rather than a research problem.

## What this does and does not license

**Does:** patch-level verification of scalar hot loops is on the table. A miner
optimising a scan, a decoder's inner loop, a small sort, a table-driven encoder or
an in-place transform can be asked for a proof about the code that ships.

**Does not:** SIMD is not covered — no `std::simd`, no intrinsics beyond what the
Aeneas library models, and `count_ones` already shows the gap. `unsafe`,
`get_unchecked`, raw pointers and platform intrinsics are all outside. Since a
large fraction of real Rust performance work *is* SIMD and `unsafe`, this bounds
the competition sharply and has to shape target selection: pick targets where the
available win is algorithmic rather than vectorial, or accept that the proved tier
and the fastest tier diverge.

**Untested here:** generics and trait dispatch, `Option`/`Result` heavy code
(v1 showed `?` on `Option` needs hand-written models), lifetimes beyond simple
`&`/`&mut` slices, and whether proofs about these loops are *cheap* — that last
one is the subject of `docs/PROOF_COST.md`.
# Candidate survey

Measured, not recalled. Every number here comes from a command in the `justfile`.

## Provability screen

`docs/AENEAS_REACH.md` establishes that `unsafe`, SIMD and iterator adapters are
outside the provable subset, while imperative index-based Rust is inside. So the
first cut is mechanical — how much of each crate's own source is out of reach:

| crate | lines | `unsafe` | SIMD | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `serde_json` 1.0.128 | 18,022 | 9 (0.05%) | 0 | in reach |
| `base64` 0.22.1 | 7,048 | 4 (0.06%) | 0 | in reach |
| **`miniz_oxide` 0.8.0** | **5,988** | **4 (0.07%)** | **0** | **in reach** |
| `arrow-arith` 53.2.0 | 7,718 | 15 (0.19%) | 2 | in reach |
| `arrow-ord` 53.2.0 | 9,990 | 28 (0.28%) | 0 | in reach |
| `lz4_flex` 0.11.3 | 4,422 | 87 (1.97%) | 2 | marginal |
| `memchr` 2.7.4 | 14,461 | 341 (2.36%) | 254 (1.76%) | **out of reach** |

This corrected a prior I held going in. I expected mature Rust performance code to
be pervasively `unsafe` and vectorised, and for `memchr` that is exactly right —
which is the irony, since the one proof in `docs/PROOF_COST.md` is of a *naive*
`memchr` that the real crate does not contain. But compression, JSON and Arrow's
compute kernels are essentially pure safe Rust.

## Metric determinism (rubric 4)

The criterion that killed v1. Measured on `miniz_oxide`:

```
level 1: sizes [370547 x5]  all_equal=true  bytes_identical=true
level 6: sizes [264602 x5]  all_equal=true  bytes_identical=true
level 9: sizes [263710 x5]  all_equal=true  bytes_identical=true
```

**Compressed output is bit-identical across runs.** A ratio metric is an exact
integer that two validators on different hardware compute identically. No pinned
governor, no isolated cores, no variance gate, no trimmed median, no
validator-disagreement failure mode. This single property removes the apparatus
that made v1's ladder fragile.

Throughput metrics (JSON parsing, Arrow kernels) do not have this property and
inherit the whole ±10% problem.

## Headroom (rubric 1)

`miniz_oxide` against system zlib, 1.1 MB of real source/prose/markup, best of 5:

| level | miniz_oxide | zlib | speed | **size** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 260.7 MiB/s, 370,547 B | 178.8 MiB/s, 321,664 B | mo 1.46x faster | **mo 15.2% worse** |
| 6 | 42.3 MiB/s, 264,602 B | 49.9 MiB/s, 264,229 B | zlib 1.18x faster | +0.1% |
| 9 | 25.2 MiB/s, 263,710 B | 18.1 MiB/s, 262,623 B | mo 1.39x faster | +0.4% |

The interesting cell is level 1: `miniz_oxide` is *faster* than zlib and gives up
**15.2% compression ratio** to get there. That is an algorithmic deficiency in
match finding, not a missing vector instruction — precisely the kind of gap that
is reachable inside the provable subset. Levels 6 and 9 are at parity with zlib,
which is itself well behind libdeflate and zstd, so the ladder has room above too.

A first attempt at this used a synthetic repetitive corpus and measured nothing:
8 MiB compressed ~300:1 and the run was dominated by match emission, showing
`miniz_oxide` as 6x faster than zlib. Recorded because the mistake is easy and the
conclusion would have been backwards.

## Structure (rubric 5 — can the slot publish invariants?)

`miniz_oxide/src/deflate/core.rs` decomposes into kernels with independent
contracts, which is what gives miners flexibility rather than one monolithic
target:

| kernel | contract | difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| `radix_sort_symbols` | output is a permutation of input, sorted by key | small — good first slot |
| `enforce_max_code_size` | code lengths stay a valid Kraft-sum prefix code | small |
| `calculate_minimum_redundancy` | package-merge produces optimal lengths | medium |
| `optimize_table` | emitted table decodes to the given code lengths | medium |
| `find_match` | reported `(dist, len)` genuinely matches at that distance | medium — the ratio lever |
| `compress_lz_codes` | the token stream reconstructs the input | large |

The top-level obligation, `inflate(deflate(x)) == x` for all `x`, is what these
compose to.

## Rejected, and why

**`memchr`** — out of the provable subset (2.4% `unsafe`, 1.9% SIMD). The proof
in `PROOF_COST.md` is of a naive scan, and closing the gap to the real crate means
SIMD, which cannot be proved here.

**`serde_json` / Arrow kernels** — pass the provability screen comfortably, but
the metric is throughput, so they inherit v1's measurement problem in full; and
the remaining headroom over `serde_json` is largely `simd-json`'s, i.e. SIMD.
Kept as runners-up, not leaders.

**Redis** — **not Rust.** It is C, so it is out of scope for the stated
competition. The Rust-ecosystem substitutes are worse candidates on this rubric,
not better: `sled`, `redb`, `fjall` and TiKV are I/O- and concurrency-bound, which
makes the metric noisy (rubric 4), and their interesting correctness properties are
about durability, crash consistency and transaction ordering — dramatically harder
to state and prove than a pure function's, and mostly *not* what a performance
patch would threaten.

**DataFusion again** — the logical optimizer is exhausted for this purpose; see
the v1 post-mortem. Its physical operators and Arrow's kernels are in reach but
land in the throughput-metric bucket above.
# Experiment 1: is the ratio headroom real and reachable?

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Reproduce:** `just knobs`, `just pareto`.
**Verdict: yes, but it is ~6% and not 15%, and it lives somewhere other than
where I said it did.**

## First, a retraction

`docs/CANDIDATES.md` reported that `miniz_oxide` gives up **15.2% compression
ratio** to zlib at level 1. That number is correct and the conclusion drawn from
it was not. Level 1 was also **46% faster** than zlib. Comparing two different
points on a speed/ratio tradeoff curve says nothing about which implementation is
better, and I had picked the point that flattered the argument.

Measuring the whole curve says something different.

## Knob test: does re-parameterising the existing code close the gap?

Level 1 gets exactly two handicaps from
`create_comp_flags_from_zip_params`: `NUM_PROBES[1] == 1` (one hash-chain probe)
and `TDEFL_GREEDY_PARSING_FLAG` (no lazy matching). Both are the classic non-SIMD
levers, so the cheap question first — no new code, just different constants:

| configuration | bytes | vs zlib L1 | speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| level 1 as shipped (1 probe, greedy) | 370,547 | +15.2% | 264 MiB/s |
| 4 probes, greedy | 300,222 | **−6.7%** | 184 MiB/s |
| 16 probes, greedy | 279,803 | −13.0% | 135 MiB/s |
| 1 probe, lazy | 311,886 | −3.0% | 161 MiB/s |

zlib level 1 is 321,664 B at 183 MiB/s. So **`miniz_oxide` with `NUM_PROBES[1]`
changed from 1 to 4 is simultaneously faster than zlib (184 vs 183 MiB/s) and
6.7% smaller.** The entire "gap to zlib" is a mistuned constant, not an
algorithmic deficit.

Which is bad news for the competition as I originally framed it: a one-constant
patch captures the whole win, upstream would simply take it, and rubric criterion
2 (*the gap must be durable*) fails.

## Pareto test: against the actual state of the art

zlib is the 1995 reference implementation and the wrong bar. libdeflate is the
current one. Sorted slowest first; **YES** marks a point nothing else beats on
both axes:

| implementation | MiB/s | bytes | frontier |
|---|---|---|---|
| libdeflate L12 | 6 | **249,742** | YES |
| zlib L9 | 19 | 262,623 | |
| miniz_oxide 128 probe lazy | 42 | 264,602 | |
| libdeflate L9 | 48 | 259,861 | YES |
| zlib L6 | 51 | 264,229 | |
| miniz_oxide 32 probe lazy | 70 | 268,408 | |
| miniz_oxide 32 probe greedy | 103 | 275,046 | |
| libdeflate L6 | 129 | 263,473 | YES |
| miniz_oxide 8 probe lazy | 130 | 280,332 | |
| miniz_oxide 16 probe greedy | 135 | 279,803 | YES |
| miniz_oxide 4 probe lazy | 147 | 288,280 | YES |
| miniz_oxide 1 probe lazy | 161 | 311,886 | |
| miniz_oxide 8 probe greedy | 171 | 289,820 | YES |
| zlib L1 | 183 | 321,664 | |
| miniz_oxide 4 probe greedy | 184 | 300,222 | |
| miniz_oxide 2 probe greedy | 192 | 334,151 | |
| miniz_oxide 1 probe greedy | 262 | 370,547 | |
| libdeflate L1 | **349** | 292,667 | YES |

Two things stand out.

**`miniz_oxide`'s fast end is strictly dominated.** libdeflate L1 is 1.33x faster
*and* 21% smaller than `miniz_oxide` level 1 as shipped. No tradeoff, just worse.

**`miniz_oxide` cannot reach libdeflate's ratio at any speed.** Its best output at
any setting is 264,602 B (128 probes, 42 MiB/s). libdeflate reaches 249,742 B —
**5.9% smaller than anything `miniz_oxide` can produce**, and 259,861 B at 48
MiB/s, which beats `miniz_oxide`'s best while being faster.

That second gap is the real one. Unlike the zlib gap it is *not* a constant: more
probes have diminishing returns and `miniz_oxide` runs out of ratio before it runs
out of time.

## Why the remaining gap is algorithmic, and therefore in reach

libdeflate's higher levels use **near-optimal parsing** — a dynamic program over
the match graph choosing the globally cheapest sequence of literals and matches —
plus **block splitting**, choosing where to end a Huffman block. `miniz_oxide`
does greedy or lazy matching and fixed-ish blocks.

The argument that this is reachable is stronger than "it looks algorithmic":

> **SIMD cannot improve compression ratio.** Vectorisation makes the *same*
> decisions faster. It never changes which match is chosen. So best-achievable
> ratio is a pure function of the algorithm.

SIMD only enters when a speed budget is binding — it buys more search per second.
So a competition scored on **smallest output under a generous speed floor** is
purely algorithmic, and the fact that SIMD is outside the provable subset stops
mattering. That is a design consequence, not a nice-to-have: it is what makes the
target compatible with `docs/AENEAS_REACH.md`.

## What this does to the recommendation

**Survives, with the framing corrected:**

* The bar is **libdeflate, not zlib**. Against zlib there is nothing to win.
* The target is **best achievable ratio under a generous speed floor**, not ratio
  at high speed. The floor must be loose enough that SIMD is not the binding
  constraint — something like "within 8x of the shipped level-9 time", which
  admits optimal-parsing work and still excludes zopfli-style unbounded search.
* The technique to compete on is **optimal parsing and block splitting**, not
  match-finder tuning. That is a real, open design space — zopfli, zstd's
  `btopt` and libdeflate's near-optimal parser are all different tradeoff points
  and none is final.
* **Fix `NUM_PROBES[1]` upstream and do not make it a slot.** It is a one-constant
  improvement worth 15% at level 1; it belongs in a pull request to
  `miniz_oxide`, not in a competition. Leaving it in as the first "win" would
  teach miners that the game is finding untuned constants.

**Headroom, honestly stated:** ~6% ratio at the good end, against a strong
baseline, via a technique nobody has finished exploring. That is smaller than the
15% I first claimed and it is real, durable, and inside the provable subset.
Whether 6% is worth a subnet is a business question, not a technical one — but it
should be decided against 6%, not 15%.
# Experiment 2: does the reach result survive contact with real code?

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Reproduce:** `just real-kernel`.
**Verdict: partly. The crate does not extract; a single kernel does, but in a much
harder form than my own probe code suggested.**

This was the experiment I flagged as testing "the single largest untested
assumption in this report" — that `docs/AENEAS_REACH.md`'s 9-of-12 result, obtained
on twelve functions I wrote myself, would generalise to third-party code. It
mostly does not, and the way it fails is specific and actionable.

## Result 1: the whole crate does not extract

Charon handles `miniz_oxide` 0.8.0. **Aeneas crashes on it** — an uncaught
`CFailure` in `translate_fun_sigs` — and before crashing it discards the bodies of
exactly the five functions that matter most:

| function | why | why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `DictOxide::find_match` | `continue 'outer` to an outer loop | **the ratio lever** |
| `compress_fast` | early return inside a loop | the level-1 driver |
| `inflate::core::decompress` | `continue` to outer loop | needed for the round trip |
| `inflate::core::decompress_fast` | `continue` to outer loop | same |
| `inflate::core::init_tree` | return inside nested loops | Huffman table build |

Plus `Dynamic trait types are not supported yet` for `CallbackFunc`. Marking the
offenders `--opaque` does not help: Aeneas still crashes.

So the Aeneas limitations are **labeled control flow across nested loops, early
returns from nested loops, and trait objects** — none of which appeared in my
probe, all of which appear in real optimised Rust. `find_match` uses
`continue 'outer` and `break 'found`; that is idiomatic for a hash-chain search
and it is precisely what cannot be translated.

## Result 2: a single kernel does extract — verbatim, unmodified

`HuffmanOxide::radix_sort_symbols`, copied byte for byte out of
`src/deflate/core.rs` into a standalone crate, translates completely: all four
loops get real definitions and only two symbols are opaque
(`Step::forward_overflowing`/`backward_overflowing`, the `0..256` range
internals).

So the failure above is **the crate, not the kernel**. That distinction is the
good news in this report.

## Result 3: but the extracted form is much harder than my probe's

This is the finding that actually revises the plan. The extracted signature:

```lean
def radix_sort_symbols (symbols0 symbols1 : Slice SymFreq) :
  Result ((Slice SymFreq) × (Slice SymFreq → ((Slice SymFreq) × (Slice SymFreq))))
```

That arrow in the return type is a **closure** — Aeneas's backward-function
encoding, forced because the Rust returns `&'a mut [SymFreq]` borrowed from *both*
arguments. The body also threads three real iterator state machines
(`Slice.iter`, `Iterator.enumerate`, `Iterator.take`) and calls `.next()`, because
the source says `for (pass, hist_item) in hist.iter().enumerate().take(n_passes)`.

Proving sortedness of *that* means reasoning about a higher-order borrow encoding
and three nested iterator automata on top of the permutation argument. It is not
the 38-line experience of `find_byte`, and I am no longer willing to estimate it
from the outside.

**The optimism in `AENEAS_REACH.md` was an artifact of my own coding style.** I
wrote index-based, value-returning functions, which is exactly the style that
extracts cleanly. Real code returns borrows and iterates.

## Result 4: the mitigation works, and it is mechanical

Rewriting the same algorithm in prover-friendly style — indices instead of
iterators, and a `bool` saying which buffer holds the answer instead of returning
one of two `&mut` borrows — changes the extracted signature to:

```lean
def radix_sort_indexed (symbols0 symbols1 : Slice SymFreq) :
  Result (Bool × (Slice SymFreq) × (Slice SymFreq))
```

First-order, no closure, no iterators. The rewrite is checked equivalent to the
original on 200 randomised inputs (`cargo test` in `probes/real-kernel`), and
that check is the thing that makes the rewrite legitimate rather than a different
function wearing the same name.

## What this changes

**The incumbent code does not need to extract — only the miner's replacement
does.** This is the key realisation and it rescues the design. A miner competing
on `find_match` is *replacing* it; they submit a de-labeled, index-based
implementation and prove it satisfies the published contract ("the reported
`(distance, length)` really does match at that distance"). Whether the *old*
`find_match` used `continue 'outer` is irrelevant — nobody has to prove the
incumbent.

**But the round-trip theorem via extraction is dead.** `inflate::core::decompress`
cannot be translated, so `inflate(deflate(x)) == x` cannot be proved about
miniz_oxide's actual decoder.

The resolution is to change what the theorem is about. Write **inflate in Lean as
a specification of RFC 1951**, not as a model of miniz_oxide's decoder, and prove
that a patched compressor's output decodes to the input *under the standard*. That
is the right statement anyway — the format is the authority, and it is what v1 did
with `Slot/RelAlg.lean`. It is also the several weeks of substrate work already
flagged, now confirmed as unavoidable rather than merely likely.

**Prover-friendly Rust becomes a submission requirement**, enforced by the
verifier: no labeled `break`/`continue`, no early return from nested loops, no
trait objects, indices over iterator chains. That is a real constraint on miners
and it must be documented up front with a worked example, not discovered by
them. It is narrower than "write Rust" and wider than "write Lean".

## Revised proof-cost estimate

`docs/PROOF_COST.md`'s 38 lines stands for what it measured — a scan loop with a
scalar invariant. It does **not** generalise to kernels whose contracts are about
permutations and array contents. Those need the permutation machinery on top of
the loop invariants, and the honest position is that the cost is **unmeasured**.
Measuring it — by proving `radix_sort_indexed` sorted-permutation end to end — is
now the highest-value next experiment, because it is the number that decides
whether per-patch proofs are affordable for anything beyond a scan.


---

## Addendum, 2026-09-02: the verbatim kernel is worse than "awkward"

[Experiment 3](EXP3_PERMUTATION.md) tried to *compile* the extraction of
`radix_sort_symbols`, which this experiment only inspected. It does not compile.
`just real-kernel` now shows why, as part (c):

```
what Aeneas emits:
      let (current_symbols1, new_symbols2, swap_back) :=
        core.mem.swap current_symbols new_symbols1
what its own model of the function is:
def mem.swap {T : Type} (a b : T): T × T := (b, a)
```

Aeneas's borrow encoding destructures a three-tuple — value, value,
backward-function — out of a model that returns a pair, and Lean rejects
`Kernel/Funs.lean` with *expected a product type*. So the conclusion above should
be read one notch stronger: `mem::swap` on two `&mut` slices does not merely
produce a shape that is hard to reason about, it produces Lean that cannot be
loaded at all. This looks like an upstream Aeneas bug and is worth filing.

The prover-friendly rewrite is therefore not a convenience for the miner. Without
it there is no proof to write.
# Experiment 3 — what does a permutation proof about extracted Rust cost?

**Run 2026-09-02.** Reproduce with `just sort-extract`, `just sort-proof`,
`just sort-cost`.

## The question, and the criterion set before running it

Every cost estimate in [`RECOMMENDATION.md`](RECOMMENDATION.md) extrapolated from
a single data point: the 38-line `memchr` proof in
[`PROOF_COST.md`](PROOF_COST.md), about a scan loop with a scalar invariant.
Nothing was known about a kernel whose contract ranges over the *contents* of an
array. `RECOMMENDATION.md` committed to a threshold in advance:

> If that proof costs 200 lines, the competition works. If it costs 2,000, it does
> not, and no amount of harness engineering will fix it.

So: prove that `radix_sort_indexed` — the prover-friendly rewrite of
`miniz_oxide`'s `radix_sort_symbols`, extracted from real Rust by Charon and
Aeneas — returns a **sorted permutation** of its input.

## The answer

**Proved, in 699 lines of Lean, and the split matters more than the total.**

```
the kernel, in Rust                 70 lines of code
extracted model (generated)        177 lines of code
specification -- paid ONCE         250 lines of code
refinement -- paid PER PATCH       449 lines of code
```

`Sort/Model.lean` (250) is what a *substrate* proves once: what a stable counting
sort pass is and why two of them sort a `u16` key. `Sort/Refine.lean` (449) is
what a *miner* proves per patch: that this particular extracted program is such a
pass. The theorem is total correctness — Aeneas's `spec` excludes both `fail` and
divergence, so "no `usize` overflows and no index is out of bounds" is part of
what was proved, not an assumption.

```lean
theorem radix_sort_indexed_spec (s0 s1 : Slice SymFreq) (hlen : s1.length = s0.length) :
    radix_sort_indexed s0 s1 ⦃ r =>
      (rd r.1 r.2.1 r.2.2).val.Perm s0.val ∧
      (rd r.1 r.2.1 r.2.2).val.Pairwise (fun a b => a.key.val ≤ b.key.val) ⦄
```

`#print axioms` reports `[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]` and nothing
else. No `sorryAx`, which matters because Aeneas's own Lean library contains
`sorry` in `Std/Slice.lean` and `Std/StringIter.lean` — build success is not the
check, the axiom list is.

**Against the pre-registered threshold: 449 is between the two numbers, nearer
the workable end.** Not the clean pass 200 would have been, not the kill 2,000
would have been. What that means for the design is in
[`RECOMMENDATION.md`](RECOMMENDATION.md); the honest summary is *feasible, and
expensive enough that the substrate has to carry more of the weight than
originally planned.*

## Where the 449 lines went

Per-obligation, counted from the file so these include each theorem's doc comment
and trailing blank line; they sum to `Sort/Refine.lean`'s 569 total lines rather
than to its 449 lines of code.

| obligation | lines |
|---|---|
| `loop1_loop1_spec` — the scatter | 137 |
| `loop0_spec` — the histogram | 100 |
| `loop1_loop0_spec` — the prefix sums | 71 |
| `radix_sort_indexed_spec` — the top level, both `n_passes` branches | 61 |
| `loop1_spec` — the pass loop | 57 |
| bit-twiddling bridge (`key & 0xFF`, `key >> 8`, the `usize` cast) | 29 |
| histogram-cell helpers (`hv`, `hv_set`) | 17 |
| collapsing the two `if in1` branches (`rd`/`wr`/`put0`/`put1`) | 28 |

The scatter is the expensive one, exactly as expected: it is the only loop whose
invariant mentions the destination *contents*. Nothing else is a surprise, and
nothing in the list is padding — but `loop0_spec`'s 100 lines include four nearly
identical 8-line blocks re-deriving that a masked byte is below 256, which a
sharper set of helper lemmas would collapse. Call the honest floor for this proof
~400 lines rather than 449.

## The single biggest lever: how the contract is stated

**This is the transferable result, and it is worth more than the number.**

The obvious formulation of a counting-sort pass is *the output is the
concatenation of the buckets*: `(range 256).flatMap (fun b => xs.filter (digit · = b))`.
Proving the extracted loop meets that means an invariant about **list segments**
under `List.set` — which segment of the destination currently holds which filtered
sublist. Every step needs `take`/`drop`/`set` juggling, and the final assembly
needs a lemma about indexing a `flatMap` at prefix-sum offsets. I started there
and abandoned it.

What the proof actually uses says instead *where each source element lands*:

```lean
def posAt (d : α → Nat) (xs : List α) (b j : Nat) : Nat :=
  start d xs b + cnt d xs b j        -- my bucket's start, plus how many like me came before

def IsPass (d : α → Nat) (src dst : List α) : Prop :=
  dst.length = src.length ∧
  ∀ (j : Nat) (_ : j < src.length), dst[posAt d src (d src[j]) j]? = some src[j]
```

Every obligation is then index arithmetic, which `omega` closes, and the
destination invariant is pointwise — no segments anywhere. Permutation and
sortedness both come out of one lemma (`IsPass.mono`) via the observation that
`posAt` is strictly monotone in *digit first, source index second*; the
`Equiv.Perm` needed for "every position is written" is 25 lines
(`perm_of_bij`) and is paid once.

Order-of-magnitude guess for the abandoned formulation: 1,000+ lines. So **the
choice of contract shape moved the cost by roughly 2x**, before any tactic
cleverness. A competition must therefore publish contracts in the form that is
cheap to prove against, and treat that as a substrate design task rather than
leaving each miner to rediscover it.

## Aeneas's `step*` is load-bearing

The three inner loops were driven by `step*`, which chains the extracted `let`s,
introduces the outputs with their `_post` hypotheses, and discharges the
side conditions it can. It left exactly the obligations that need real content:
index bounds, `usize` overflow, and the invariant step. Without it, each loop body
would need a hand-written `spec_bind` chain per statement — the loop-0 body alone
has thirteen. A rough count of that plumbing puts the proof 150–200 lines larger.

Two places `step*` needed help, both worth knowing:

* It does not enter a `do` block whose first statement is an `if`. Both scatter
  branches (`if in1 { … } else { … }`) had to be rewritten into a *choice of
  slice* first — `Slice.index_usize (if in1 then sb else sa) j` — which is also
  what keeps the proof from being written twice, once per value of `in1`.
* The extracted `¬ in1` is `decide (¬ in1 = true)`, not `!in1`, and needs
  normalising before any lemma about `!` applies.

## Three things the proof found that testing did not

**1. The verbatim kernel's extraction does not even typecheck.**
Experiment 2 reported that `radix_sort_symbols` translates *badly* — a
backward-function closure in its return type. Stronger result: the translation is
**ill-typed Lean**. Aeneas emits

```lean
let (current_symbols1, new_symbols2, swap_back) := core.mem.swap current_symbols new_symbols1
```

destructuring a three-tuple, while its own model is
`def mem.swap {T} (a b : T) : T × T := (b, a)`. `Kernel/Funs.lean` fails to
compile with *expected a product type*. So `mem::swap` on two `&mut` slices is not
merely awkward for the prover; nothing can be proved about that extraction at all
until Aeneas is fixed. The prover-friendly rewrite is not a nicety, it is the
only route. (Reported as-is: this is an upstream bug, and worth filing.)

**2. Zero hand-written axioms.** Extracting `src/lib.rs` needs two
`core::iter::range::Step` axioms, because the verbatim function iterates. The
indexed rewrite reaches nothing outside Aeneas's model of `core`, so
`FunsExternal.lean` does not exist and the trusted base grows by nothing. That is
a direct, measured argument for the prover-friendly submission rule.

**3. A soundness subtlety in the real algorithm.** `radix_sort_symbols` computes
both histograms *once*, from the original buffer, and pass 1 uses the second
histogram against the *output of pass 0*. That is only sound because pass 0 is a
permutation and `countP` does not care about order. The proof cannot proceed
without saying so:

```lean
theorem total_of_perm (d : SymFreq → Nat) {ys xs : List SymFreq} (h : ys.Perm xs)
    (b : Nat) : total d ys b = total d xs b := h.countP_eq _
```

Nothing in the Rust records this, and a miner who "optimised" by recomputing a
histogram from the wrong buffer, or who broke the permutation property in pass 0,
would produce a mis-sorted table that still looks plausible. This is the kind of
thing the gate is for.

## What was *not* proved, and it is a design question

The contract is sorted-permutation. It is **not** stability of the whole sort:
two symbols with equal keys may come out in either order. The machinery for
stability exists (`IsPass.mono`'s second disjunct is exactly it) but the
composed theorem does not state it.

That is deliberate, and it is the substrate's call, not the miner's. A
non-stable-but-sorted replacement produces a *different but still valid* Huffman
table, so the compressed stream stays decodable while the output bytes stop
matching the reference. For a competition scored on **ratio** that is fine and
even desirable. For one that pins bit-exact output it is a failure. The contract
has to say which, up front.

## Caveats on the number

* **The 449 is a second draft.** It is what the proof costs *knowing the right
  formulation*. A miner handed the contract and a worked example pays something
  close to it; a miner discovering the shape themselves pays much more, which is
  the same lesson as the prover-friendly-Rust rule from experiment 2.
* **I wrote both the contract and the proof.** That is the friendliest possible
  case, and a real competition does not have it. The substrate publishing the
  contract is what makes the friendly case reproducible for everyone.
* **This is the hard end of the kernel ladder, not the typical one.** A permutation
  over array contents is about the most global contract a small kernel can have.
  `find_match`'s contract — *the returned `(distance, length)` really does match,
  within the window* — is local: a bounded compare loop plus window arithmetic,
  with no counting argument and no global bijection. Extrapolating from `memchr`
  (38) and this (449), I would estimate `find_match` at **150–300 lines**. That is
  an estimate, not a measurement, and it is the next thing worth measuring
  because `find_match` is where the ratio win actually lives.
* **Skill, not just lines.** The proof uses Aeneas's WP layer, `step*`, `Finset`
  sums, `Equiv.ofBijective` and `Finite.injective_iff_surjective`. Line count
  understates what it asks of a contributor.
# Writing a submission

You change **two files**:

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `competition/slot/src/parse.rs` | your LZ77 parser |
| `competition/lean/Proof/Parse.lean` | your proof that it is correct |

Everything else is pinned by hash and the verifier will reject a submission that
touches it.

## What you are competing on

Total compressed bytes over a held-out corpus. Lower wins. The number is an exact
integer, so two validators compute the *same* score; there is no measurement noise
to argue about.

Your parser produces a **token stream**. A trusted, fixed entropy coder
(`harness/src/deflate.rs`) turns that into real DEFLATE bytes. You cannot change
the entropy coder, so the score measures exactly one thing: how good your parse is.

There is also a **speed floor**: 8x the incumbent's parse time. It is loose on
purpose, because a tight floor would make SIMD decisive and SIMD cannot be proved.
It exists only to stop the degenerate submission, which is to spend unbounded time
for a fraction of a percent.

## The contract, in one sentence

> The token stream you write must decode back to the input, and `parse` must never
> panic and always terminate.

Formally, `LZ77.Obligation` in `lean/Lz77/Interface.lean`. A token is a `u32`:

* `t < 256` — the literal byte `t`
* `t = 2^24 + (dist-1)*256 + (len-3)` — copy `len` bytes from `dist` back,
  with `1 ≤ dist ≤ 32768` and `3 ≤ len ≤ 258`

## What is *not* constrained — read this before optimising

**Nothing about how you find matches.** The hash chains in the reference
submission could be a suffix automaton, a binary search tree, a full optimal-parse
dynamic program, or a lookup in a table you precomputed from the corpus shape
statistics. The proof does not grow, because correctness depends only on the bytes
you actually compared before emitting a match.

Concretely, in the reference proof:

* `hash3_spec` proves that the hash lands in `0..32768`. It says **nothing** about
  what the hash computes. A worse hash finds worse matches; it cannot find invalid
  ones.
* `parse_loop0_loop0_spec` — the loop that maintains the chains — has the
  postcondition `True`. All it has to prove is that it terminates and does not
  index out of bounds.
* `Found` is the entire interface between the search and the emission. If you
  replace the search, `find_match_spec` is the only lemma you rewrite.

That is the design. The expensive half of the proof is the *emission*, and the
emission is the part you are least likely to want to change.

## Prover-friendly Rust — the rules

These are enforced by `verifier/verify.py` stage 1, and every one of them was
found by something failing rather than by reading a manual.

**1. No labelled `break`/`continue`, no `for`, no iterator adapters, no trait
objects, no `unsafe`, no SIMD.** Indices, `while`, and plain `if`. Aeneas
translates 9 of 12 common hot-loop shapes; the three it does not are all
iterator-shaped. (`docs/AENEAS_REACH.md`)

**2. Prefer `i <= n - k` to `i + k <= n`.**

```rust
// rejected: in the extracted model a slice may have length usize::MAX, and
// then this addition overflows, so `parse` is not total
if pos + 3 <= n { … }

// accepted
let has3 = n >= 3;
let lim = if has3 { n - 3 } else { 0 };
if has3 && pos <= lim { … }
```

**3. Bound array indices with `%`, not `&`.** `h % 32768 < 32768` is one `omega`
step. The same fact about `h & 0x7fff` is a bitvector argument, and you will pay
for it in every index you write.

**4. Give every loop a counter that decreases regardless of the data.** The chain
walk terminates because `probes` counts up to 16, *not* because the chain is
acyclic — and it must not need the chain to be acyclic, because a truncated
`as u32` can point anywhere. That is also why walking a corrupt chain is harmless:
`match_len` compares the bytes.

**5. Lift a nested loop into its own function if it reads an array from the
enclosing scope.** Aeneas reports `Unimplemented` for a second loop nested in the
body of `parse`'s outer loop when that loop also reads a local array. The fix is
to make it a function taking `&[u32]`:

```rust
// rejected
pub fn parse(input: &[u8], out: &mut [u32]) -> usize {
    let mut prev = [0u32; 32768];
    while pos < n {
        …
        while probes < 16 && cur > 0 {        // Unimplemented
            cur = prev[cur % 32768] as usize;
            probes += 1;
        }
    }
}

// accepted
pub fn find_match(input: &[u8], prev: &[u32], pos: usize, cap: usize,
                  start: usize) -> (usize, usize) { … }
```

**6. `if b { x } else { y }` assigned to a variable is fine; a fallible
computation inside a `while` guard is not.** Move the arithmetic into the body.

## Working on the proof

Two Aeneas facts will cost you an afternoon if nobody tells you:

* **`step*` will not enter a `do` block whose first statement is an `if`.** Cut it
  with `Std.WP.spec_bind` and an explicit intermediate postcondition. In practice
  that cut lands exactly where you want a named property anyway — `Found` is one
  such cut, and it is the better structure.
* **`if b then ok x else ok y` must be rewritten to `ok (if b then x else y)`**
  before `step*` continues:

  ```lean
  rw [show ((if cap > 258#usize then ok 258#usize else ok cap) : Result Std.Usize)
      = ok (if cap > 258#usize then 258#usize else cap) from by split <;> rfl]
  ```

* Register your own lemmas with `@[local step]`. Once `hash3_spec`,
  `match_len_spec`, `find_match_spec` and `parse_loop0_loop0_spec` are registered,
  `step*` discharges almost all of the plumbing and every range obligation of the
  token encoding by itself.

## The loop you will actually iterate

```bash
just score          # ratio only, no proof — cheap, run this while tuning
just slot-extract   # regenerate lean/Slot/ from your parse.rs
just slot-proof     # build the Lean side
just verify-proof   # the full proof gate, without scoring
just verify         # what a validator runs
```

Tune with `just score` until the ratio is worth having, then pay for the proof.
Do not do it the other way round.

## What it costs

Measured, on this repository, with `just slot-cost`:

| | lines |
|---|---|
| the slot, in Rust | 90–156 |
| the contract and its lemmas — **paid once, by the operator** | 131 |
| **your proof** | 236–263 |

And the number that matters most: moving the reference submission from a
single-slot hash head to 16-deep hash chains — a **10.8%** ratio win — cost
**32 additional proof lines**.
# The competition, as a working thing

**Date:** 2026-09-03. **Reproduce:** `just verify` (competition/).

`RECOMMENDATION.md` argued for a compression-ratio competition gated on Lean
proofs. This is that competition, built and run end to end on one real
submission. Everything below is a measurement from `competition/`, not a design
sketch.

## What exists

```
   slot/src/parse.rs                 the miner's Rust — the whole LZ77 parsing stage
        │
        ├── charon + aeneas ────────► lean/Slot/{Types,Funs}.lean   (verifier re-runs this)
        │                                    │
        │                             lean/Proof/Parse.lean         the miner's proof
        │                                    │
        │                             lean/Lz77/*.lean              the contract, paid once
        │                                    │
        │                             lean/Verify/Obligation.lean   the gate (3 lines)
        │
        └── cargo ──► tokens ──► harness/src/deflate.rs ──► DEFLATE bytes
                                        │
                miniz_oxide + zlib ◄────┘        round-trip check
                                        │
                                   compressed bytes, vs the incumbent
```

## The result

One submission, taken all the way through:

```
1 policy      ok — the submitted Rust is inside the subset
2 pins        ok — 18 contract and harness files unchanged
3 extract     ok — charon+aeneas re-run by the verifier, no new axioms
4 statement   ok — `LZ77.Obligation slot.parse` typechecks
5 axioms      ok — ['Classical.choice', 'Quot.sound', 'propext']
6 score       running…

file                              raw   incumbent  submission    delta
binary.bin                    2000000      888358      833460   0.938x
json.txt                      1000000      195680      164110   0.839x
lean.txt                       152156       51733       43123   0.834x
prose.md.txt                   783633      349993      294431   0.841x
source.rs.txt                 1067137      367034      317953   0.866x
TOTAL                         5002926     1852798     1653077

  miniz_oxide level 1          2011928
  miniz_oxide level 9          1583615
  libdeflate level 12          1487126   <- the state of the art

score      0.89221x   parse time 2.43x   ACCEPTED — 10.779% smaller
```

## The four things this settles

### 1. The slot is not a sliver

The unit a miner replaces is the **entire LZ77 parsing stage** — 90 to 156 lines
of Rust containing the hash function, the match verifier, the chain walk, the
greedy decision and the emission. It translates through Charon and Aeneas with
**zero hand-written axioms**.

`EXP2_REAL_CODE.md` found that `miniz_oxide` itself does not extract. That does
not matter, because a miner *replaces* `find_match` rather than proving the
incumbent's version — the realisation that rescues the design, now demonstrated
rather than argued.

### 2. Correctness is independent of the search

This is the design decision that makes the economics work, and it is worth stating
precisely.

`hash3_spec` proves that the hash lands in `0..32768` and says nothing about what
it computes. `parse_loop0_loop0_spec` — the loop that maintains the chains — has
the postcondition `True`. Between the search and the emission sits one predicate:

```lean
def Found (input : Slice Std.U8) (n pos best_len best_dist : Std.Usize) : Prop :=
  best_len.val < 3 ∨
    (3 ≤ best_len.val ∧ best_len.val ≤ 258 ∧ pos.val + best_len.val ≤ n.val ∧
      1 ≤ best_dist.val ∧ best_dist.val ≤ 32768 ∧ best_dist.val ≤ pos.val ∧
      Matches input (pos.val - best_dist.val) pos.val best_len.val)
```

A submission may compute its matches with a suffix automaton, a binary tree, or a
full optimal-parse dynamic program. It rewrites `find_match_spec` and nothing
else. Nothing in the proof says the hash chain is acyclic, or that `prev` points
anywhere sensible, or that the match found is the best available — only that the
bytes were compared.

### 3. The marginal cost of a real improvement is about 30 lines

| | lines |
|---|---|
| the slot, in Rust | 90 → 156 |
| extracted model (generated) | 190 → 241 |
| the contract, its lemmas and interface — **paid once** | 131 |
| the gate — **paid once** | 4 |
| **the proof — paid per patch** | **231 → 263** |

The submission moved from a single-slot hash head to 16-deep hash chains, won
10.8% on ratio, and its proof grew by **32 lines**. Against
`EXP3_PERMUTATION.md`'s 449 lines for a radix sort, a whole parser at 263 is the
result that decides the economics, and it comes from two deliberate choices:

* **The contract was designed for the proof.** `copyN` describes a back-reference
  as the accumulator extended one byte at a time, so `copyN_take` reduces the
  whole obligation to `∀ k < len, input[pos-dist+k] = input[pos+k]` — exactly what
  a match-length loop already computes. A miner never mentions `copyN`. This is
  EXP3's "shape of the contract" lever applied on purpose; it was worth more than
  any tactic.
* **`Found` is a firewall.** The search's cost does not propagate into the
  emission's proof.

### 4. The seam is not exhausted

libdeflate reaches 1,487,126 bytes on this corpus: **19.7% under the incumbent and
10.0% under the accepted submission**, and the gap is algorithmic — lazy matching,
better block splitting, near-optimal parsing — all of it inside the provable
subset, because *SIMD cannot improve compression ratio*. Vectorisation makes the
same decisions faster; it never changes which match is chosen.

## The gate

Six stages, and the order is the design. **Nothing is compiled for speed and
nothing is timed until the proof has been accepted**, so a submission cannot buy
validator time with a program that has no proof.

| stage | what it does | what it stops |
|---|---|---|
| 1 policy | scans the submitted Rust | code outside the translated subset |
| 2 pins | hashes 18 contract and harness files | editing the contract you are judged against |
| 3 extract | **the verifier re-runs charon+aeneas itself** | an extraction that is a claim by the claimant |
| 4 statement | `LZ77.Obligation slot.parse` typechecks | a weakened theorem |
| 5 axioms | `#print axioms accepted` | `sorryAx` — Aeneas's own library contains `sorry` |
| 6 score | round-trip, bytes, speed floor | everything else |

Stage 4 is v1's statement check done as a **type check** rather than a string
comparison, and that is the only version of it that cannot be gamed. The
verifier — not the miner — writes:

```lean
theorem accepted : LZ77.Obligation slot.parse :=
  fun input out h => Submission.parse_spec input out h
```

If the miner proved something weaker, this does not compile. Checked negatively:
substituting a proof of `⦃ fun _ => True ⦄` produces

```
Type mismatch: weak input out h has type
  slot.parse input out ⦃ x => True ⦄
but is expected to have type
  slot.parse input out ⦃ r => ↑r.1 ≤ input.length ∧ r.2.length = out.length ∧
                              LZ77.Valid (LZ77.bytes input) (LZ77.toks r.2 ↑r.1) ⦄
```

Stage 1 checked the same way: inserting `'outer: while` is rejected with
`line ~90: "'outer: while" — labelled loops`.

## Why the proof is load-bearing rather than decorative

A compressor that emits a stream which does not decode back is a silent,
catastrophic and *delayed* failure. Fuzzing finds most of the ways to get there;
`decode(parse(x)) = x` finds all of them. The harness still runs a differential
round-trip check against two independent inflaters — `miniz_oxide` and the system
zlib — because the harness must stay sound even if the contract has a bug, and a
disagreement between an accepted proof and the differential check is evidence
about the *contract*, which is exactly the failure worth catching loudly.

## What is deliberately not in the MVP

* **The entropy coder is trusted, not proved.** Huffman coding is a bijection the
  harness implements once and no miner touches, so nothing about it is in the
  obligation. Extending the competition to that layer means a second slot with its
  own contract.
* **Block splitting is in the harness**, so it is identical for everyone. It is
  worth ratio and it is a natural second slot.
* **`inflate` is not modelled.** The obligation is stated against `LZ77.decode`,
  the LZ77 layer of RFC 1951 with the Huffman coding stripped off. That is
  `RECOMMENDATION.md`'s own mitigation — *"ship the LZ77-layer property as a
  complete smaller gate first"* — and the reason it works is that the harness owns
  the entropy layer. A complete small theorem beats an incomplete large one.
* **The corpus is reproducible rather than held out**, so that the numbers here
  can be checked. A real round commit-reveals it and publishes shape statistics
  only.
* **Stability is not decided.** The score is a ratio, so a different-but-valid
  parse is fine. A bit-exact score would need the slot definition to say so.

## Honest risks

**The speed floor is a guess.** 8x the incumbent, and the accepted submission used
2.4x of it. If a later submission is a near-optimal parser it will want much more,
and raising the floor eventually puts SIMD back on the critical path, at which
point the target dies. The constant is load-bearing in both directions and it has
not been calibrated against a real frontier.

**The incumbent is weak.** It is a single-slot hash head — roughly level-1
quality. Early submissions will win easily, which is good for demonstrating that
the pipeline registers wins and bad as a measure of how hard the competition is.
The bar moves each time a submission is promoted.

**The trusted base includes Aeneas.** Its Lean library contains `sorry`, Charon
must be rebuilt against a pinned Aeneas, and the pair drifts. Stage 5 is what
stands between that and an unsound acceptance, and it is not optional.

**Two implementations of the token encoding.** `token.rs` and `LZ77.emit` are the
same function written twice, once to run and once to reason about. Keeping them in
step is a real obligation of the operator; the correspondence is tabulated in
`harness/src/token.rs` and the arithmetic half is checked exhaustively by a test
over every legal `(dist, len)`.

## Reproducing

```bash
just corpus-comp    # build the scoring corpus
just verify         # the whole gate, then the score
just verify-proof   # the proof gate alone
just score          # ratio only, no proof (what a miner runs while tuning)
just slot-cost      # what one submission costs, in lines
```
# What one patch-level proof costs

**Date:** 2026-09-02. **Artifact:** `probes/aeneas-reach/Proof/FindByte.lean`.

`docs/AENEAS_REACH.md` establishes that hot-loop Rust *translates*. Translating is
not proving, and the decision-relevant number is the second one: a competition
whose proof burden exceeds the value of the optimisation cannot function, however
elegant the pipeline.

So: the full `memchr` specification, proved about Charon/Aeneas-extracted Rust.

## The result

```
theorem find_byte_spec (xs : Slice U8) (n : U8) :
    find_byte xs n ⦃ r => FoundFirst xs n r ⦄
```

where `FoundFirst` is the real contract, not a weakened one:

```
| none   => n ∉ xs.val                                    -- absent everywhere
| some k => xs.val[k]? = some n ∧ n ∉ xs.val.take k        -- present, and FIRST
```

The `take k` clause matters: "returns *an* index where the needle occurs" is the
spec a buggy `memchr` also satisfies. This is the one that pins down first-match.

**Cost: 38 lines**, including the specification and comments. Axioms
`[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]`. No `sorry`.

## How it went

The proof is four obligations and no invention:

1. `loop.spec_decr_nat` with `measure = xs.length - i` and
   `inv i = i ≤ xs.length ∧ n ∉ take i`. Aeneas ships this rule; the invariant is
   the one anybody would write.
2. In-range branch: `Slice.index_usize_spec` gives the element, then a `split`.
3. Match found: discharged by the invariant directly.
4. No match: `take (i+1) = take i ++ [xs[i]]`, so neither part contains the needle.

Two friction points, both trivia rather than obstacles: `↑(1#usize)` does not
reduce to `1` on its own, so `List.take_add_one` will not fire until it is
normalised; and the `Usize.add_spec` side condition needs `scalar_tac`. Both are
learn-once, not per-proof.

## What this says about feasibility

38 lines for a real search-loop contract is **affordable**. Extrapolating with
appropriate suspicion:

| patch shape | expected proof cost | confidence |
|---|---|---|
| scan / search loop | tens of lines | measured |
