## Relationship to conjectures-validator

The sibling repository is the proof infrastructure this one stands on: the
static policy scanner, the Comparator, `lean4export`, the second `nanoda`
kernel, and the landrun + seccomp sandbox are all inherited rather than
reinvented. The genuinely new parts are that the statement is parameterised by
the miner's own definition (solved by putting the obligation inside
`Slot.VerifiedRule`), that miner code is *executed* and not merely type-checked,
and that the verdict is continuous rather than binary.

## Layout

```
lean/Slot/        spec library — miners import this, and only this
lean/SlotHost/    wire codec — trusted, miners never import it
lean/Main.lean    rule host process
crates/relalg/    Rust mirror of the IR and codec (no dependencies)
crates/df-bridge/ LogicalPlan ⟷ Rel, conservative; the real TCB
crates/df-rule-host/  DataFusion OptimizerRule driving the Lean host
crates/bench/     two-arm benchmark, differential check, bridge self-check
verifier/         the submission gate: policy scan, proof check, bench driver
verify/           Aeneas proofs about crates/relalg — separate package, not the slot
tasks/            slot definitions: challenge, header, footer, scoring manifest
examples/         reference submissions
tests/            semantics guards, adversarial gates, verifier tests
scripts/          submission assembly and task hash pinning
```
# Queries for the predicate-normalisation rules

The set `examples/normalise/Main.lean` was developed and measured against. Each
group is deliberately shaped so the measurement is about the rewrite:

* `contra`, `contra_join` — the contradiction rule. `l_linenumber` runs 1..7, so
  every Parquet row group has min=1 max=7 and statistics pruning cannot skip
  anything: the champion has to read and filter all 6M rows. Note that the
  *ratio* these report is a property of the scale factor — the challenger plan is
  an `EmptyRelation` and does no work at all — so it measures how much waste was
  removed, not how good the rule is.
* `coalesce_int`, `coalesce_date` — the interval rule. Both forms select the same
  rows, so the difference is the cost of the per-row filter: two comparisons
  instead of four and an `OR`. Measured at ~1.27x and ~1.32x.
* `coalesce_prune` — **a refuted hypothesis, kept as a record.** It was written to
  show that a contiguous range prunes row groups where a disjunction does not.
  It measures no effect: DataFusion prunes a disjunction correctly, by testing
  each disjunct against the row-group statistics and skipping a group only when
  every one fails. The predicate also selects ~5/6 of `lineitem`, so there was
  little to skip either way. Retained because a query that refutes a plausible
  story about the engine is worth more checked in than deleted.
* `control` — satisfiable and *not* coalescable, because the two intervals have a
  gap between them. Nothing should change. A speedup here is measuring something
  other than the rewrite.

## Run it against a null control

A speedup is uninterpretable without knowing what this machine reports when
nothing changes, and on a developer machine that is a lot: four null runs of the
set below spanned **0.888x to 1.094x** per query with identical plans, and
`control` alone reached 1.120x on zero rewrites. Any single reading inside about
±10% is noise. So always run both arms of the experiment:

```bash
QS=contra,contra_join,coalesce_int,coalesce_date,coalesce_prune,control

# the rule
just bench examples/normalise/Main.lean --scale 1 --reps 15 --max-cv 9.9 \
  --queries crates/bench/queries/normalise --only $QS --json .work/bench/real-1.json

# the null: same queries, a submission that declines every one of them, so both
# arms optimize to identical plans and the result is pure measurement noise
just bench examples/filter-merge/Main.lean --scale 1 --reps 15 --max-cv 9.9 \
  --queries crates/bench/queries/normalise --only $QS --json .work/bench/null-1.json
```

Repeat each a few times and divide the real geomean by the null geomean per
query; that cancels any systematic asymmetry between the arms. `--max-cv` is
loosened here because the gate is calibrated for the validator's pinned governor
and isolated cores, and voiding the run would hide the numbers this README is
about. `docs/STATUS.md` has the full table.
# Simplifier probes

Not a workload. Each file is a predicate with a known simplification, written
using only the types and operators the v1 fragment can lower — `Int`, `Date32`,
`Utf8View`, and `Eq`/`Lt`/`Gt`/`And`/`Or`/`Not`/`IsNull`. No decimals, no `<=`.

The point is to find out what DataFusion 50 *already* does, mechanically, rather
than guessing. Run them and read the dumped champion plan:

```bash
just bench examples/filter-merge/Main.lean --scale 0.01 --check-only \
  --queries crates/bench/queries/probe --plans .work/probe-plans \
  --only absorption,contra_eq,contra_isnull,contra_lt_eq,date_interval_or,interval_or,isnotnull_redundant,or_eq_same_col,redundant_lt,taut_isnull
for f in .work/probe-plans/*.champion.txt; do echo "== $f"; grep -E 'Filter:|EmptyRelation' $f; done
```

Results as of DataFusion 50.3 are tabulated in `docs/STATUS.md`. Six of the ten
are already handled and are therefore worth nothing on the ladder; three are real
gaps. Re-run this after any engine version bump: a gap closing upstream silently
turns a champion into a rule that no longer earns.
# Verifying the Rust mirror with Aeneas

`crates/relalg` is trusted and unproved. It is the Rust side of the wire: the
`Rel` the Lean proof is about, mirrored constructor for constructor, plus the
codec. `CLAUDE.md` says of it that "nothing above it can be more correct than the
claim that a `Rel` here means the same thing as the `Slot.Rel` the Lean proof is
about" — and until now that claim was defended by a five-plan roundtrip corpus
and two assertions.

This is one function of it proved, with [Aeneas](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas):
`Rel::width`, against `Slot.Rel.width`.

## Why `width` and not the codec

Because `width` is where a disagreement is a *soundness* bug rather than a wrong
answer. `crates/df-rule-host` accepts a rewritten plan only when its width equals
the submitted plan's, and the justification is `Slot.Sound`, which proves width
preservation over `Slot.Rel.width`. That check means something only if the Rust
`width` computes the same function as the Lean one, and nothing in the proof
pipeline says it does: `Slot.Sound` is a statement about `Slot.Rel`, and the Rust
is on the other side of the wire.

The codec is the other half of the same claim and is **not** proved here. Aeneas
cannot translate it: `sexpr::parse_at` walks a `&str`, and `rel_of_sexp` passes
`nat` to `Iterator::map` as a function value, which is outside the tool's subset
(closures as trait objects with lifetime constraints). It is left opaque, as an
axiom, and `just wire-roundtrip` remains the only thing checking it.

## What was found

`Rel::width` returned `u32` and added with a bare `+`:

```rust
Rel::Join { left, right, .. } => left.width() + right.width(),
```

`Slot.Rel.width` is over `Nat` and cannot overflow. The Rust can, and the widths
reaching it are not bounded by anything: a rewrite response is parsed by
`rel_of_sexp`, which accepts any `u32` for a scan's width. So

```
Join(Scan{ w = 4294967295 }, Scan{ w = 9 })
```

has a true arity of `2^32 + 8` and computed one of **8** — a perfectly ordinary
arity, and exactly the kind of value the host is comparing against. A rewrite
response describing a completely different plan could therefore pass the width
check. The schema-drift check downstream is what actually stopped it, which is
defence in depth working, but the width check is supposed to be the primary
guard and it was defeatable.

In a build with overflow checks the same expression *panics*, inside
`OptimizerRule::rewrite`. That fails the query rather than declining the rewrite,
which breaks the property `crates/df-rule-host` documents about itself: every
failure mode degrades to "keep the original plan".

`width` now returns `Option<u32>`, `None` meaning "no representable arity", and
both call sites treat `None` as a width violation — which is right, because
`Slot.Sound` says a rewritten plan's width equals the original's, and the
original's came from a real schema.

## What is proved

In [`verify/Verify/RelAlg.lean`](../verify/Verify/RelAlg.lean), against the
Charon+Aeneas translation of the shipping Rust:

| theorem | statement |
|---|---|
| `width_spec` | `width r` always succeeds, and reports `Slot.Rel.width` of the plan `r` denotes exactly when that is representable |
| `width_sound` | if `width r` reports an arity, that arity **is** `Slot.Rel.width` — the direction the host depends on, and the one that was false before |
| `width_complete` | it reports one whenever the specification's arity fits, so nothing correct is rejected |
| `width_never_fails` | it neither fails nor diverges |

All four depend on exactly `[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]` — the
slot's own permitted axiom set. No `sorryAx`. That is checked, not assumed, in
[`verify/Verify/Axioms.lean`](../verify/Verify/Axioms.lean), and it matters here
more than usual because **Aeneas's own standard library contains `sorry`** in
`Aeneas/Std/Slice.lean` and `Aeneas/Std/StringIter.lean`; a proof that reached
those parts of it would inherit `sorryAx` and still compile.

The proof is load-bearing rather than decorative, and this is worth checking
rather than asserting: reintroduce the bare `+`, re-extract, and the Join case of
`width_spec` no longer closes. There is no way to prove it for the wrapping
version, because it is not true.

## What it rests on

Four things, and dropping any of them makes "verified by Aeneas" mean more than
it should.

1. **Charon and Aeneas are trusted.** `verify/Relalg/{Types,Funs}.lean` is
   generated from `crates/relalg/src/lib.rs`, not transcribed, so the proof is
   about the shipping code — but only as far as the translation is faithful.
2. **`verify/Relalg/FunsExternal.lean` is hand-written**, and is the only such
   file. Rust's `?` on `Option` desugars into `Try::branch` and
   `FromResidual::from_residual`, which Aeneas models for `Result` and not for
   `Option`, so three definitions had to be supplied. They are transliterations
   of Aeneas's own `Result` versions and `from_residual` has no freedom at all
   (`Infallible` is an empty inductive). Three definitions, all reducible by
   `rfl`. That is the trusted surface.
3. **`toSpec` is a translation this repository defines.** It is not arbitrary —
   it is the denotation the wire codec already commits to, since
   `wire::rel_to_sexp` and `SlotHost.relOfSexp` compose to exactly this map. That
   they do compose to it is *tested*, by `just wire-roundtrip`, not proved. So
   the full claim "the host's width check is meaningful" is a proof composed with
   a test, and the test is the weaker half.
4. **The extraction can go stale.** `verify/Relalg/{Types,Funs}.lean` is
   generated and checked in; nothing warns you when the Rust moves underneath it
   and the proofs keep passing about code that no longer exists.
   `just verify-extract-check` is the guard, and it fails loudly.

## Why this is a separate Lake package

Aeneas's Lean library requires **Mathlib** and pins **Lean v4.31.0**.
`lean/Slot/` requires neither and pins v4.27.0, which the slot's `manifest.json`
records and every champion's proof is verified against. "No Mathlib, no
Batteries" is one of the project's settled decisions: it keeps the cold build at
~2 s and the verifier's trusted checkout small.

So `verify/` is its own package with its own toolchain, and nothing in it is
imported by `lean/`, by a miner, or by the verifier. What crosses the boundary is
a *conclusion*, restated here.

The spec is not copied across the boundary either. `verify/lakefile.toml` builds
`Slot.Value` and `Slot.RelAlg` from `srcDir = "../lean"` — the same bytes the
slot pins, compiled a second time by a second toolchain. There is one definition
of what correctness means.

## What this says about v3

[`PLAN.md`](PLAN.md) files Aeneas under v3, compression codecs, where "the proved
artifact is *not* the shipped artifact" and the manifest must say the guarantee
is weaker than v1's. Doing it once, small, says how much weaker, concretely:

* **The subset is narrow.** Of `crates/relalg` — a dependency-free crate of ~500
  lines — Aeneas translated the type definitions and two functions, 126 lines of
  Lean. The codec failed on iterator combinators and `&str` and is 16 axioms. A
  SIMD codec is much further outside the subset than that.
* **The trusted surface is real but small and inspectable.** Three definitions
  here. It will be bigger for anything using slices or iterators, and Aeneas's
  slice support is where its `sorry`s live.
* **The extraction is fragile in ways that touch design.** Aeneas mistranslates
  the `Debug` derive on mutually recursive types (a forward reference Lean
  rejects) and mistranslates `PartialEq` on an enum with a variant named `Bool`
  (it emits `Result Bool`, where Lean resolves `Bool` to the *constructor*
  instead of `_root_.Bool`). Neither has anything to do with arity, so both are
  excluded from extraction — but the second one is a tool bug triggered by
  ordinary Rust, and the alternative was renaming a constructor in a trusted
  crate to suit a tool.
* **Version pinning is exact and unforgiving.** Aeneas refuses LLBC from any
  Charon but the one it was built against, and Charon needs a specific Rust
  nightly with `rustc-dev`. The pins live in `scripts/extract.sh` and must move
  together.

None of that argues against v3. It argues for budgeting the extraction work
honestly and for writing the guarantee down as "this function, under these
axioms, given this translation" rather than "verified".

## Reproducing

```bash
just verify                # check the proofs, print their axioms
just verify-extract        # regenerate the model from the Rust
just verify-extract-check  # fail if the checked-in model is stale
```

`just verify` needs Lean v4.31.0 and Mathlib's olean cache — a few GB on first
run. `just verify-extract` additionally needs a Rust nightly with `rustc-dev` and
builds Charon, which is a rustc driver and takes ten minutes or so. Neither is
part of `just test`.
# Architecture

## What this subnet buys

conjectures-validator pays for **proofs of fixed statements**: the task names a
theorem, the miner supplies a proof, the Comparator says yes or no. The answer
is binary and the reward is a bounty.

conjectures-rust pays for **proof-gated performance**. The task names a *slot*
in a real query engine. A miner submits a replacement component together with a
Lean proof that it preserves semantics. The proof is a gate, not the product:
among artifacts that pass the gate, the one that runs a workload fastest wins.
Correctness is pass/fail; the competition is on the continuous axis behind it.

That only works if the artifact the proof is about is the artifact that runs.
Everything below follows from defending that one sentence.

## Why a query optimizer rule, and not a B-tree

A rewrite rule runs **at plan time**: once per query, in microseconds, deciding
seconds of execution. So the Lean-compiled function can *be* the shipping
implementation. Its own speed is irrelevant; only the plan it produces matters.

Nothing else in a database has that property. A B-tree, a compression codec, a
hash-join kernel — those run in the inner loop, need native SIMD, and would have
to be re-implemented in Rust after being proved in Lean. That gap is where
verified-systems projects go to die. v1 refuses to open it. (Codecs are still
worth doing; see [`PLAN.md`](PLAN.md) v3, where the gap is bridged by Aeneas plus
differential fuzzing rather than wished away.)

## The pipeline

```
                 miner
                   │  Main.lean  (rule + soundness proof, no imports)
                   ▼
       ┌───────────────────────┐
       │ static policy check   │  token scan: no import/axiom/sorry/macro/
       │ (verifier/)           │  set_option/native_decide/implemented_by/...
       └───────────┬───────────┘
                   ▼
       ┌───────────────────────┐   header + submission + footer = Solution.lean
       │ Comparator + kernel   │   the footer builds Bounty.target : Slot.VerifiedRule
       │ + lean4export         │   ── statement match is plain type equality
       │ + nanoda (2nd kernel) │   ── axioms ⊆ {propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice}
       │ under landrun+seccomp │
       └───────────┬───────────┘
                   ▼  VERIFIED
       ┌───────────────────────┐   SlotEntry.lean names Bounty.target
       │ rule host process     │   lean --run Main.lean, line-delimited s-expr
       └───────────┬───────────┘
                   ▼
       ┌───────────────────────┐   lower : LogicalPlan → Option Rel     (trusted)
       │ DataFusion + bridge   │   Slot.repeatN fuel                    (proved)
       │ crates/df-*           │   lift  : Rel → Option LogicalPlan     (trusted)
       └───────────┬───────────┘
                   ▼
       ┌───────────────────────┐   public workload + held-out workload
       │ benchmark + diff test │   result-set equality vs. the baseline plan
       │ crates/bench          │   geomean speedup, trimmed median of N
       └───────────┬───────────┘
                   ▼
             champion ladder
```

## The statement-pinning trick

The Comparator in conjectures-validator checks that the solution's theorem has
the *same type* as the challenge's. That works when the statement is closed. A
rule's soundness statement is not closed — it mentions the miner's own
definition, so `Sound rule` differs between challenge and solution and the type
hashes would never match.

The fix is to move the obligation inside a structure:

```lean
structure VerifiedRule where
  rule  : Rule
  sound : Sound rule
```

Now both files declare `Bounty.target : Slot.VerifiedRule`. The types are
identical and hash-comparable, so **the existing Comparator applies unchanged**,
while the proof obligation rides inside the value where it cannot be weakened:
you cannot construct a `VerifiedRule` without supplying `sound`.

`Sound` itself is pinned by the hash of `lean/Slot/Rule.lean`, which the task
manifest commits to alongside the challenge files.

## Trusted computing base

Proved, not trusted:

* the bottom-up traversal (`Slot.everywhere`) and the fuel-bounded fixpoint
  (`Slot.repeatN`) — `Slot.optimize_sound` derives whole-plan soundness from the
  miner's local obligation, so the driver is not in the TCB;
* the miner's rule, obviously.

Trusted:

| Component | Size | Why it is trusted, and what defends it |
|---|---|---|
| `lean/Slot/Value.lean`, `RelAlg.lean` | ~180 lines | The semantics *is* the specification. Reviewed, versioned, hash-pinned per slot. |
| `lean/SlotHost/Wire.lean` + `crates/relalg` | ~300 lines each | Two codecs must agree. `just wire-roundtrip` diffs them over a shared corpus on every CI run. |
| `crates/df-bridge` | ~350 lines | No proof reaches it. Defended by conservatism (`None` for anything unsupported), scan identity (originals are carried, not rebuilt), and differential execution. |
| Lean kernel, `lean4export`, `nanoda` | vendored | Inherited from conjectures-validator, including the second independent kernel. |
| `landrun` + seccomp sandbox | vendored | Inherited, including the live fail-closed self-test. |

Everything in the middle column is either small enough to read in an afternoon
or already trusted by the sibling validator. That is the design budget.

## What changes relative to conjectures-validator

| | conjectures-validator | conjectures-rust |
|---|---|---|
| Statement | closed, fixed by the task | `Slot.VerifiedRule`, obligation inside the value |
| Miner code | type-checked only | type-checked **and executed** |
| Reward | bounty per target | champion ladder per slot, scored on Δ speedup |
| Verdict | accept / reject | accept / reject, then a continuous score |
| Lean deps | Mathlib via formal-conjectures | Lean 4 core only |

Executing miner code is the genuinely new risk, and it is why the rule host runs
under the same landrun+seccomp isolation as the Comparator. See
[`THREAT_MODEL.md`](THREAT_MODEL.md).
# Competition design: how submissions should arrive

`SCORING.md` says how a submission is *judged*. This says how it should *arrive*,
who reviews what, and which of the project's problems are economic rather than
technical. It exists because the obvious answer — miners open pull requests
against a repository — is wrong for the scored channel and right for a different
one, and the distinction is easy to get backwards.

## Pull requests cannot carry scored submissions

Four reasons, in descending order of how badly they bite.

**1. A public pull request destroys commit–reveal.** `SCORING.md`'s anti-gaming
table answers "copy another miner's proof" with "commit–reveal, first-seen-wins
on the normalised proof-term hash". A pull request publishes the proof term
before it has been scored. Anyone watching can lift it and submit it through a
faster channel. This is not friction, it is the removal of the only defence
against copying, and no amount of process discipline restores it — the artifact
is the whole submission and it is now public.

**2. Review adds latency and subjectivity to a mechanical decision.** The gate is
a Lean type-check, an axiom allowlist, a second independent kernel, a differential
execution check, and six numeric thresholds. There is nothing for a reviewer to
contribute except a delay and an opportunity for bias. The design's central claim
is that correctness is *decidable here*; putting a human in front of it concedes
the claim.

**3. A merge has no economic meaning.** Emission is set by validator consensus on
a held-out query set that rotates per epoch. A maintainer pressing a button is
not that, and building a flow where it looks like it is invites exactly the
governance capture the subnet is supposed to avoid.

**4. Serialization.** One champion per slot, promotion measured against whoever
currently holds it. N open pull requests against a moving champion is N rebases
that change nothing.

The live flow is therefore: develop locally, commit to a hash on-chain, reveal,
and let the gate run. `crates/bench` already produces the validator's report from
the validator's code, so a miner can predict the verdict before submitting —
which is the property that makes a mechanical gate humane rather than opaque.

## But pull requests are right for the substrate, and that matters more than it looks

M1 measured something that reframes the whole competition: on TPC-H SF1 the
bridge **declines 1656 of the 2744 plan nodes it is offered**, and of the 1088 it
does lower, the reference rule finds nothing — because DataFusion's own
`push_down_filter` and `eliminate_filter` got there first. Most TPC-H predicates
are decimal comparisons, which are excluded on purpose and soundly.

Two consequences.

* **The ceiling is low and it is not the miners' fault.** A miner writing Lean
  rules cannot widen the fragment, cannot teach `lower` about decimals, and
  cannot make DataFusion's existing rules worse. The binding constraint on how
  much value this slot can produce lives in `crates/df-bridge` and
  `lean/Slot/RelAlg.lean`, not in the quality of submissions.
* **That work is unproved Rust in the trusted computing base**, which is exactly
  the kind of change that *does* need a human reviewer. Refusing to lower a node
  is always correct; approximating one never is. Every `None` in `df-bridge` is
  load-bearing and a patch that removes one has to argue why.

So run two economies with different mechanics:

| | the ladder | the commons |
|---|---|---|
| what | a proved rewrite rule | bridge coverage, new operators, proof combinators, query generation, sandbox |
| arrives as | commit–reveal to the validator | a public pull request |
| reviewed by | nothing — the gate is mechanical | a human, because it is the TCB |
| paid from | emission, by displacement and tenure | fixed bounties |
| copying | fatal; prevented by commit–reveal | the point |
| skill | Lean proof + query optimisation | Rust + DataFusion internals |

The second column is not charity. It removes the ceiling the first column
competes under, and it draws on a completely different and much larger pool of
people. Funding it out of a separate budget rather than out of emission keeps the
two from bidding against each other.

## The real constraint is the size of the talent pool

Everything above is secondary to this. The slot as it stands asks for someone who
can write a Lean 4 proof about relational algebra under three-valued logic *and*
knows what makes a query plan fast. That intersection is very small, and no
amount of reward design makes it bigger.

Four things that do, in order of leverage:

**1. Ship proved combinators, not just a specification.** Today a miner proves
`Sound` from scratch; `Slot/Lemmas.lean` is a start and no more. If the slot
shipped proved building blocks — per-operator congruence, `remap` and
`Scalar.shift` correctness, filter/join commutation with its NULL side
conditions, predicate-normalisation lemmas — then a submission becomes a
*composition* of proved pieces rather than a proof. That converts the requirement
from "Lean expert" to "optimiser person willing to learn some Lean", which is a
much larger set. I would put this ahead of M3: a verifier service with no
submissions to verify is not progress.

**2. Publish each champion's proof once it has been displaced.** Commit–reveal
stays intact — the proof is public only after it can no longer be stolen for the
position it held — and it builds the corpus of worked examples that is the best
documentation this project could have. Right now there is exactly one example and
it loses.

**3. Run a training slot with no money on it.** `production_eligible: false`
already exists in the manifest. Make a slot whose scored set *is* the public set,
with no emission and immediate feedback, so someone can learn the pipeline
without waiting an epoch to find out their axioms were wrong. It costs a manifest
and a queue.

**4. Pay for negative results.** A reproducible "I wanted this rewrite and the
fragment cannot express it" report is worth more at this stage than a marginal
rule. Every substantive thing learned so far came from that shape of observation:
that `lower_literal` accepted `Utf8` but not `Utf8View`, so no string predicate
in TPC-H could be lowered; that no date type was lowered at all; that `apply_order`
meant the rule only ever saw the plan root. None were visible from inside the
Lean, and none would have been reported by a miner who is only paid for wins.

## Two mechanical things to fix before going live

**The promotion bar is close to the measurement floor.** ε = 0.02, and three
runs on an ordinary machine with the two arms executing *identical plans*
returned 1.0068x, 1.0169x and 1.0056x. `SCORING.md`'s answer is the fixed
hardware profile, and it is the right answer, but it is a single point of failure:
one mis-provisioned validator promotes noise. Cheap second defence — **require
the improvement to replicate across two independent runs** before promoting. It
costs one extra run per candidate and it removes the whole class of "won by
variance" outcomes.

**Gate cheaply before gating expensively.** The Lean check is seconds, the
differential check at SF0.01 is a minute, a timed SF1 run on pinned hardware is
minutes of a scarce resource. Run them in that order and reject on the first
failure. Most bad submissions — unfinished proofs, wrong axioms, rules that never
fire — die in the first two stages for almost nothing.

## If what you actually want is miners editing the engine

Worth naming the alternative, because "miners submit improvements to the dataflow
engine" reads naturally and means something quite different.

If submissions were patches to a Rust query engine, the proof gate would be gone.
Nothing in Lean covers arbitrary Rust, so correctness would fall back to
differential testing and fuzzing — the same thing every performance competition
does, with no formal guarantee and a much larger attack surface (a patch that is
subtly wrong on data the test set does not cover is now a wrong answer in
production). The premise stated at the top of `CLAUDE.md` — that a rewrite rule
runs at plan time, so the Lean-compiled rule can be the shipping implementation,
with no extraction step and no gap between the proved program and the running one
— would be discarded, and with it the reason this subnet is different from a
leaderboard.

That is a coherent subnet. It is not this one, and the two should not be blended:
a slot that accepts both proved rules and unproved patches is a slot whose
guarantee is the weaker of the two, advertised as the stronger.

The honest middle path already exists in the plan as **v3**, where the shipped
artifact is not the proved one and the manifest says so out loud. See
[`AENEAS.md`](AENEAS.md) for what that costs, measured rather than guessed.
# Miner guide

## What you submit

One Lean file. No imports, no `set_option`, no tactics that leave the kernel.
It must define exactly two things by name:

```lean
def rule : Rule := ...
theorem rule_sound : Sound rule := ...
```

Auxiliary definitions and lemmas are fine — the reference submission has five.
The slot's footer assembles `Bounty.target := ⟨rule, rule_sound⟩`, so those two
names are the interface.

Your file is spliced between a fixed header and footer:

```lean
import Slot          -- header
namespace Bounty
open Slot
                     -- your file
def target : Slot.VerifiedRule := ⟨rule, rule_sound⟩   -- footer
end Bounty
```

## What you must prove

```lean
def Sound (rule : Rule) : Prop :=
  ∀ e e' : Rel, rule e = some e' → Equiv e e' ∧ e'.width = e.width
```

`Equiv e e'` is `∀ db, (eval db e).Perm (eval db e')` — same bag of rows on every
database. `e'.width = e.width` is arity preservation. Read
[`SPEC_V1.md`](SPEC_V1.md) for the fragment and its semantics.

## Getting started

```bash
just build                                  # spec library + rule host, ~2 s cold
just check examples/filter-merge/Main.lean  # type-check and print the axioms
just run   examples/filter-merge/Main.lean  # rewrite plans from stdin
just wire-roundtrip                         # codec agreement, Rust ↔ Lean
```

`just check` prints the axiom list. Anything other than a subset of
`propext`, `Quot.sound`, `Classical.choice` is a rejection — in particular
`sorryAx`, which is what an unfinished proof looks like.

```bash
$ just check examples/filter-merge/Main.lean
'Bounty.target' depends on axioms: [propext, Quot.sound]
```

## Two things that will cost you a submission

**Pattern order in `rule`.** Lean compiles overlapping patterns into nested
matches that do not reduce, and then the soundness proof will not go through for
the arm you care about. In the reference submission the two arms selected by the
*child's* constructor come first, and the arm selected by a specific *predicate*
comes last — written the other way round, the third arm shadows the first two
for one particular `p` and nothing reduces. If a case of `rule_sound` will not
close and the goal still shows an unreduced `match`, this is why.

**Order-sensitivity.** `Equiv` is bag equality. Every operator in the v1
fragment is permutation-congruent, so this is safe — but if you find yourself
wanting `LIMIT` or `ORDER BY`, they are absent on purpose and the bridge will
not lower them.

## What makes a rule win

The gate is correctness; the competition is speed. Read
[`SCORING.md`](SCORING.md) before optimising for the wrong thing — in
particular, scoring is on a **held-out** query set seeded from a chain block
hash, no single query may regress by more than 1%, and plan time is budgeted.

Rules that only ever fire on the published TPC-H queries will score nothing.

## Where the headroom is

Predicate pushdown through joins, join reassociation, predicate normalisation
under three-valued logic, union distribution, column pruning. The ranked list
with notes is at the end of [`SPEC_V1.md`](SPEC_V1.md).
# Implementation plan

## Position

[`STATUS.md`](STATUS.md) is the live board — it distinguishes what has
been *run* from what merely compiles, and carries the environment notes and
open questions. This section is the summary.

Done, in this repository, and verified locally:

* the Lean spec library — semantics, congruence, and the proved traversal
  (`lean/Slot/`, builds clean in ~2 s with **no Mathlib and no Batteries**);
* the rule host process and its wire protocol (`lean/SlotHost/`, `lean/Main.lean`);
* the Rust mirror of the IR and codec, with a cross-implementation roundtrip
  check that both codecs agree (`crates/relalg`);
* the DataFusion bridge and the `OptimizerRule` that drives the Lean host
  (`crates/df-bridge`, `crates/df-rule-host`), verified end to end against real
  plans over 6M rows by the M1 positive control;
* the two-arm benchmark, differential check and bridge self-check
  (`crates/bench`), run at TPC-H SF1;
* the slot's task bundle and the submission assembler (`tasks/`, `scripts/`);
* a reference submission with three real rewrites, proved, whose only axioms are
  `propext` and `Quot.sound` (`examples/filter-merge/`).

Not done: the verifier service, the ladder, and the subnet integration. Those are
M2–M7 below.

What M1 also established, and what redirects the work: the reference submission
does **not** beat stock DataFusion — zero rewrites on all ten public TPC-H
queries, and a geomean indistinguishable from 1.0, because its three rewrites are
things `push_down_filter` and `eliminate_filter` have already done by the time the
rule is asked. The pipeline works; that rule does not win. See
[`STATUS.md`](STATUS.md#m1-results-what-the-number-says).

## Milestones

### M1 — benchmark harness (`crates/bench`) — **done**

Built and run. TPC-H generation, content-addressed; two-arm interleaved runner;
differential check as bags; a bridge positive control; a `BenchReport` and the
gates 2–6 of [`SCORING.md`](SCORING.md) as a verdict.

**Exit criterion — the reference submission produces a measurable, repeatable
speedup on at least one TPC-H query — was not met**, and the reason is the
submission, not the harness. The differential check passes everywhere; the
positive control shows all three rewrites round-tripping through a real plan at
SF1; the fragment lowers 1088 of 2744 offered TPC-H nodes. The rule simply finds
nothing left to do after DataFusion's own rules.

Four bugs found along the way. Three presented as "no speedup" rather than as
errors: `LeanRule` never saw anything but the plan root (`apply_order` at its
default), `lower_literal` rejected `Utf8View` and every date type, and a lowered
date literal could not be lifted back into a plan DataFusion would type. The
fourth was worse — `lift` was not fail-closed, because `Filter::try_new`
type-checks only on a best effort, so a malformed lifted plan failed the *query*
at physical planning time instead of degrading to "keep the original plan". All
fixed; details in [`STATUS.md`](STATUS.md#four-bugs-m1-found-all-fixed).

**Follow-on, and now the highest-value work:** a reference submission that wins.
Predicate pushdown through a join is the first item on the headroom list in
[`SPEC_V1.md`](SPEC_V1.md#where-the-headroom-is). Until one exists there is
nothing to test the ladder with, because the current reference rule can never
displace a champion.

### M2 — held-out query generation (`scripts/genqueries.py`)

* A grammar over the v1 fragment: scans, filters over 3VL predicates,
  projections, inner joins, `UNION ALL`. Seeded, reproducible.
* Seed derived from a future chain block hash, so the query set is unpredictable
  at submission time and reproducible afterwards.
* A shape report, so it is visible when the generator drifts away from
  TPC-H-like plans and starts rewarding rules nobody wants.

**Exit criterion:** a slot's held-out set can be regenerated from its manifest
plus one block hash, byte for byte.

### M3 — verifier service

Port from conjectures-validator rather than rewrite. Most of it applies verbatim.

* Vendor `verifier/static_checks.py`, `comparator.py`, `process.py`,
  `environment.py`, `hashing.py`, `submission.py`, and the `landrun` + seccomp
  security assets.
* Adapt `workspace.py`: the Lake package graph is this repository's, not
  formal-conjectures'; the solution is assembled by `scripts/slotpack.py`.
* Adapt `verification.py`: replace the `fcTypeOfName%` source-type inspection —
  which has no analogue here — with a spec-library hash check, and keep the
  Comparator statement-match and axiom checks unchanged.
* Add a `PERF` stage after `VERIFIED`, and the reason codes for it:
  `WIDTH_VIOLATION`, `DIFFERENTIAL_MISMATCH`, `REGRESSION_CAP_EXCEEDED`,
  `PLAN_TIME_EXCEEDED`, `BENCH_VARIANCE`.

**Exit criterion:** `just verify examples/filter-merge/Main.lean` returns an
accepted report under the production sandbox, on Linux, fail-closed.

### M4 — the rule host under the sandbox

* Run `lean --run lean/Main.lean` under the same landrun + seccomp profile as the
  Comparator, in a fresh disposable workspace.
* Using the interpreter rather than a compiled binary is deliberate: it keeps
  `leanc` off the miner-derived path entirely. Plan-time cost is irrelevant, so
  the safer option is also the free one. Measure it in M1 and revisit only if
  the data says otherwise.
* Wire `RuleStats.width_violations` to a hard failure, not a warning.

**Exit criterion:** a submission that loops forever, allocates without bound, or
returns garbage is contained and scored as a rejection, not as a validator
outage.

### M5 — champion ladder and storage

* `slots`, `slot_champions`, `slot_runs` tables. One champion per slot; every
  run immutable and auditable, matching the sibling's posture.
* Promotion is transactional and idempotent: retrying a job must never promote
  twice or double-pay.
* Content-addressed artifact storage for submissions, reports, and the exact
  held-out query set a run scored against.

**Exit criterion:** a challenger displaces a champion, and the whole decision —
inputs, timings, verdict — can be replayed from storage.

### M6 — rewards

* Displacement reward proportional to the geomean improvement Δ.
* Tenure stream to the sitting champion, decaying with age. v1 ships the decay
  as a constant: fit the curve once there is real submission volume, not before.
* Reuse the sibling's payment, payout, and emissions workers wholesale.

### M7 — public API and miner tooling

* `GET /v1/slots`, `GET /v1/slots/{id}/champion`, `POST /v1/submissions`,
  `GET /v1/submissions/{id}/report`, mirroring the sibling's surface.
* Ship the public workload and a local `just bench` so a miner can measure
  before paying. Every submission that fails for a reason the miner could have
  found locally is wasted TAO and a support ticket.

## Beyond v1

**v2 — widen the fragment.** Aggregation, `DISTINCT`, `LIMIT`, outer joins. Each
needs its congruence story first: `LIMIT` and `ORDER BY` are order-sensitive, so
they need an ordered semantics alongside the bag one, and a rule must then state
which it preserves. This is the largest single increase in reachable speedup and
also the easiest place to introduce an unsoundness. Do it slowly.

**v2.5 — join enumeration as a second slot.** The obligation is different in
kind and easier: the output must be a valid plan for the query graph — same
relation multiset, all predicates applied — rather than semantically equivalent
to a specific input plan. High headroom, and it exercises the ladder against a
slot whose scoring is dominated by plan quality rather than operator count.

**v3 — compression codecs.** `decode (encode xs) = xs` is a one-line spec, and
the speedups are large. But codecs run in the inner loop and want native SIMD,
so this is the first slot where the proved artifact is *not* the shipped
artifact. Bridge it with Aeneas (Rust → Lean functional model) plus differential
fuzzing, and be explicit in the slot manifest that the guarantee is weaker than
v1's. Do not open this gap until v1 has run long enough to trust the rest of the
pipeline.

The Aeneas half of that has now been tried, small, on `crates/relalg`, and
[`AENEAS.md`](AENEAS.md) records what it cost and what it caught — including a
soundness bug in `Rel::width` that no amount of Lean proof about `Slot.Rel` could
have reached. Read it before budgeting v3: the translatable subset is narrower
than it looks (the wire codec in a dependency-free 450-line crate is already
outside it), the trusted hand-written surface is small but real, and Aeneas's own
standard library is not `sorry`-free.

**v4 — a second engine.** The spec library is engine-independent; only
`crates/df-bridge` is not. A second bridge — Turso, or Materialize's
`MirRelationExpr` — would let one proved rule earn on two ladders, and would
prove out the claim that the IR is not secretly DataFusion-shaped.

## Sequencing note

M1 before M3, and M1 has now run. The bet was that a working number on a real
workload would tell you whether the premise holds before spending weeks on the
verifier service, and it paid: three bugs that no proof could have caught, and a
clear answer that the pipeline is sound and the reference *rule* is not
competitive. Neither of those would have surfaced from more infrastructure.

The same reasoning applies to what comes next. A reference submission that wins
is the cheapest remaining thing that can invalidate a downstream assumption —
the ladder cannot be tested without one — so it comes before M3 too.
# Research: what the v2 target survey settled

**Written 2026-09-02.** The work summarised here was done in the sibling
repository `../conjectures-research`, and every number in it is reproducible —
but by a recipe in *that* repository's `justfile`, not this one. The command is
named beside each claim, and the "Reproducing" section at the bottom has them in
one block.

Nothing in this document has been run in this checkout, and no code here depends
on it. It exists because whoever picks the work up next needs to know what was
measured elsewhere, which of this repository's parts survive it, and what is
still unknown.

## Why this document is in this repository

This repository's *mechanism* is validated and its *target* is exhausted. The
post-mortem is in [`STATUS.md`](STATUS.md): `examples/normalise` proves two real
rewrites, clears every scoring gate on a development set, is worth ~200x on
queries containing the shape it attacks — and fires **zero** times on public
TPC-H, scoring 0.9897x, a reject. The wall-clock metric has a ±10% noise floor
against a 2% reward bar, and two arms running *identical* plans once reported
1.120x.

So the research repository asked the next question — *what should such a
competition target instead?* — and answered it with measurements rather than
argument. The answer implies a v2 that differs from this repository in one
structural way (the extraction gap reopens, see below), which is why the answer
cannot just be filed away in the other repo.

## What is settled

| question | answer | command |
|---|---|---|
| Can Aeneas translate hot-loop Rust? | **Yes, 9 of 12 patterns.** Imperative index-based code is in. Iterator adapters (`fold`, `chunks`), `count_ones`, SIMD and `unsafe` are out. | `just reach` |
| What does one patch proof cost? | **38 lines** for the full `memchr` first-match contract about extracted Rust. Axioms `[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]`. | `just proof` |
| What does a proof over array *contents* cost? | **449 lines per patch plus 250 paid once.** Sorted-permutation, total correctness, about Charon/Aeneas-extracted Rust. Axioms clean. | `just sort-proof`, `just sort-cost` |
| Which crates are inside the provable subset? | `miniz_oxide` 0.8.0: 4 `unsafe` in 5,988 lines (0.07%), no SIMD. `serde_json`, `base64`, Arrow compute likewise. `memchr` is not: 2.36% `unsafe`, 1.76% SIMD. | `just survey` |
| Can the metric be exact? | **Yes.** Compressed size is bit-identical across runs — 370,547 / 264,602 / 263,710 B at levels 1/6/9, five runs each. | `just determinism` |
| Is there headroom? | **~5.9%, and it is durable.** `miniz_oxide`'s best output is 264,602 B; libdeflate reaches 249,742 B, which `miniz_oxide` cannot match *at any speed*. | `just knobs`, `just pareto` |
| Does real third-party code extract? | **The crate: no.** Aeneas crashes on `miniz_oxide` and drops `find_match`, `compress_fast`, `decompress`, `decompress_fast` and `init_tree`. A prover-friendly *rewrite* of one kernel: yes, with zero hand-written axioms. | `just real-kernel`, `just sort-extract` |
| So what should be built? | `miniz_oxide` DEFLATE, scored on **compression ratio under a generous speed floor**, miners submitting prover-friendly Rust against published per-kernel contracts. | that repo's `docs/RECOMMENDATION.md` |

## The four results that change how a v2 would be built here

**1. The metric can be an exact integer, and that is the unlock.** A ratio score
is a number two validators on different hardware compute *identically*. That
deletes the pinned governor, the isolated cores, the variance gate, the trimmed
median, the interleaved arms and — the one that actually matters for a
decentralised subnet — the possibility of two honest validators disagreeing.
Roughly half of `crates/bench`'s complexity and all of the scoring fragility in
[`SCORING.md`](SCORING.md) exist to fight wall-clock noise. In v2 wall clock
returns only as a *coarse floor gate*, where ±10% is harmless.

**2. The extraction gap reopens, and is closed the other way round.** This
repository's premise, stated in [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](ARCHITECTURE.md) and in
`CLAUDE.md`, is that a rewrite rule runs at plan time, so the Lean-compiled rule
*is* the shipping implementation. That does not transfer to a hot loop:
Lean-compiled code would be far too slow. v2 closes the gap from the other
direction — Charon and Aeneas prove **the Rust that ships**.

The consequence for this repository is a change of status, not a change of tool.
`verify/` and `scripts/extract.sh` are a side quest here, held deliberately
outside the trusted boundary because they prove things about a *mirror*. In a v2
that same machinery **is the gate**. Everything that is currently a caveat about
it becomes a trusted-base and governance concern: Aeneas's own Lean library
contains `sorry`, Charon must be rebuilt against a pinned Aeneas and the pair
drifts, and the extracted model can go stale silently. This repository already
records all three; v2 has to *act* on them.

**3. The incumbent does not need to extract.** This is the realisation that
rescues the design from result 7 in the table above. A miner competing on
`find_match` is *replacing* it: they submit a de-labelled, index-based
implementation and prove it against the published contract. Nobody ever proves
the old code. Aeneas crashing on the shipped crate therefore does not matter —
but it makes prover-friendly Rust a **submission requirement** rather than a
preference, with a documented worked example, because a miner who discovers the
rule by failing is a miner who leaves.

**4. The shape of the published contract is the substrate's highest-leverage
task.** Measured, not asserted: stating a counting-sort pass as *"the output is
the concatenation of the buckets"* forces an invariant about list segments under
`List.set` and was abandoned mid-proof; stating it as *"element `j` lands at its
bucket start plus how many earlier elements share its digit"* turns every
obligation into index arithmetic that `omega` closes. Same theorem, roughly **2x
the cost**, before any tactic work.

This is the same lever this repository already pulls — `Slot/Lemmas.lean` is why
`examples/normalise`'s submission site is three lines and no tactics — and it is
the strongest transferable finding of the whole survey.

## What carries over from this repository

* **`verifier/`, nearly unchanged.** Task-commitment and pinned-hash checks, the
  tokenising policy scanner, elaboration, the statement check, the axiom check,
  and above all the ordering — *nothing is timed until the proof is accepted*.
  The axiom check becomes **more** important, not less: Aeneas's `Std/Slice.lean`
  and `Std/StringIter.lean` contain `sorry`, so build success is not the check
  and `#print axioms` is the only thing that distinguishes a real proof from one
  that reached a sorried lemma.
* **`scripts/slotpack.py`, `tasks/…/manifest.json`, and the hash-pinning
  discipline.** Unchanged in shape; what gets pinned becomes the contract library
  and the extracted model instead of the spec library.
* **`scripts/extract.sh`, `verify/`, and `just verify-extract-check`.** These
  become central. One thing must change: in v2 the artifact being proved is
  *generated from the miner's Rust*, so **the verifier must re-extract**, and
  never trust an extraction that arrives in the submission.
* **[`COMPETITION.md`](COMPETITION.md)'s commit–reveal argument.** Unchanged: a
  public pull request cannot carry a scored submission, because it publishes the
  proof term before it is scored.
* **`crates/bench`'s differential check, shrunk.** The round-trip check
  `inflate(deflate'(x)) == x` over the corpus is the empirical half; the proof is
  what generalises it from a corpus to all inputs. Same division of labour as
  [`WIRE.md`](WIRE.md) describes for the codec.
* **The habit of separating "compiles" from "works".** The research repo copied
  it and it caught a bad synthetic corpus; see the traps below.

**What does not carry over**, so that nobody spends time trying: `lean/Slot/`'s
bag semantics of relational algebra and three-valued logic, `lean/SlotHost/`'s
wire codec, `crates/relalg`, `crates/df-bridge`, `crates/df-rule-host`, and the
whole "a Lean process *is* the rule" host protocol. Nor does the **"no Mathlib,
no Batteries"** decision in [`STATUS.md`](STATUS.md)'s *Decided* list: it is
correct for this slot and cannot survive a change of target, because Aeneas
requires Mathlib and pins Lean v4.31.0 where this repository pins v4.27.0. In v2
the prover's toolchain *is* the slot's toolchain, and the ~2 s cold build goes
with it.

## What is still missing

In the order I would do them.

1. **`find_match`'s contract cost. This is the number that decides v2's
   economics and it is not measured.** Every estimate rests on two data points:
   38 lines for a scan loop with a scalar invariant, 449 for a permutation over
   array contents. `find_match`'s contract is *local* — the returned
   `(distance, length)` really does match, within the window — with no counting
   argument and no bijection, so interpolation puts it at **150–300 lines**. That
   is an estimate. It is where the whole ratio win lives, and it is cheaper to
   measure than the permutation proof was.
2. **The Lean RFC 1951 `inflate` specification.** On the critical path, priced in
   *weeks*, and now confirmed unavoidable — `miniz_oxide`'s own `decompress` does
   not translate, so the round-trip theorem cannot be stated against another
   implementation and must be stated against the standard. This is the analogue
   of this repository's spec library, and it is the item most likely to be
   underestimated. The mitigation is already chosen: ship the LZ77-layer property
   (*the token stream reconstructs the input*, no Huffman model needed) as a
   complete smaller gate first. A complete small theorem beats an incomplete
   large one.
3. **A contract library designed on the "where does each element land" principle.**
   Nobody has built one. This is the 2x lever from result 4, and leaving each
   miner to rediscover the right formulation is the difference between a
   competition and a hazing ritual.
4. **The stability decision.** What was proved is sorted-permutation, *not*
   stability. An unstable-but-sorted replacement yields a different-but-valid
   Huffman table: fine under a ratio score, fatal under a bit-exact one. The slot
   definition has to say which, up front — the machinery for stability exists and
   is not free.
5. **A prover-friendly-Rust checker.** The rule (no labelled `break`/`continue`,
   no early return from nested loops, no trait objects, indices rather than
   iterator chains) is measured but not enforced. `verifier/`'s policy scanner is
   the right place, and the slot must ship a worked example.
6. **Corpus governance.** Held out, commit-revealed, mixed text/source/binary,
   with published *shape* statistics but not contents. The v1 lesson applies
   directly: publish the shape report from the start or the generator drifts into
   rewarding overfitting.
7. **The speed-floor constant.** "~8x the shipped level-9 time" is a proposal,
   not a measurement. It is load-bearing in both directions: without a floor the
   degenerate submission is zopfli (unbounded time for a fraction of a percent),
   and with a *tight* floor SIMD returns to the critical path and the target
   dies, because SIMD is outside the provable subset.
8. **Two upstream items, worth doing whatever is decided here.** File the
   ill-typed `core::mem::swap` extraction against Aeneas — it emits a three-tuple
   destructuring for a model that returns a pair, so the verbatim kernel's
   extraction does not typecheck at all. And send `NUM_PROBES[1] = 1 → 4` to
   `miniz_oxide` as a pull request: it makes the crate simultaneously *faster*
   and 6.7% *smaller* than zlib. A one-constant win is a pull request, not a
   competition, and it should be sent as one.
9. **Whether v1 continues in parallel — an open decision, not a settled one.**
   Nothing in the research says this repository must stop. What stands between
   `examples/normalise` and a win is the *fragment* — decimals, `<=`/`>=` as
   primitives — not the proof burden, and that is a bounded amount of work here.
   The research says v1 should not be the flagship; it does not say it is dead.

## Retractions to carry across

These were claims I held confidently and that measurement overturned. They are
recorded because they are exactly the sort of thing that gets rediscovered
expensively.

* *"Aeneas is useless for hot loops."* No. This repository's codec failure was
  about walking a `&str` and passing a function to `Iterator::map` — neither
  characteristic of a hot loop. [`WIRE.md`](WIRE.md)'s limit is real but local.
* *"Mature Rust performance code is pervasively `unsafe` and vectorised."* True
  of `memchr`, false of compression, JSON and Arrow compute.
* *"There is a 15.2% ratio gap to zlib to close."* Unfair comparison — that
  configuration was also 46% faster — and the whole gap is one mistuned constant.
  The real, durable gap is ~5.9% against libdeflate.
* *"Hot-loop Rust extracts cleanly."* Only code written in a particular style.
  Real third-party code uses labelled `continue` and returns `&mut` borrows.
* *"`radix_sort_symbols` is a cheap first slot because it is small and
  self-contained."* Backwards. Its contract is a permutation over array
  contents — the most global thing a small kernel can ask for — making it the
  *most* expensive contract on the ladder, not the least. This one matters for
  ordering the work: starting there means starting with the least-understood
  cost.

## Traps found there, worth knowing here

* **Aeneas's own Lean library contains `sorry`.** Check the axiom list, not the
  build. This repository's habit of printing `#print axioms` on every submission
  is not optional in v2 — it is the whole gate.
* **`Slice` is a `List`, not memory.** The extracted model says what the code
  computes, not how fast. A proof cannot see cache behaviour or allocation, so
  performance stays an empirical claim and "verified performance" would be a lie.
  The proof only says the optimisation did not change the answer. Same division
  of labour this repository already uses; it must be *stated*, because the phrase
  is tempting.
* **A synthetic corpus measures nothing.** A first headroom run on repetitive
  data compressed ~300:1, was dominated by match emission, and reported
  `miniz_oxide` as 6x faster than zlib. The conclusion would have been backwards.
* **Aeneas's `step*` has two sharp edges.** It will not enter a `do` block whose
  first statement is an `if` (both branches must be rewritten into a choice of
  value first), and the extracted `¬ b` is `decide (¬ b = true)` rather than
  `!b`, which needs normalising before any lemma about `!` applies.
* **Charon and Aeneas drift as a pair.** Charon must be rebuilt against a pinned
  Aeneas. This project lost time to exactly that skew once already.
* **Proof cost is not only line count.** The 449-line proof uses Aeneas's WP
  layer, `step*`, `Finset` sums, `Equiv.ofBijective` and
  `Finite.injective_iff_surjective`. Lines understate what it asks of a
  contributor, and it was a *second draft* written by the same person who wrote
  the contract — the friendliest possible case, which a real competition does not
  have.

## Reproducing

```bash
cd ../conjectures-research
just reach        # what Aeneas translates, and what it leaves opaque
just proof        # the memchr proof, with its axioms
just survey       # unsafe/SIMD density across candidates
just determinism  # is the metric exact?
just headroom     # miniz_oxide vs zlib: speed and ratio
just knobs        # do probe depth and lazy matching close the gap?
just pareto       # the frontier, against libdeflate
just real-kernel  # the crate fails to extract; one rewritten kernel succeeds
just sort-extract # extract the prover-friendly kernel alone
just sort-proof   # the sorted-permutation proof, with its axioms
just sort-cost    # lines paid once vs lines paid per patch
just all
```

Charon and Aeneas are built by *this* repository's `scripts/extract.sh`; the
research repo points `AENEAS_WORK` at them rather than keeping a second copy.

## Where to pick it up

The next four steps, in order, and where they belong:

1. Measure `find_match`'s contract cost. Still a *probe* — it belongs in
   `../conjectures-research/probes/`, not here.
2. Prototype the LZ77 reconstruction property as the first complete gate.
   Also a probe.
3. Design the contract library on the principle from result 4.
4. Only then the substrate: `inflate` in Lean, and composing kernel contracts up
   to `inflate ∘ deflate = id`.

Steps 1 and 2 can still invalidate the recommendation, which is why no harness
work should start before them — that is the mistake v1 made, and the reason this
repository has a complete, working pipeline aimed at a target that could not
contain a win.
# Scoring and the champion ladder

Correctness is a gate. Everything in this file happens *after* a submission has
been accepted by the Lean pipeline.

## The ladder

Each slot has one **champion**: the accepted artifact with the best held-out
score. A challenger displaces it only by clearing every bar below. The baseline
champion of a fresh slot is `Slot.baseline`, the rule that never fires, so the
ladder is well-founded from block zero.

A challenger is promoted when all of the following hold:

1. **Verified.** Lean pipeline accepted; axioms within the permitted set; second
   kernel (`nanoda`) agreed.
2. **No width violations.** `Slot.Sound` proves these are impossible, so a
   non-zero count means the executed binary is not the proved rule. The run is
   void, not merely slow, and the submission is quarantined for review.
3. **Differentially correct.** Every scored query is executed twice — with the
   rule and with the champion — and the result sets must be equal as bags. This
   is the only check that exercises `crates/df-bridge`, which no proof reaches.
4. **Faster on held-out.** `geomean(champion_time / challenger_time) ≥ 1 + ε`,
   ε = 0.02 in v1.
5. **No cherry-picking.** No individual held-out query regresses by more than
   δ = 1%. A rule that wins the geomean by wrecking one query is not an
   improvement, it is a trade the subnet did not ask for.
6. **Plan-time budget.** Total host round-trip time under 250 ms per query, and
   the rule host still alive at the end of the run. A rule that burns plan time
   to win execution time is a real trade-off, but a bounded one.

## Measurement protocol

Nothing here is novel; it is the standard set of precautions, written down so
that a validator operator cannot quietly skip one.

* **Fixed hardware profile.** Validator-side only. Pinned CPU governor,
  isolated cores, `numactl` binding, no other tenant. The profile is part of the
  slot manifest, and a run from a host that does not match it is not scored.
* **Deterministic data.** TPC-H `dbgen` at a pinned scale factor and seed,
  materialised to Parquet once and content-addressed. Both arms read the same
  files.
* **Repetitions.** 7 runs per query, one discarded warm-up, trimmed median.
  Champion and challenger are interleaved rather than run in blocks, so thermal
  drift hits both.
* **Public and held-out workloads.** The public set (10 TPC-H queries) is
  published so miners can develop. Scoring uses the held-out set: 64 queries
  generated by `scripts/genqueries.py` from a seed derived from a future chain
  block hash, so it is unpredictable at submission time and reproducible
  afterwards. Rotated every scoring epoch.

## Anti-gaming

The failure modes worth naming, and what stops each:

| Attack | Defence |
|---|---|
| Overfit to the published queries | Scoring is on held-out queries, seeded from a block hash the miner cannot predict, rotated per epoch |
| Win the geomean by tanking one query | Per-query regression cap (δ) |
| Prove a weaker statement | `Sound` is pinned by the spec-library hash in the task manifest; the footer, not the miner, builds `Bounty.target` |
| `sorry` / `native_decide` / custom axiom | Axiom allowlist checked on the exported environment by the Comparator, plus a second independent kernel |
| Execute something other than the proved rule | `SlotEntry.lean` names `Bounty.target`; width violations are counted and void the run |
| Rule that never terminates in practice | Host fuel bound, per-request timeout, sandbox wall-clock and memory caps |
| Burn plan time to look good | Plan-time budget is scored, not free |
| Copy another miner's proof | Commit–reveal, first-seen-wins on the normalised proof-term hash |
| Time the benchmark host into noise | Interleaved arms, trimmed median, fixed hardware profile, run rejected if variance exceeds a threshold |

## Rewards

Emission for a slot is split between:

* a **displacement reward**, proportional to the geomean improvement Δ the
  challenger achieved over the champion it displaced; and
* a **tenure stream** to the sitting champion, decaying with age so that a slot
  which stops improving stops paying.

The decay is what prevents a slot from becoming an annuity for whoever got there
first, and it is the knob to tune once real submission volume exists. v1 ships
with tenure decay stubbed at a constant so that the first ladder can be observed
before the curve is fitted; see [`PLAN.md`](PLAN.md) M6.
# Slot `datafusion-logical-rewrite-v1`

## The obligation

A submission is a Lean file that defines `rule` and `rule_sound`. The slot's
footer assembles them:

```lean
def target : Slot.VerifiedRule := ⟨rule, rule_sound⟩
```

so the submitted rule and the proved rule are the same constant, by construction.

```lean
abbrev Rule := Rel → Option Rel          -- `none` = "I decline to rewrite this node"

def Sound (rule : Rule) : Prop :=
  ∀ e e' : Rel, rule e = some e' → Equiv e e' ∧ e'.width = e.width
```

Two obligations, both load-bearing:

* **`Equiv e e'`** — for every database, the two plans return the same *bag* of
  rows. Equality is `List.Perm`, never list equality: a rule may not depend on
  the order rows come back in, because no DataFusion operator in this fragment
  guarantees one.
* **`e'.width = e.width`** — the rewritten plan has the same arity. The bridge
  splices the result into an enclosing plan whose schema must not move
  underneath it. A rule that changed arity would produce a plan DataFusion
  accepts and answers wrongly.

## The fragment

```lean
inductive Rel where
  | scan    (table : Nat) (width : Nat)
  | filter  (p : Scalar) (r : Rel)
  | project (cols : List Nat) (r : Rel)
  | join    (p : Scalar) (l r : Rel)      -- inner, concatenating
  | union   (l r : Rel)                   -- UNION ALL
```

Rows are positional: `Row = List (Option Value)`, `none` is `NULL`. Predicates
evaluate under three-valued logic, and `WHERE` keeps a row only when the
predicate is exactly `TRUE` (`Slot.truthy`) — the single point where 3VL becomes
2VL, and the point where most real-world pushdown bugs live.

Every operator in the fragment is permutation-congruent. That is not a
coincidence, it is the entry criterion. **`LIMIT`, `ORDER BY`, `DISTINCT`,
aggregation, window functions and outer joins are absent on purpose**: bag
equivalence is not a sound correctness notion for an operator that observes row
order or row multiplicity in a way `Perm` cannot see. They arrive in v2 with the
congruence machinery that makes them safe, not before. The bridge declines to
lower them, so a plan containing them is simply left alone.

Totality is deliberate everywhere:

* out-of-range column reads are `NULL`, not an error;
* `DB` is a total function `Nat → List Row`, so there is no "table exists" side
  condition;
* every 3VL operator is defined on every input, with non-boolean operands
  behaving as `NULL`.

The result is that `eval` needs no well-formedness hypothesis, so `Sound` has no
escape hatch: a miner cannot discharge it by assuming the plan is well-formed.

## What the host guarantees on top

The miner proves a *local* rewrite sound. The host applies it *everywhere*, to a
fuel bound. Both steps are proved in `lean/Slot/Rewrite.lean`:

```lean
theorem optimize_sound (v : VerifiedRule) (n : Nat) (e : Rel) :
    Equiv e (repeatN v.rule n e) ∧ (repeatN v.rule n e).width = e.width
```

Fuel is a host constant (64 in v1), not a miner input. Lean rejects `partial`,
so a rule is always total — but a rule that maps `a → b → a` would still make an
unbounded fixpoint spin. Fuel bounds that: oscillation costs plan time and
nothing else, because every intermediate step is equivalent to the one before.

## Submission policy

Inherited from `verifier/static_checks.py` in conjectures-validator, which
token-scans the submission and rejects `import`, `axiom`, `sorry`, `elab`,
`macro`, `syntax`, `notation`, `set_option`, `native_decide`, `implemented_by`,
`extern`, `unsafe`, `partial`, `instance`, `attribute`, `run_cmd`, and the rest.

Permitted axioms: `propext`, `Quot.sound`, `Classical.choice`. Anything else —
in particular `sorryAx` and `Lean.ofReduceBool` — is a rejection. The reference
submission in `examples/filter-merge/` uses only `propext` and `Quot.sound`.

Two rules that matter more here than in the sibling validator, because this code
is *executed*:

* **`partial` stays banned.** It is the difference between "slow" and "hangs".
* **`native_decide` stays banned.** It adds `Lean.ofReduceBool`, which trusts the
  compiler rather than the kernel, and it is the standard soundness escape hatch.

## Reference submission

`examples/filter-merge/Main.lean` — three rewrites, ~110 lines including proofs:

| Rewrite | Value |
|---|---|
| `filter p (filter q r) → filter (p ∧ q) r` | one predicate per row instead of two |
| `filter p (project cs r) → project cs (filter (remap cs p) r)` | the projection runs on fewer rows and the filter reaches the scan |
| `filter TRUE r → r` | removes a whole operator |

The second is the one with real value, and the one where the subtlety lives:
`remap` rewrites `col i` to the column the projection reads it from, and maps an
index the projection does not cover to a literal `NULL` — which is exactly what
reading past the end of a projected row already yields. That is why the rewrite
needs no well-formedness side condition.

Verified end to end:

```
$ printf '(rewrite 64 (filter (lt (col 0) (lit (int 10))) (project (2 0 5) (scan 7 8))))\n' | <host>
(ok (project (2 0 5) (filter (lt (col 2) (lit (int 10))) (scan 7 8))))
```

## Where the headroom is

The M1 benchmark measured the reference submission against stock DataFusion 50.3
on TPC-H SF1 and it does not win: **zero rewrites** on all ten public queries,
and a geomean indistinguishable from 1.0. The reason is not that the fragment fails to reach the
workload — 1088 of 2744 offered plan nodes lower cleanly — but that all three of
the reference rewrites are things DataFusion's own `push_down_filter` and
`eliminate_filter` have already done by the time the rule is asked. Turn
`push_down_filter` off in both arms and the rule does fire on Q3, which is the
control that proves the shapes are reachable.

So the reference submission is a demonstration of the *pipeline*, not a
competitive rule, and the list below is where a miner has to go to beat a mature
optimizer. Anything already in `Optimizer::new().rules` is worth nothing on the
ladder no matter how well it is proved.

**Firing is not the same as paying.** Pushing a filter below a *pure
column-selection* projection is nearly free in a columnar engine. The wins come
from pushdown that reduces cardinality upstream of something expensive — below a
join, where hash-join cost is superlinear in its input, or into a scan, where
Parquet row-group pruning skips I/O outright. A rule can rewrite every plan it is
shown and move no time at all.

Left for miners, in rough order of expected payoff:

1. **Predicate pushdown through joins**, including the NULL-safety conditions
   that make it wrong for some predicates.
2. **Join reassociation and commutation.** Commutation changes tuple layout, so
   it is only expressible with a compensating projection — `Scalar.shift` is in
   the spec library for exactly this.
3. **Predicate normalisation** — CNF/DNF, constant folding, absorption,
   contradiction detection. Cheap to state, and the 3VL cases are a minefield
   that a proof navigates and a test suite does not.
4. **Union distribution** — pushing filters and projections through `UNION ALL`.
5. **Column pruning** — narrowing a projection to what the parent actually reads.
