## Environment notes

* **Lean toolchain.** `lean-toolchain` pins `leanprover/lean4:v4.27.0`. There is
  no system-wide elan on this machine; the justfile takes `ELAN_HOME` from the
  environment and falls back to a local `.elan/`. The sibling validator has a
  vendored copy that works:

  ```bash
  export ELAN_HOME=/home/robert/repos/s66_repositories/conjectures-validator/.elan
  ```

* **Cargo workspace.** Only `crates/relalg` is a workspace member, so
  `cargo test` works with no network. `df-bridge`, `df-rule-host` and `bench` are
  `exclude`d and built separately by `just df-build` — a workspace member that
  cannot resolve its dependencies fails resolution for the whole workspace.

* **`LEAN_PATH` ordering matters.** The assembled entry directory must come
  *before* `.lake/build/lib/lean`, or the baseline `SlotEntry.olean` shadows the
  miner's and every rewrite silently becomes the identity. The justfile gets
  this right; anything hand-rolled must too.

## M1 results: what the number says

`crates/bench` is built and has been run against DataFusion 50.3 on TPC-H SF1,
12 partitions, the ten public queries from `slot.json`, 7 repetitions with one
discarded warm-up, arms interleaved and their order alternated per repetition.

### The bridge works

This is the first thing M1 established and the more important one. The positive
control (`--self-check`) builds plans in each of the three shapes the reference
rule rewrites, using `LogicalPlanBuilder` rather than SQL — SQL cannot produce
them, because `WHERE` is planned *below* `SELECT`, so a filter is never above a
projection until an optimizer rule puts it there. Both control arms run with
DataFusion's own logical rules switched off, so nothing else can reach the shape
first. At SF1:

| case | plan shape | rows | rewrites | answers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `filter/project` | `Filter(Projection(Scan))` | 3 251 845 | 1 | agree |
| `filter/filter`  | `Filter(Filter(Scan))`     |   541 362 | 1 | agree |
| `filter/true`    | `Filter(TRUE, Scan)`       | 6 001 215 | 1 | agree |

`lower → wire → Lean rule → wire → lift → execute` therefore works against real
plans over real data. Every claim in this repository about `crates/df-bridge` was
unverified before this ran.

The differential check also passes on all ten TPC-H queries, in every
configuration tried.

### The reference submission does not win

```
query        rows    plan?  rw   champion   challenger    speedup    cv (c/x)
q1               4    same    0    219.5ms      218.1ms    1.007x   1.9%/2.0%
q3              10    same    0     73.6ms       69.4ms    1.060x   3.4%/3.9%
q5               5    same    0    113.1ms      115.0ms    0.984x   4.0%/5.4%
q6               1    same    0     44.5ms       41.4ms    1.074x  10.3%/9.9%
q7               4    same    0    168.5ms      165.8ms    1.016x   3.1%/2.9%
q8               2    same    0     88.2ms       88.9ms    0.992x   0.8%/3.9%
q10             20    same    0    114.8ms      115.5ms    0.994x   2.3%/2.8%
q12              2    same    0     82.0ms       84.5ms    0.971x   3.5%/6.1%
q14              1    same    0     45.1ms       43.9ms    1.027x   2.4%/6.3%
q19              1    same    0     85.7ms       81.7ms    1.050x   2.9%/2.1%

geomean speedup      1.0169x
rule stats           attempts 2744 · lowered 1088 · declined 1656
                     rewritten 0 · unchanged 1088 · errors 0 · width violations 0
host round trips     168.0 ms total
```

**Exit criterion not met.** The geomean is not a small win, it is noise — see
[the noise floor](#the-2-bar-is-below-this-machines-noise-floor) below, and note
`plan? same` and `rw 0` on every row: the two arms ran identical plans. Not for
lack of a harness, and not because the fragment cannot reach TPC-H: 1088 of 2744
offered nodes lower cleanly. All three of the reference rewrites are things
DataFusion's own `push_down_filter` and
`eliminate_filter` have already done by the time the rule is asked. `rewritten 0`
with `unchanged 1088` says precisely that — the bridge handed the rule 1088 real
subtrees and the rule found nothing in any of them.

A third reason, found while trying to construct a query where the reference rule
*would* pay: **`SubqueryAlias` is not lowered**, and it sits between the filter
and everything below it in any query with an aliased subquery — Q7 and Q8 in the
public set, and every hand-written attempt to produce a filter-over-projection
shape from SQL. Lowering it as a pass-through is not obviously safe: the alias
supplies the qualifier the enclosing predicate resolves against, so dropping it
in `lift` would leave `t.l_shipdate` unresolvable and the schema-drift check
would reject the plan. Making it work means teaching `lift` to restore the alias.
Small, real bridge work, and a concrete item for the commons.

**And firing is not the same as paying.** Pushing a filter below a *pure
column-selection* projection is nearly free in a columnar engine: the projection
is column selection, not per-row work, so doing it on fewer rows saves little.
The wins in this fragment come from pushdown that reduces cardinality upstream of
something expensive — below a join, where hash-join cost is superlinear in input
size, or into a scan, where Parquet row-group pruning skips I/O outright. Two of
the reference rule's three rewrites cannot reach either, so even in a world where
DataFusion did not get there first, they would be close to free.

That the shapes are reachable at all is shown by turning `push_down_filter` off
in both arms: Q3 then gets 2 rewrites. The timing from that configuration is not
usable (the queries triple in cost and the variance goes to 50–68% on this
machine), but the counter is the point.

### The 2% bar is below this machine's noise floor

Worth writing down because it will otherwise be rediscovered as a bug. Three
identical scored runs — same data digest, same configuration, **zero rewrites in
all three, so the two arms are executing plans that are identical node for
node** — returned geomeans of 1.0068x, 1.0169x and 1.0056x. Nothing measurable
separates the arms in any of them, so that ±1% spread is purely the measurement
floor of an ordinary developer machine.

`min_improvement` is 0.02. A 1.7% phantom improvement is most of that, which is
what `SCORING.md`'s fixed hardware profile — pinned governor, isolated cores, no
other tenant — is actually for; it is not ceremony. Two consequences:

* The variance gate is doing real work and must not be loosened on a validator.
  This board's numbers come from runs with `--max-cv 0.15`, which is a developer
  setting and not a scoring one.
* Any future claim of a marginal win needs more than one run behind it. Reporting
  the per-query `cv` alongside the speedup is there so that a 1.05x on a query
  with 10% variance is visibly not a result.

**So the answer to "can a rule in this fragment move TPC-H" is: the machinery
can, this rule cannot.** The reference submission is a demonstration of the
pipeline, and a competitive rule has to attack something DataFusion does not
already do — the headroom list in [`SPEC_V1.md`](SPEC_V1.md#where-the-headroom-is),
starting with predicate pushdown through joins.

### Plan-time cost is not a problem

2–12 ms per query against a 250 ms budget, 159 ms of host round trips across a
whole 7-repetition run of 10 queries. Open question 3 — interpreter or compiled
host — is answered: `lean --run` is comfortably cheap enough, and `leanc` stays
off the miner-derived path.

### Four bugs M1 found, all fixed

The first three were invisible to the proof pipeline and each presented as "no
speedup" rather than as an error, which is why the harness now reports a
diagnosis rather than a bare geomean. The fourth was worse than that.

1. **`LeanRule` never saw anything but the plan root.** `OptimizerRule::rewrite`
   does not recurse, and `apply_order()` was left at its `None` default, which
   tells DataFusion the rule handles recursion itself. Every real query has
   something out of the fragment at its root — an aggregate, a sort, a limit — so
   `lower` declined once per query and the rule never fired. Fixed by returning
   `Some(ApplyOrder::TopDown)`; top-down because `lower` already walks the whole
   subtree beneath the node it is handed, so the first node that lowers is the
   largest and the rule sees the most context.
2. **`lower_literal` rejected every type TPC-H filters on.** It accepted `Utf8`
   and `LargeUtf8` but not `Utf8View`, which is what DataFusion 50 gives strings
   read from Parquet, and it accepted no date type at all. Between them that is
   every predicate in the public workload. `Utf8View` and `Date32`/`Date64` are
   now lowered; the argument for why dates are not the decimal case is in
   [`THREAT_MODEL.md`](THREAT_MODEL.md).
3. **A lowered date could not be lifted back.** `Slot.Value` has no date, so a
   `Date32` literal lowers to an `Int` and returns as an `Int64`. `TypeCoercion`
   is an *analyzer* rule and has already run, so nothing repairs
   `l_shipdate > Int64(9497)`: the rebuilt plan fails to type, `lift` returns
   `None`, and the rewrite is dropped silently. `lift_expr` now restores a
   literal's type from the column it is compared against, and only where the
   restoration is exact.
4. **`lift` was not fail-closed.** The sentence above — "the rebuilt plan fails
   to type, so `lift` returns `None`" — was not actually true, and finding that
   out was the most valuable thing in M1. `Filter::try_new` validates its
   predicate's type on a *best effort*: it calls `get_type` and, when that
   **errors**, skips the check and builds the node anyway, because correlated
   subqueries genuinely cannot be typed at construction time. An untypeable
   predicate from a bad lift takes that same path. So the malformed plan was
   accepted, propagated, and failed during *physical* planning — a failed query,
   not a declined rewrite, which is exactly the outcome
   `crates/df-rule-host`'s own documentation promises can never happen. (The
   invariant check that would have caught it, `check_invariants(Executable)`,
   runs only in debug builds; a scored run is a release build.) `lift` now
   resolves the predicate's type itself and refuses anything that is not
   boolean. Verified by disabling the fix from bug 3 and confirming that the
   date cases drop to zero rewrites with correct answers rather than erroring.

A fifth, smaller thing: `RuleStats` had no way to distinguish "the bridge could
not lower this node" from "the bridge lowered it and the rule declined". They
call for opposite work and both read as zero rewrites, so `unchanged` is now
counted separately from `declined`.

### Using the harness

```
slot-bench [options] -- <host-argv>...
```

The trailing argv is the rule host, already wrapped in whatever sandbox the
caller wants; this crate has no opinion about the sandbox, so the local
`just bench` passes a bare `lean --run` and the validator will pass its landrun
invocation. Options worth knowing:

* `--self-check` — the bridge positive control described above. Run it after any
  change to `crates/df-bridge`; it is seconds at `--scale 0.01`.
* `--rule-position append|prepend` — where in the logical optimizer's rule list
  the miner's rule goes. `append` is what a scored run uses and what `slot.json`
  describes; `prepend` exists because a rule that duplicates a DataFusion rule
  scores zero when appended and its true effect is otherwise invisible.
* `--disable-df-rule <name>` — switches a DataFusion rule off in **both** arms.
  For measuring headroom, not for scoring.
* `--max-cv <fraction>` — the variance gate, 5% by default. `SCORING.md` requires
  a pinned CPU governor, isolated cores and no other tenant; a developer machine
  is none of those and wants this loosened to ~0.15, not the gate ignored.
* `--check-only`, `--json <path>`, `--only <names>`, `--plans <dir>`.

The `RuleStats` counters in the report are meant to be read as a decision tree,
because a zero in the rewrite column has five causes that call for different
work: `declined` (the bridge cannot lower it — work on `crates/df-bridge`),
`unchanged` (it lowered and the rule found nothing — work on the rule), `errors`
(the host is not answering — a protocol or `LEAN_PATH` problem), `lift_failures`
(a real rewrite that could not be rebuilt — work on `lift`), and
`width_violations` (the running artifact is not the proved rule — void the run).

Exit status is the verdict: 0 promote, 1 reject, 2 void, 3 differential
mismatch, 4 setup error.

## A rule that wins: predicate normalisation

The first submission this project has produced that clears every gate.
`examples/normalise/Main.lean`, two proved rewrites composed, **verdict
`Promote`** on its development set — and `Reject` on the public TPC-H set, which
is the more important half of the sentence.

### The method: probe first, guess never

Two initial hypotheses were wrong. I expected DataFusion to miss the factoring in
Q19 and the disjunctive single-side inference in Q7; it does both, and Q7's plan
shows `n_name = 'FRANCE' OR n_name = 'GERMANY'` pushed to each nation scan
unprompted. So the rule was chosen by measurement instead:
`crates/bench/queries/probe/` is ten predicates with known simplifications,
written in only the types the fragment can lower, and the answer is read off
DataFusion's dumped plan.

| probe | DataFusion 50.3 | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `x = 'A' AND x = 'B'` | `EmptyRelation` | already done |
| `x IS NULL AND x = 5` | `EmptyRelation` | already done |
| `x IS NULL OR NOT(x IS NULL)` | filter deleted | already done |
| `p OR (p AND q)` | `p` | already done |
| `x < 100 AND x < 500` | `x < 100` | already done |
| `x = 5 AND NOT(x IS NULL)` | `x = 5` | already done |
| **`x < 100 AND x = 100`** | **left verbatim** | **gap** |
| **`(x>10 ∧ x<1000) OR (x>500 ∧ x<2000)`** | **left verbatim** | **gap** |
| same on `Date32` | left verbatim | gap |
| `x='A' OR x='B'` | not an `InList` | gap, no value |

Six of ten already handled. Anything in that column is worth zero on the ladder
however well it is proved, and this table is worth re-running on every engine
bump: a gap closing upstream silently turns a champion into a rule that no longer
earns.

### The two rewrites

**Contradiction.** `x < a ∧ x = b` with `a ≤ b` is unsatisfiable; rewrite to
literal `FALSE`. DataFusion catches `Eq ∧ Eq` and not `Lt ∧ Eq` — that is the
seam. The output looks useless on its own, and is not: DataFusion's own
`eliminate_filter` turns `Filter(false)` into an `EmptyRelation` and
`propagate_empty_relation` deletes the subtree above it. **The proved rule
supplies reasoning the engine lacks; the engine supplies plan surgery the v1
fragment cannot express.** That composition is the most interesting thing
validated here.

**Interval coalescing.** `(a < x ∧ x < b) ∨ (c < x ∧ x < d)` with `a ≤ c < b` is
one interval, so the row filter evaluates two comparisons instead of four and an
`OR`. It works on dates for free, with no date case in the rule, because the bridge
lowers `Date32` to its epoch offset as a `Value.int`.

An earlier version of this note also claimed a contiguous range prunes Parquet row
groups where a disjunction of ranges does not. **That is wrong and the measurement
says so** — see `coalesce_prune` below. DataFusion prunes a disjunction perfectly
well, by testing each disjunct against the row-group statistics and skipping a
group only when all of them fail. The saving is in the per-row filter, and there
alone.

### The numbers, against a null control

A speedup means nothing without knowing what this machine reports when *nothing
changes*. So every figure below is paired with a **null run**: the same queries,
the same protocol, but `examples/filter-merge/Main.lean` as the submission, which
declines every one of these predicates. Both arms then optimize to identical plans
and every deviation from 1.000x is measurement noise.

SF1, 15 repetitions, one discarded warm-up, interleaved arms, four independent
runs of each configuration.

**The noise floor** — 24 measurements, identical plans, `rewritten 0`:

```
contra          1.047  1.001  0.982  0.978
contra_join     0.982  1.077  0.987  0.953
coalesce_int    1.077  0.888  0.991  0.953
coalesce_date   0.997  1.044  0.983  0.972
coalesce_prune  0.969  1.058  1.017  1.094
control         1.035  1.042  1.006  0.977

range 0.888 - 1.094 · geomean 1.0035 · sd(log) 0.0476
```

**On this machine a single per-query speedup anywhere in [0.89, 1.09] is
indistinguishable from no effect at all.** The per-run geomean of nothing ranged
0.987–1.017. That is the number every claim below has to clear, and it is why the
`--max-cv 0.05` default voids these runs: the observed per-query cv is 6–36%.

**The rule**, same protocol, four runs. `corrected` divides by the null geomean for
that query, which cancels any systematic asymmetry between the arms:

```
query           real speedups (4 runs)      real gm   null gm  corrected   verdict
contra          213    201    223    213    212.165     1.002    211.804   real
contra_join     1132   1183   1131   1158  1151.061     0.999   1152.529   real
coalesce_int    1.222  1.151  1.333  1.266    1.241     0.975      1.273   real
coalesce_date   1.368  1.328  1.297  1.262    1.313     0.998      1.315   real
coalesce_prune  1.101  1.023  1.029  1.086    1.059     1.034      1.025   NOISE
control         1.059  1.120  0.997  1.030    1.051     1.014      1.036   NOISE
```

Read it row by row, because the rows do not agree with each other:

* **`contra`, `contra_join` — real beyond argument.** Three orders of magnitude
  outside the noise, and the challenger does not execute at all: the plan is an
  `EmptyRelation`. But **the size of the number is a property of the table, not of
  the rule.** The champion scans SF1; at SF10 the same rewrite would report
  ~2000x. It is a ratio against work that was entirely unnecessary, so it says
  nothing about rule quality and should never be read as if it did.
* **`coalesce_int`, `coalesce_date` — real, ~1.27x and ~1.32x.** These are the
  honest findings. The worst of the four real runs (1.151) is above the best of
  all 24 null measurements (1.094), so the distributions are disjoint.
* **`coalesce_prune` — no effect.** Its range sits inside the null's. This query
  existed to test the row-group-pruning hypothesis and it refutes it: the earlier
  1.131x reading was noise, and the query tests nothing `coalesce_int` does not.
* **`control` — no effect, as designed.** It also hit **1.120x with zero
  rewrites**, which is the single most useful number here: it is proof by
  construction that one observation of "+12%" on this hardware is worth nothing.

Two claims from the first write-up of this section are withdrawn: the coalescing
figures were given as 13–16% from one run when the effect on int and date is
larger (~27–32%) and the effect on `coalesce_prune` is zero, and the pruning
mechanism was asserted without evidence and is now contradicted by it.

The **geomean 8.2930x** first reported for this set should also be read for what it
is: an artifact of putting two synthetic 200x+ queries in a six-query set. It
describes the query set, not the rule. Aggregating a structural elimination and a
per-row saving into one geometric mean is not meaningful, and a ladder that scores
this way is trivially gamed by a submission that turns one query empty.

**And on the public TPC-H set: 0.9897x, zero rewrites, `Reject`** — which is inside
the ±1.7% the null run showed for a geomean of nothing. Neither shape occurs there
in a type the fragment can lower; Q19 contains the interval shape and it is on
`l_quantity`, a decimal.

So, precisely: **both rewrites clear the noise on queries built to contain them,
and neither produces any measurable effect on a real workload, because neither
fires there.** What is validated is the mechanism — proof, wire, bridge, gates, and
the composition with DataFusion's own rules. What is not validated is that a rule
in the v1 fragment can earn on TPC-H, and that is blocked by the fragment
excluding decimals and `<=`, not by anything about these rules.

### Three harness bugs, found by running a second submission

None were visible with only the reference rule, which is the lesson.

1. **The bridge self-check cried wolf.** It failed any submission that did not
   target its three control shapes, conflating "the rule declined" with "the
   bridge is broken". It now distinguishes them: `unchanged` counts a plan that
   went out over the wire and came back, which proves the round trip for the
   decline path, and only a silent host is a failure.
2. **Both scoring gates fired on noise.** The variance gate voided a run with a
   181x speedup because a 5 ms query jittered by 20%, and the regression cap
   flagged a 16% "regression" on a query whose two arms ran *identical plans*.
   Noise only invalidates a measurement when it could explain it, so both gates
   now require the effect to be clear of the combined coefficient of variation.
   This matters beyond the demo: on a real ladder the old gates would have voided
   good submissions and rejected good ones at random.
3. **`lift` produced a plan that failed the query — again, and worse.** A
   comparison against an `Int32` column came back as an `Int64` literal. Unlike
   the date case this *type-checks*, because DataFusion's comparison coercion
   widens to `Int64`, so the fail-closed guard passed and the plan was accepted —
   then the range analysis failed the query with "Only intervals with the same
   data type are comparable". Fixed twice over: `retype_against_sibling` now
   narrows integers exactly, and the guard additionally requires both operands of
   a comparison to have the *same* type rather than merely coercible ones.

That third one is the third instance of one structural fact, and it is worth
naming: **`Slot.Value` has one integer type and `ScalarValue` has twelve**, so
`lift` must reconstruct a type it threw away. Every type it does not know is
either a declined rewrite, which is fine, or a failed query, which is not. The
guard now makes the first outcome the default.

### Reproducing

```bash
just check examples/normalise/Main.lean     # axioms: [propext, Quot.sound]
QS=contra,contra_join,coalesce_int,coalesce_date,coalesce_prune,control
# the rule
just bench examples/normalise/Main.lean --scale 1 --reps 15 --max-cv 9.9 \
  --queries crates/bench/queries/normalise --only $QS --json .work/bench/real-1.json
# the null control: same queries, a rule that declines all of them
just bench examples/filter-merge/Main.lean --scale 1 --reps 15 --max-cv 9.9 \
  --queries crates/bench/queries/normalise --only $QS --json .work/bench/null-1.json
just bench examples/normalise/Main.lean --scale 1 --reps 7 --max-cv 0.2 --self-check
```

`crates/bench/queries/probe/README.md` has the command for the gap table.

## Aeneas: `Rel::width` proved, and the bug it found

Full account in [`AENEAS.md`](AENEAS.md); the short version and what it changes.

**What was verified.** `crates/relalg`'s `Rel::width`, extracted from the
shipping Rust by Charon and Aeneas and proved against `Slot.Rel.width`. Four
theorems in [`verify/Verify/RelAlg.lean`](../verify/Verify/RelAlg.lean); the one
that matters is `width_sound` — *if the Rust reports an arity, that arity is the
specification's*. All four depend on exactly
`[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]`, the slot's own permitted set, checked
in `verify/Verify/Axioms.lean` rather than assumed. That check is not ceremony:
Aeneas's standard library contains `sorry` in `Aeneas/Std/Slice.lean` and
`Aeneas/Std/StringIter.lean`, so a proof reaching the wrong part of it would
inherit `sorryAx` and still compile.

**Why that function.** It is where a disagreement with Lean is a *soundness* bug
and not a wrong answer. The host accepts a rewritten plan only when its width
matches the submitted one's, and the justification for that is `Slot.Sound` —
a theorem about `Slot.Rel.width`, on the other side of the wire from the Rust
that actually runs the check.

**The bug.** `width` returned `u32` and added with a bare `+`, while
`Slot.Rel.width` is over `Nat`. Widths are not bounded on the way in:
`rel_of_sexp` accepts any `u32` for a scan's width. So
`Join(Scan{w = u32::MAX}, Scan{w = 9})` had a true arity of `2^32 + 8` and
computed **8** — an ordinary arity, and exactly the sort of value being compared
against, so a response describing a different plan passed the check. Only the
downstream schema-drift check stopped it. With overflow checks on, the same
expression panics inside `OptimizerRule::rewrite`, which fails the query rather
than declining the rewrite. `width` now returns `Option<u32>` and both call sites
treat `None` as a width violation.

**The proof is load-bearing.** Put the bare `+` back, re-extract, and the Join
case of `width_spec` does not close. It cannot: the statement is false for the
wrapping version. Verified by doing it.

**A second bug, found by accident.** Changing `width`'s signature perturbed
timing enough to expose that `LeanRule`'s 250 ms per-request timeout was being
charged the Lean interpreter's *startup* cost on the first request — and a
timeout disables the host permanently. One slow first request silently turned the
rule into the identity for a whole run, presenting as "declined everything".
`LeanRule::spawn` now warms the host with a trivial request under a separate
30 s budget, so the scored budget is steady-state cost only, and a host that
cannot run at all fails at spawn instead of quietly. This is the kind of thing
that would have made a validator void submissions at random.

**A diagnostic gap closed alongside it.** `RuleStats.errors` conflated a protocol
failure with a rewrite that `lift` could not rebuild. They mean opposite things —
the host is broken, versus the bridge is the limit and a real rewrite was
dropped — so `lift_failures` is now counted separately, and the bridge
self-check prints every counter rather than just the rewrite count. Diagnosing
the warm-up bug took three rounds of instrumenting that the counters should have
answered immediately.

**What it says about v3.** [`PLAN.md`](PLAN.md) files Aeneas under v3 with the
note that the guarantee will be weaker than v1's. It is now possible to say how
much weaker, and the honest answer is mixed: the tool caught a real soundness bug
that no proof about `Slot.Rel` could reach, and the translatable subset is
narrower than it looks — the wire codec, in a dependency-free 450-line crate, is
already outside it. Budget the extraction work, and write the guarantee down as
"this function, under these axioms, given this translation" rather than
"verified".

## Next action: M2, held-out query generation

M1's conclusion redirects the work. The premise holds — the pipeline runs
end to end and the fragment reaches TPC-H — so M3 is no longer at risk of being
wasted. But two things now want doing before the verifier service, and they are
cheaper than it:

1. **A reference submission that actually wins** (`examples/`). Predicate
   pushdown through a join is the first item on the headroom list and the one
   with the clearest payoff: DataFusion does it, so the shape is known to matter,
   and a Lean proof of it needs the NULL-safety side conditions that make it
   interesting. Without such a submission there is nothing to test a ladder
   with, because the reference rule can never displace a champion.
2. **M2, the held-out set.** `scripts/genqueries.py` over the v1 fragment. M1
   showed the public workload is the wrong tool for developing a rule — TPC-H
   plans are already normalised by the time the rule is asked — so the generated
   set needs a shape report from the start, or it will drift into rewarding rules
   that only fire on plans nobody runs.

Do these in either order; do them before M3.

**And a third that the normalisation exercise moved up the list:** add `Le` and
`Ge` to the fragment as *primitives* with their own three-valued semantics — not
as `NOT (b < a)`, which is genuinely unsound. Between them and decimals they are
what stands between the coalescing rule, which wins 13–16% where it fires, and
TPC-H, where the same shape appears on `l_quantity`. That is a slot version bump
and re-pin, so it is substrate work, not a submission.

**The thing that used to outrank all of them has largely landed.** The argument in
[`COMPETITION.md`](COMPETITION.md) was to ship *proved combinators*, not just a
specification, because a submission that proves `Sound` from nothing needs a Lean
expert while a submission that composes proved pieces needs an optimiser person
willing to learn some Lean. `Slot/Lemmas.lean` now carries that library:
per-operator `Equiv` congruence, `Scalar.remap` with `evalScalar_remap`,
`evalScalar_shift`, `filter_congr_pred` and `join_congr_pred`, `merge_filters`,
`drop_true_filter`, `filter_comm`, and push-down through project, join and union.

`examples/normalise/Main.lean` is the evidence that this changes submissions
rather than only the substrate: it used to prove its own copy of
`filter_congr_pred` and now imports it, which is a lemma and eight lines of proof
deleted from a submission that was already the shortest interesting one. The
remaining gap for a would-be miner is not congruence any more — it is the
three-valued arithmetic facts (`lt_eq_never` and friends), which are specific to
a rewrite and probably belong in submissions.

What that leaves genuinely open is above: a submission that wins on a *real*
workload, which is blocked by the fragment (decimals, `Le`/`Ge`) rather than by
the proof burden.

Two smaller things the Aeneas work leaves open, neither blocking:

3. **`just verify-extract-check` is not wired to anything.** It is the only guard
   against the proofs passing about a `crates/relalg` that no longer exists, and
   nothing runs it. It cannot go in `just test` — it needs a Rust nightly with
   `rustc-dev` and builds Charon — so it belongs in CI, or in a pre-release
   check. Until then it is a command someone has to remember.
4. **`Rel::size` has `Rel::width`'s shape and is unproved.** `1 + left.size() +
   right.size()` in `usize`, and the reason it is safe is that a plan with `2^64`
   nodes cannot be parsed — an argument about what fits in memory rather than
   about the values, which is the argument that was wrong for `width`. It bounds
   `max_plan_nodes`, so an overflow would defeat a denial-of-service guard rather
   than a soundness one. Lower stakes, same fix, and the extraction already
   covers the function.

## Open questions that need a decision

All of these want an answer before M5. Question 3 is now answered by M1's
measurement and is kept here with the answer rather than deleted, so a future
session does not reopen it.

1. **DataFusion version policy.** Pinned to `50` today. DataFusion moves fast and
   the `OptimizerRule` trait has changed shape before. A slot's manifest already
   records the engine version — decide whether a version bump opens a new slot
   (champions reset) or migrates the existing one (champions carry over, and
   every champion must be re-benchmarked).
2. **Scale factor for scoring.** SF1 keeps a scoring run to minutes; SF10 gives a
   cleaner signal and a heavier validator. Depends on how many submissions per
   epoch you expect. Concrete numbers from M1: SF1 is 310 MB of Parquet, about a
   minute to generate, and a 7-repetition run of the ten public queries takes
   roughly two minutes. SF0.01 is useless for timing — the queries run in 2–6 ms
   and the variance swamps everything — but it is the right scale for
   `--self-check` and the differential gate.
3. ~~**Interpreter or compiled host.**~~ **Answered: interpreter.** `lean --run`
   costs 2–12 ms of plan time per TPC-H query against a 250 ms budget, and 159 ms
   of host round trips across a whole 7-repetition run of ten queries. `leanc`
   stays off the miner-derived path and the safer option is also free. Revisit
   only if a slot appears whose plans are orders of magnitude larger.
4. **Tenure decay curve.** Shipped as a constant. Fit it once there is real
   submission volume, not before.
5. **Launch eligibility.** `manifest.json` has `production_eligible: false`.
   Flipping it is the go-live gate and should require the full sandbox posture
   from M4 to be in place.
6. **How submissions arrive.** Answered in [`COMPETITION.md`](COMPETITION.md), and
   the short version is that a public pull request cannot carry a scored
   submission: it publishes the proof term before it is scored, which removes
   commit–reveal, the only defence against copying. Two decisions still open
   there — whether substrate work is bountied out of a separate budget rather
   than emission, and whether promotion requires an improvement to replicate
   across two independent runs (recommended: the 2% bar is close to the
   measurement floor, and one mis-provisioned validator otherwise promotes
   noise).

## Decided — do not re-litigate

Recorded here so a future session does not spend an afternoon rediscovering the
reasoning.

* **No Mathlib, no Batteries.** Everything needed is in Lean 4 core:
  `List.Perm.filter/map/append/flatMap_right`, `rcases`, `omega`. The one gap —
  pointwise `flatMap` congruence — is four lines in `Slot/Lemmas.lean`. Cold
  build stays at ~2 s and the verifier's trusted checkout stays small.
* **`LIMIT`, `ORDER BY`, `DISTINCT`, aggregation, outer joins are out of the v1
  fragment.** Bag equivalence is not a sound correctness notion for
  order- or multiplicity-observing operators. They arrive in v2 *with* their
  congruence story, not before. The bridge declines to lower them.
* **`<=`, `>=`, `!=` are not lowered.** `NOT (b < a)` is wrong under three-valued
  logic, because `NOT NULL` is `NULL`, not `TRUE`.
* **Floats and decimals are not lowered.** Widening to `Int` would let a proof
  about integer comparison licence a rewrite over money columns.
* **Dates are lowered, to their epoch offset.** Not a re-litigation of the line
  above: a `Date32` *is* a day count and DataFusion compares dates by comparing
  those integers, so the agreement is exact rather than approximate. A decimal's
  integer is a *scaled* representation and agreement would depend on both sides
  carrying the same scale — a property of DataFusion's coercion rules, which the
  bridge does not get to assume. Full argument in
  [`THREAT_MODEL.md`](THREAT_MODEL.md); M1 found that without dates the fragment
  cannot express a single TPC-H predicate.
* **The obligation lives inside `Slot.VerifiedRule`.** That is what makes the
  sibling's type-hash statement check apply unchanged to a statement that
  mentions the miner's own definition. See [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](ARCHITECTURE.md).
* **`crates/df-bridge` is unproved and stays unproved in v1.** Proving it would
  need a formal model of DataFusion's `LogicalPlan` semantics, which does not
  exist. It is defended by conservatism, scan identity, and differential
  execution — see [`THREAT_MODEL.md`](THREAT_MODEL.md).

* **Aeneas verification lives in `verify/`, a separate Lake package.** It needs
  Mathlib and Lean v4.31.0; the spec library needs neither and pins v4.27.0,
  which `manifest.json` records and champions are verified against. Bumping the
  slot's toolchain to suit a tool would invalidate every existing proof's
  pinning. The two coexist instead, and `verify/` compiles the spec from its real
  path rather than copying it.

## Traps worth remembering

* **Pattern order in a miner's `rule`.** Lean compiles overlapping patterns into
  nested matches that do not reduce, and the soundness proof then will not close
  for the arm you care about. In the reference submission the arms selected by
  the *child's* constructor come first and the arm selected by a specific
  *predicate* comes last. Written the other way round, nothing reduces. This is
  documented in [`MINER.md`](MINER.md) because miners will hit it too.
* **`apply_order` is not optional.** A rule that does not recurse and returns
  `None` from `apply_order()` is offered the plan root and nothing else, and
  every real query has something out of the fragment at its root. The failure is
  silent — it reads as "found no improvement". Anything else added to the
  optimizer rule list needs the same consideration.
* **A rewrite that cannot be lifted is invisible.** `lift` returning `None`
  means "keep the original plan", which is correct and is also indistinguishable
  from a rule that declined. The date-literal bug lived in that gap. When a
  change to `crates/df-bridge` seems to have no effect, check the `errors`
  counter before concluding the rule found nothing.
* **DataFusion's plan constructors are not a validator.** `Filter::try_new`
  type-checks its predicate only when `get_type` succeeds, and silently accepts
  it when `get_type` errors. `.ok()?` on a builder call therefore does *not*
  mean "DataFusion approved this plan". Anything `lift` builds has to be checked
  by `lift`; a malformed plan that gets past it becomes a failed query at
  physical planning time, in release builds where `check_invariants` does not
  run.
* **A `u32` mirror of a `Nat` definition is a soundness gap, not a detail.**
  `Rel::width` is the case that bit; `Rel::size` has the same shape and is only
  safe because a plan with `2^64` nodes cannot be parsed. Any new function in
  `crates/relalg` that mirrors a `Nat`-valued definition in `lean/Slot/` needs the
  same treatment, and the argument has to be about the values reaching it, not
  about what a reasonable plan looks like — the values come off a wire a miner
  controls.
* **Timeouts that disable a host permanently need a warm-up.** Charging process
  startup to a per-request budget makes the first request of a run fail on a busy
  machine, and disabling the host on timeout makes that failure permanent and
  silent. `LeanRule::spawn` warms up for this reason; anything else given a
  per-request deadline needs the same split.
* **Out-of-range columns are `NULL`, not an error.** This is what makes `eval`
  total and lets `Sound` have no well-formedness escape hatch. It also means a
  pushdown past a narrow projection legitimately produces `(lit null)` — that is
  correct behaviour, not a bug, and the host demonstrates it.
# Threat model

Most of this is inherited. conjectures-validator already runs hostile Lean under
landrun + seccomp, with a live fail-closed isolation probe, an axiom allowlist
checked against an exported environment, and a second independent kernel. That
posture carries over unchanged and is not re-argued here.

What follows is only what is **new**, and it comes from one change: this subnet
*executes* miner code, where the sibling only type-checks it.

## New: the miner's code runs

A rule is a total, pure Lean function. It cannot perform IO — `unsafe`,
`extern`, `implemented_by`, `partial` and `initialize` are all rejected by the
static policy, and the type `Rel → Option Rel` lives in `Id`, not `IO`. So the
threat is not exfiltration; it is resource exhaustion and wrong output.

| Threat | Control |
|---|---|
| Rule is total but astronomically slow (`ackermann 5 5`) | Per-request timeout (250 ms), sandbox wall-clock and memory caps, host killed and rule disabled on breach |
| Rule oscillates `a → b → a` | Fuel bound of 64 in `Slot.repeatN`, set by the host |
| Rule allocates without bound | `RLIMIT_AS` on the host process, same as the Comparator |
| Rule emits an enormous plan | `max_plan_nodes` checked before the request and the response decoded with a depth cap |
| Half-spoken pipe desynchronises request/response | Any protocol error kills the host and disables the rule for the rest of the run — a resynchronised pipe could pair one plan's request with another's response |

The rule host runs under the same landrun + seccomp profile as the Comparator,
in a fresh disposable workspace, with no network, no validator keys, and no
database. It is a separate security context from the benchmark orchestrator.

## New: the bridge is unproved

`crates/df-bridge` translates between DataFusion's `LogicalPlan` and the slot IR,
and **no Lean theorem covers it**. This is the honest weak point of the design,
and pretending otherwise would be the actual danger. Three defences:

1. **Conservatism by construction.** `lower` returns `None` for anything it does
   not fully understand, and the caller then leaves that subtree untouched. Most
   of the file is refusals. Approximating an unsupported node is never allowed.
2. **Scan identity.** `Rel::Scan { table }` indexes a side table of the original
   `LogicalPlan` scan nodes; `lift` rebuilds from those verbatim. Table sources,
   pushed-down filters and projections inside a scan are carried through rather
   than re-derived, so the bridge cannot lose them.
3. **Differential execution.** Every scored query runs both arms and the result
   sets are compared as bags. A bridge bug becomes a wrong answer on a real
   workload — the only check that reaches the parts no proof does.

`crates/relalg` sits below the bridge and is trusted the same way, with one
exception: `Rel::width` is now *proved* to compute `Slot.Rel.width`, by Aeneas.
That matters because the width check is what enforces `Slot.Sound` at the wire,
and the check was defeatable — the Rust computed the arity in `u32` with a bare
`+`, so `Join(Scan{w = u32::MAX}, Scan{w = 9})` reported `8`, an ordinary arity
equal to the one being compared against. See [`AENEAS.md`](AENEAS.md). The wire
codec is *not* proved and is still defended only by `just wire-roundtrip`.

Concretely, the traps already closed in v1:

* `<=`, `>=` and `!=` are **not** lowered. Expressing `a <= b` as `NOT (b < a)`
  is wrong under three-valued logic, because `NOT NULL` is `NULL`, not `TRUE`.
* Floats and decimals are **not** lowered. Widening them to `Int` would let a
  proof about integer comparison licence a rewrite over money columns.
* Dates **are** lowered, to their epoch offset, and this is not the same move.
  `Date32` *is* a day count and `Date64` *is* a millisecond count; DataFusion
  compares both by comparing those integers, so `Slot.Value` ordering on the
  offset agrees with date ordering exactly. Type coercion has already forced both
  sides of a comparison to the same date type, so a day count is never compared
  against a millisecond one. A decimal's integer, by contrast, is a *scaled*
  representation: agreement would depend on both sides carrying the same scale,
  which is a property of DataFusion's coercion rules rather than of the values,
  and the bridge does not get to assume those. That asymmetry is the whole
  distinction, and it is why the two cases are decided differently.
* `lift` gives a literal back the type of the column it is compared against,
  where it can do so exactly — an `Int` against a date column, a `Str` against a
  `Utf8View` column. It has to: `TypeCoercion` is an *analyzer* rule and has
  already run, so nothing downstream repairs `l_shipdate > Int64(9497)`. Where
  the type cannot be reproduced exactly the literal is left alone and DataFusion
  rejects the plan, which drops the rewrite. Inventing a value to make a plan
  type-check is the one thing the bridge must never do.
* Outer joins are **not** lowered. They invent NULL rows that `Slot.Rel.join`
  does not model.
* `Limit`, `Sort`, `Distinct`, aggregation and window functions are **not**
  lowered, because bag equivalence is unsound for order- and
  multiplicity-observing operators.
* A lifted plan whose schema names or types drift from the original is rejected
  even though its width matches, because the enclosing operators are bound to
  the original field qualifiers.
* A lifted predicate that does not resolve to a boolean is rejected by `lift`
  itself, rather than left to DataFusion. `Filter::try_new` type-checks on a
  *best effort* — it skips the check when `get_type` errors, which correlated
  subqueries need and a malformed lift also gets — so a bad predicate would
  otherwise be accepted and fail during physical planning. That would turn a
  bridge bug into a failed query, and the whole posture here depends on a bridge
  bug costing at most a lost optimisation. `check_invariants(Executable)` would
  have caught it but runs only in debug builds; a scored run is a release build.

## New: the statement is parameterised

The sibling's Comparator compares a closed statement's type hash. Here the
statement mentions the miner's own definition. The obligation is therefore
carried inside `Slot.VerifiedRule`, so both files declare the same closed type
and the existing check applies unchanged.

Two things must hold for that to be worth anything, and both are enforced
outside the miner's reach:

* **`Sound` must mean what the slot says.** It is pinned by the hash of
  `lean/Slot/Rule.lean` — and of every other file in `lean/Slot/` — recorded in
  the task manifest by `scripts/slotpack.py pin`. A validator on a stale or
  edited checkout fails the hash check rather than silently accepting proofs
  about a different specification.
* **`Bounty.target` must be built by the slot, not the miner.** It is assembled
  in `SolutionFooter.lean.txt`, which the miner never sees the inside of and
  cannot modify. Elaboration fails unless `rule_sound` proves `Sound rule` for
  the same `rule` the host will execute.

## New: performance is an attack surface

A scoring pipeline is a thing to be gamed even when every proof is honest. See
the anti-gaming table in [`SCORING.md`](SCORING.md); the load-bearing items are
held-out queries seeded from an unpredictable block hash, a per-query regression
cap, and interleaved repetitions on a pinned hardware profile.

## Explicitly out of scope for v1

* Proving `crates/df-bridge` correct. It would need a formal model of
  DataFusion's `LogicalPlan` semantics, which does not exist.
* Proving anything about DataFusion's *physical* planning or execution. The slot
  only claims the logical plan means the same thing.
* Side channels between the rule host and the benchmark orchestrator. They are
  separate processes but not separate machines.
# The verifier

`verifier/` is the submission gate: it decides whether a miner's Lean file is
accepted, and only then whether it is fast. Ported from `verifier/` in the sibling
`conjectures-validator`, keeping its module names so further porting stays a diff
rather than a translation.

```bash
just gate    examples/normalise/Main.lean   # proof gate only, ~1s
just verdict examples/normalise/Main.lean --bench-arg=--scale --bench-arg=1
just verifier-test                          # 34 tests, mostly adversarial
```

## The order is the design

```
load task
  -> task commitment          (is this the task the network committed to?)
    -> trusted files          (is the spec library the pinned one?)
      -> toolchain            (is this the pinned Lean?)
        -> load submission    (size, UTF-8, hash)
          -> static policy    (tokens, before anything elaborates)
            -> sandbox        (does the isolation actually deny?)
              -> elaborate    (the footer is the statement check)
                -> statement  (is the type `Slot.VerifiedRule`?)
                  -> axioms   (`#print axioms`, strictly parsed)
                    -> [second kernel]
                      -> differential check
                        -> timing
```

**Nothing is timed until the proof has been accepted.** That is the whole point:
a submission cannot buy speed with an unsound rule, and a fast wrong answer is
not a low score but no score. The cheap checks also come first, so the common
rejections cost milliseconds rather than minutes.

Every stage is recorded whether or not it ran, so a report says how far a
submission got, not only where it stopped.

## Exit status, and whose fault it is

| code | meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | accepted |
| 1 | rejected — the submission's fault, and scoreable |
| 2 | could not verify — the **validator's** fault; retry, never penalise |

The split matters more than it looks. `errors.py:OPERATOR_FAULT` lists the reasons
that indict the operator: a missing sandbox, a stale checkout, an unbuilt harness,
a void benchmark. Scoring a miner down because the validator's CPU governor was
unpinned is the kind of bug that destroys a subnet's credibility, so the reason
codes carry the distinction rather than leaving it to the caller.

## Why a static scan, when the axioms are checked anyway

Because several fatal constructs produce no axiom at all:

* `set_option` can disable the checks that make the axiom list meaningful.
* `implemented_by` and `extern` replace a declaration's *compiled* behaviour
  while leaving its proof intact. That breaks the premise of this whole slot —
  that the proved program **is** the running program — and `#print axioms` would
  show nothing wrong.
* `elab` / `macro` / `notation` can make the source text mean something other
  than what it reads as, which defeats review by a human.
* `partial` makes a definition opaque to the proof that is supposed to be about
  it.

The scanner is a tokenizer, not a regex, and that is not fastidiousness:
`examples/normalise/Main.lean` contains a docstring reading "instances of this",
and `instance` is a prohibited token. A regex rejects a real submission for a
comment. Comments and string literals are excluded from the scan; `s!"..."`
interpolation is rejected outright rather than scanned into.

## What the footer buys

The submission is sandwiched between the slot's fixed header and footer, byte for
byte. The footer reads

```lean
def target : Slot.VerifiedRule := ⟨rule, rule_sound⟩
```

so elaboration fails unless `rule` has type `Slot.Rule` and `rule_sound` proves
`Slot.Sound rule` **for that same rule**. The miner never writes the type of the
artifact, so there is no "does the theorem say the right thing" pass to get wrong.
`tests/test_verifier.py::test_an_unsound_rule_cannot_be_proved` submits a rule
that deletes a filter — innocuous to the scanner, false as a theorem — and
checks it dies at elaboration.

The `#check` against `manifest.target_type` is belt and braces: the footer is a
*task file*, and a task assembled with a mismatched header/footer pair would build
happily while proving something else.

## What is *not* here

**The second kernel.** `lean4export` + `nanoda` — the independent re-check of the
proof term — lives in `conjectures-validator`. The manifest sets
`enable_nanoda: true`, and this verifier treats that as a requirement: if the
tooling is absent it reports `nanoda_passed: false` and refuses, unless
`--allow-insecure-development` is passed. It does not silently downgrade.

**The sandbox.** `hardened-landrun.sh` and `seccomp-launcher.c` are also the
sibling's. `sandbox.py` locates them and runs the sibling's *live* fail-closed
probe rather than checking that a file exists — a landrun binary that does not
actually deny is worse than none, because the report would claim isolation that
was not there. In this checkout the probe reports:

```
absent | no built seccomp launcher at ../conjectures-validator/.tools/seccomp-launcher
```

so every run here needs `--allow-insecure-development`, which stamps the report.
Point `CONJECTURES_VALIDATOR` at the sibling and build its launcher to get a real
run.

**The scoring rules.** They live in `crates/bench`, because that is where the two
DataFusion arms live. `performance.py` is a driver, not a second implementation;
duplicating the ladder in Python would create two versions that could disagree.
The one thing the driver adds is putting the workspace **first** on `LEAN_PATH`,
so a baseline `SlotEntry.olean` cannot shadow the submission and turn the rule
into the identity — which would report an honest-looking 1.000x.

## The governance check

`check_trusted_files` compares every hash in `manifest.trusted_file_hashes`
against the working tree on every run, and that includes the spec library. This is
the invariant `CLAUDE.md` calls a governance boundary: `Slot.VerifiedRule` is only
a meaningful obligation while `Slot.Sound` means what the slot says it means. A
miner cannot edit `lean/Slot/RelAlg.lean` — but a validator running a stale or
patched checkout can, and would then accept proofs of a different statement with
every check still green.
`tests/test_verifier.py::test_spec_library_tampering_is_detected` appends a
comment to `RelAlg.lean` in a copy of the tree and requires the run to stop.

Similarly, a production task requires `--expect-task-sha256`: a validator that
verifies against a task it fetched itself has proved nothing about the task the
network agreed on.

## Status

Working and tested end to end against all four example submissions:

| submission | gate | benchmark |
|---|---|---|
| `filter-merge` | accepted | `NOT_FASTER` (declines everything) |
| `combinators` | accepted | not measured |
| `contradiction` | accepted | not measured |
| `normalise` | accepted | `promote`, geomean 9.03x on its dev set |

Rejection paths exercised: `sorry` → `SUBMISSION_POLICY_VIOLATION` (exit 1);
an unsound rule → `SOLUTION_BUILD_FAILED` (exit 1); no sandbox →
`INSECURE_SANDBOX` (exit 2, operator fault); a wrong commitment →
`TASK_COMMITMENT_MISMATCH` (exit 2); oversized and non-UTF-8 submissions.

Remaining before this is a validator rather than a verifier: the second kernel
and sandbox wired up from the sibling, a worker loop and queue, the held-out
query generator (M2), and commit–reveal for task distribution. None of those
change the gate; they surround it.
# The wire codec: what is proved, and what is not

`docs/STATUS.md` recorded the Rust ⟷ Lean agreement as **tested, not proved**, on
the strength of `just wire-roundtrip` — both codecs run over a shared corpus and
the outputs are diffed. This document replaces that single line with the actual
division of labour, because the two halves of the claim now have very different
standing.

The codec matters more than its size suggests. `Slot.optimize_sound` is a theorem
about the `Rel` the host decoded, not about the `LogicalPlan` DataFusion holds.
Those are the same object only if the codec is faithful, so a codec that decodes a
plan into a `Rel` meaning something *else* invalidates every proof above it
without any proof failing.

## Proved: the Lean codec, on every input

`lean/SlotHost/WireProof.lean` (680 lines, 48 theorems). Built by
`just wire-proof`, which also prints the axioms.

| theorem | statement |
|---|---|
| `natOfString_natToString` | decimal naturals round-trip |
| `intOfString_intToString` | decimal integers round-trip, sign included |
| `decodeHex_encodeHex` | the string escape round-trips, UTF-8 included |
| `cellOfSexp_cellToSexp` | every `Cell` survives the structured layer |
| `scalarOfSexp_scalarToSexp` | every `Scalar` survives it |
| `relOfSexp_relToSexp` | every `Rel` survives it |
| `tokenize_render` | `tokenize ∘ render` is the intended token stream |
| `parse_render` | every `SafeSexp` survives the textual layer |
| `safeSexp_relToSexp` | everything the encoder emits *is* a `SafeSexp` |
| **`roundtrip`** | **`parse (render (relToSexp r)) >>= relOfSexp = .ok r`, for every `r`** |

`roundtrip` is the one to read. It has no hypothesis: `parse_render` needs the
atoms to avoid parentheses and whitespace, and `safeSexp_relToSexp` discharges
that for every `Sexp` the encoder can build, so the alphabet promise `render`
used to make in a comment is now checked.

Axioms: `[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]`, all three in the slot
manifest's `permitted_axioms`. No `sorry`, no `native_decide`.

### What had to change to make it provable

Four things, all in trusted host code, none of them changing the bytes on the
wire (`just wire-roundtrip` is what confirms that):

* **Nothing is `partial` any more.** `partial def` is opaque to the equation
  compiler, so a round-trip theorem could not even be *stated* about the old
  decoders. `render`, `tokenize`, `scalarOfSexp` and `relOfSexp` are now
  structurally recursive; the parser takes explicit fuel, because the token list
  does not shrink in a way Lean can see — `parseList` resumes wherever
  `parseTokens` stopped. `parse` passes more fuel than any input can consume and
  `parseTokens_tokensOf` proves the bound is never the reason a frame fails.
* **The numeral codec is written out** (`lean/SlotHost/Numeral.lean`). Core proves
  no lemma relating `toString` to `String.toNat?`, and without
  `(toString n).toNat? = some n` there is no route to `relOfSexp_relToSexp` at
  all. The replacement renders and parses decimal directly, so induction reaches
  it; the output is byte-identical.
* **The parser dispatches on the head token with `if`, not by matching string
  literals.** A literal pattern compiles to a `matcher` that `simp` will not
  reduce from a disequality hypothesis.
* **The hex codec works on `List UInt8`.** The old version indexed a `ByteArray`
  through `List.range` and `get!`, which is not usable in a proof.

### A defect this found

Proving `safeSexp_relToSexp` failed, correctly, on one case: **the empty string
was not transmissible.** `encodeHex ""` is `""`, so a plan containing
`Value.str ""` encoded to `(str )` with an empty atom; `Sexp.flush` emits nothing
for an empty accumulator, so `tokenize` dropped it and `(str)` came back
undecodable.

Both codecs did this *identically*, which is the interesting part: the failure was
symmetric, so `just wire-roundtrip` could never have caught it — a differential
test is blind to a loss both sides share, and the corpus had no empty string. It
failed closed (decode error → `err` → the Rust host keeps the original plan), so
it cost rewrites and never answers. Fixed on both sides: a one-element `(str)` is
the empty string, and no empty atom is ever emitted. The corpus now covers it.

## Not proved: that the *Rust* codec agrees

Still `just wire-roundtrip` only: both implementations over a shared corpus,
diffed. This is a real check — it is what caught every format skew during
development, and it now covers the empty string — but it is a test over five plan
shapes, not a theorem.

**Aeneas cannot reach the Rust codec**, so the gap is not laziness. The parser
walks a `&str` and `rel_of_sexp` hands `nat` to `Iterator::map` as a function
value; neither is in the translated subset. `verify/Relalg/FunsExternal.lean`
therefore carries the codec as sixteen opaque axioms, which is the honest
representation of "we did not model this". See [`AENEAS.md`](AENEAS.md).

So the standing of the whole claim is:

* the Lean codec is **correct** — proved, all inputs;
* the Rust codec is **consistent with it** — tested, one corpus;
* and the two implementations are deliberately written to the same shape
  (accumulator-based tokenizer, `if`-dispatched parser, same arm order) so that
  reading them side by side is a meaningful review.

Closing the remaining gap means either extending Charon/Aeneas's subset or
rewriting the Rust codec into it. The second is possible — an index-passing
parser over `&[u8]` with no closures — and is the cheaper of the two, but it
touches the real trusted computing base to buy a theorem about a component whose
failures are already fail-closed. It is recorded as future work, not as an
oversight.

## Reproducing

```bash
just wire-proof        # builds SlotHostProof, prints the axioms of 5 theorems
just wire-roundtrip    # the two codecs over the shared corpus
just verify-extract-check   # the Aeneas model is not stale
```

`just test` runs the first two.

# GitNexus CLI Commands

Commands below use `node .gitnexus/run.cjs <command>` — the project-local runner `gitnexus analyze` drops next to the index. It auto-selects an available runner at call time (global `gitnexus`, else `pnpm dlx`, else `npx`), so no package-manager assumption and no global install is required.

> **Not analyzed yet, or `node .gitnexus/run.cjs` reports `Cannot find module`** (the gitignored runner is absent — e.g. a fresh clone or `git clean`)? (Re)generate it with `npx gitnexus analyze` from the project root. On **npm 11.x**, if `npx` crashes during install (`node.target is null`), install once with `npm i -g gitnexus` (then `gitnexus analyze`) or use `pnpm --allow-build=@ladybugdb/core --allow-build=gitnexus --allow-build=tree-sitter dlx gitnexus@latest analyze`. See [#1939](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/issues/1939).

## Commands

### analyze — Build or refresh the index

```bash
node .gitnexus/run.cjs analyze
```

Run from the project root. This parses all source files, builds the knowledge graph, writes it to `.gitnexus/`, and generates CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md context files.

| Flag           | Effect                                                           |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--force`      | Force full re-index even if up to date                           |
| `--embeddings` | Enable embedding generation for semantic search (off by default) |
| `--drop-embeddings` | Drop existing embeddings on rebuild. By default, an `analyze` without `--embeddings` preserves them. |
| `--pdg` | Build the program-dependence layers used by `explain` and `pdg_query` (taint, CDG, and REACHING_DEF). |

**When to run:** First time in a project, after major code changes, or when `gitnexus://repo/{name}/context` reports the index is stale. In Claude Code, a PostToolUse hook detects staleness after `git commit` and `git merge` and notifies the agent to run `analyze` — the hook does not run analyze itself, to avoid blocking the agent for up to 120s and risking KuzuDB corruption on timeout.

### status — Check index freshness

```bash
node .gitnexus/run.cjs status
```

Shows whether the current repo has a GitNexus index, when it was last updated, and symbol/relationship counts. Use this to check if re-indexing is needed.

### clean — Delete the index

```bash
node .gitnexus/run.cjs clean
```

Deletes the `.gitnexus/` directory and unregisters the repo from the global registry. Use before re-indexing if the index is corrupt or after removing GitNexus from a project.

| Flag      | Effect                                            |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `--force` | Skip confirmation prompt                          |
| `--all`   | Clean all indexed repos, not just the current one |

### wiki — Generate documentation from the graph

```bash
node .gitnexus/run.cjs wiki
```

Generates repository documentation from the knowledge graph using an LLM. Requires an API key (saved to `~/.gitnexus/config.json` on first use).

| Flag                | Effect                                    |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `--force`           | Force full regeneration                   |
| `--model <model>`   | LLM model (default: minimax/minimax-m2.5) |
| `--base-url <url>`  | LLM API base URL                          |
| `--api-key <key>`   | LLM API key                               |
| `--concurrency <n>` | Parallel LLM calls (default: 3)           |
| `--gist`            | Publish wiki as a public GitHub Gist      |

### list — Show all indexed repos

```bash
node .gitnexus/run.cjs list
```

Lists all repositories registered in `~/.gitnexus/registry.json`. The MCP `list_repos` tool provides the same information.

## After Indexing

1. **Read `gitnexus://repo/{name}/context`** to verify the index loaded
2. Use the other GitNexus skills (`exploring`, `debugging`, `impact-analysis`, `refactoring`) for your task

## Troubleshooting

- **"Not inside a git repository"**: Run from a directory inside a git repo
- **Index is stale after re-analyzing**: Restart Claude Code to reload the MCP server
- **Embeddings slow**: Omit `--embeddings` (it's off by default) or set `OPENAI_API_KEY` for faster API-based embedding

# Debugging with GitNexus

## When to Use

- "Why is this function failing?"
- "Trace where this error comes from"
- "Who calls this method?"
- "This endpoint returns 500"
- Investigating bugs, errors, or unexpected behavior

## Workflow

```
1. query({search_query: "<error or symptom>"})            → Find related execution flows
2. context({name: "<suspect>"})                    → See callers/callees/processes
3. READ gitnexus://repo/{name}/process/{name}                → Trace execution flow
4. cypher({statement: "MATCH path..."})                 → Custom traces if needed
```

> If "Index is stale" → run `node .gitnexus/run.cjs analyze` in terminal.

## Checklist

```
- [ ] Understand the symptom (error message, unexpected behavior)
- [ ] query for error text or related code
- [ ] Identify the suspect function from returned processes
- [ ] context to see callers and callees
- [ ] Trace execution flow via process resource if applicable
- [ ] cypher for custom call chain traces if needed
- [ ] Read source files to confirm root cause
```

## Debugging Patterns

| Symptom              | GitNexus Approach                                          |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| Error message        | `query` for error text → `context` on throw sites |
| Wrong return value   | `context` on the function → trace callees for data flow    |
| Intermittent failure | `context` → look for external calls, async deps            |
| Performance issue    | `context` → find symbols with many callers (hot paths)     |
| Recent regression    | `detect_changes` to see what your changes affect           |
| "How does A reach B?" | `trace` between the two symbols — shortest call chain in one call |

## Tools

**query** — find code related to error:

```
query({search_query: "payment validation error"})
→ Processes: CheckoutFlow, ErrorHandling
→ Symbols: validatePayment, handlePaymentError, PaymentException
```

**context** — full context for a suspect:

```
context({name: "validatePayment"})
→ Incoming calls: processCheckout, webhookHandler
→ Outgoing calls: verifyCard, fetchRates (external API!)
→ Processes: CheckoutFlow (step 3/7)
```

**cypher** — custom call chain traces:

```cypher
MATCH path = (a)-[:CodeRelation {type: 'CALLS'}*1..2]->(b:Function {name: "validatePayment"})
RETURN [n IN nodes(path) | n.name] AS chain
```

**trace** — shortest call chain between two symbols ("how does A reach B?"), one call instead of chaining `context` hops:

```
trace({ from: "processCheckout", to: "fetchRates" })
→ status: ok, hopCount: 3
→ hops: processCheckout → validatePayment → verifyCard → fetchRates
→ edges: CALLS (1.0), CALLS (0.95), CALLS (1.0)
```

When no path exists, `trace` reports the furthest reachable node — exactly where the chain breaks (dynamic dispatch, reflection, or an external boundary).

## Example: "Payment endpoint returns 500 intermittently"

```
1. query({search_query: "payment error handling"})
   → Processes: CheckoutFlow, ErrorHandling
   → Symbols: validatePayment, handlePaymentError

2. context({name: "validatePayment"})
   → Outgoing calls: verifyCard, fetchRates (external API!)

3. READ gitnexus://repo/my-app/process/CheckoutFlow
   → Step 3: validatePayment → calls fetchRates (external)

4. Root cause: fetchRates calls external API without proper timeout
```

# Exploring Codebases with GitNexus

## When to Use

- "How does authentication work?"
- "What's the project structure?"
- "Show me the main components"
- "Where is the database logic?"
- Understanding code you haven't seen before

## Workflow

```
1. READ gitnexus://repos                          → Discover indexed repos
2. READ gitnexus://repo/{name}/context             → Codebase overview, check staleness
3. query({search_query: "<what you want to understand>"})  → Find related execution flows

```

> If step 2 says "Index is stale" → run `node .gitnexus/run.cjs analyze` in terminal.

## Checklist

```
- [ ] READ gitnexus://repo/{name}/context
- [ ] query for the concept you want to understand
- [ ] Review returned processes (execution flows)
- [ ] context on key symbols for callers/callees
- [ ] READ process resource for full execution traces
- [ ] Read source files for implementation details
```

## Resources

| Resource                                | What you get                                            |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `gitnexus://repo/{name}/context`        | Stats, staleness warning (~150 tokens)                  |

| `gitnexus://repo/{name}/cluster/{name}` | Area members with file paths (~500 tokens)              |

## Tools

**query** — find execution flows related to a concept:

**context** — 360-degree view of a symbol:


# GitNexus Guide

Quick reference for all GitNexus MCP tools, resources, and the knowledge graph schema.

## Always Start Here

For any task involving code understanding, debugging, impact analysis, or refactoring:

1. **Read `gitnexus://repo/{name}/context`** — codebase overview + check index freshness
2. **Match your task to a skill below** and **read that skill file**
3. **Follow the skill's workflow and checklist**

> If step 1 warns the index is stale, run `node .gitnexus/run.cjs analyze` in the terminal first.

## Skills

| Task                                         | Skill to read       |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| Understand architecture / "How does X work?" | `gitnexus-exploring`         |
| Blast radius / "What breaks if I change X?"  | `gitnexus-impact-analysis`   |
| Trace bugs / "Why is X failing?"             | `gitnexus-debugging`         |
| Rename / extract / split / refactor          | `gitnexus-refactoring`       |
| Tools, resources, schema reference           | `gitnexus-guide` (this file) |
| Index, status, clean, wiki CLI commands      | `gitnexus-cli`               |

## Tools Reference

| Tool             | What it gives you                                                        |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `query`          | Process-grouped code intelligence — execution flows related to a concept |
| `context`        | 360-degree symbol view — categorized refs, processes it participates in  |
| `impact`         | Symbol blast radius — what breaks at depth 1/2/3 with confidence         |
| `trace`          | Shortest path between two symbols — "how does A reach B?" in one call     |
| `detect_changes` | Git-diff impact — what do your current changes affect                    |
| `rename`         | Multi-file coordinated rename with confidence-tagged edits               |
| `cypher`         | Raw graph queries (read `gitnexus://repo/{name}/schema` first)           |
| `explain`        | Persisted taint findings — source→sink data flows (needs `analyze --pdg`) |
| `pdg_query`      | Control/data dependence — what gates X (CDG) / where Y flows (REACHING_DEF); needs `analyze --pdg` |
| `check`          | Check graph invariants such as circular imports                          |
| `route_map`      | API route map — which components/hooks fetch which endpoints, and the handler files that serve them |
| `shape_check`    | Response-shape drift — keys each route returns vs keys its consumers access (flags MISMATCH) |
| `api_impact`     | Pre-change report for an API route — consumers, middleware, shape mismatches, risk level |
| `tool_map`       | MCP/RPC tool definitions and the files that handle them                  |
| `group_list`     | List configured multi-repo groups, or one group's config                 |
| `group_sync`     | Rebuild a group's Contract Registry (cross-repo HTTP contract links); run after `group.yaml` changes or member re-index |
| `list_repos`     | Discover indexed repos (paginated — `limit`/`offset`)                    |

### Paginating `list_repos`

`list_repos` is paginated so a large registry is not truncated by MCP/LLM token limits. It takes optional `limit` (default **50**, max **200**) and `offset`, and returns:

```jsonc
{
  "repositories": [
    { "name": "...", "path": "...", "indexedAt": "...", "lastCommit": "...", "stats": { } }
  ],
  "pagination": {
    "total": 437,
    "limit": 50,
    "offset": 0,
    "returned": 50,
    "hasMore": true,
    "nextOffset": 50
  }
}
```

To enumerate **every** repository, keep calling with `offset` set to `pagination.nextOffset` until `hasMore` is `false`:

```text
list_repos {}               → repos 1–50,    nextOffset 50,  hasMore true
list_repos { offset: 50 }   → repos 51–100,  nextOffset 100, hasMore true
…
list_repos { offset: 400 }  → repos 401–437,                 hasMore false   (done)
```

Notes: `offset` ≥ `total` returns an empty page (with `total` still reported). Out-of-range or malformed `limit`/`offset` (non-integer, `limit` outside `[1, 200]`, `offset < 0`) are rejected with a clear error — `limit` above the max is rejected, not silently capped. The order is deterministic (lower-cased name, then path), so paging never skips or duplicates an entry while the registry is unchanged.

### Taint findings (`explain`)

`explain` returns taint findings recorded by `gitnexus analyze --pdg` — intra-procedural `TAINTED` edges plus cross-function `TAINT_PATH` hops where the interprocedural taint phase found a function-level source→sink chain. Each finding includes a sink category (command-injection, code-injection, path-traversal, sql-injection, xss), source/sink lines, and the ordered hop path with the variable carried on each hop.

- `explain {}` — enumerate all findings for the repo (bounded by `limit`, deterministic order)
- `explain { target: "src/vuln.ts" }` — findings in a file (suffix path match accepted)
- `explain { target: "runUserCommand" }` — findings in a function (resolved like `context`; ambiguous names return ranked candidates)

A repo indexed without `--pdg` returns a clear "no taint layer" note. Caveats: closure/callback, property/field, and implicit flows are not modeled, and interprocedural findings are function-level `TAINT_PATH` hops rather than statement-level path proof, so the absence of a finding is **not** proof of safety. `SANITIZES` (sanitizer-kill) edges are queryable via `cypher`.

### Control & data dependence (`pdg_query`)

`pdg_query` reads the control/data-dependence layers `gitnexus analyze --pdg` records (CDG + REACHING_DEF, basic-block granular) — the control/data analog of `explain`. It is **always anchored** (a `target` file path or symbol, resolved like `context`) and has two modes:

- `pdg_query { mode: "controls", target: "..." }` — CDG: "under what condition does X run?". Each edge is a controlling predicate block → dependent block with the branch sense (`'T'`/`'F'`) in `reason`; an edge into an early `return`/`throw` is flagged `guard: true` (guard-clause discovery — the sense depends on the predicate, so don't filter guards by a fixed label).
- `pdg_query { mode: "flows", target: "...", variable?: "..." }` — REACHING_DEF def→use edges within the function; pass `variable` to trace one binding.

A repo indexed without `--pdg` returns a "no PDG layer" note (or "status unknown" when the layer can't be confirmed). Intra-procedural only — cross-function flow is taint's domain (`explain`). The raw CDG/REACHING_DEF edges are also queryable via `cypher`. See the `gitnexus-pdg-query` skill for the full query surface.

### Shortest path between two symbols (`trace`)

`trace` answers "how does A reach B?" in one call — the shortest directed path over `CALLS` (plus `HAS_METHOD`, so a class-rooted trace descends into its methods) instead of chaining 3–8 `context`/`impact` hops by hand.

- `trace { from: "validateUser", to: "executeQuery" }` — shortest path between two symbols.
- Disambiguate common names with `from_uid`/`to_uid` (zero-ambiguity) or `from_file`/`to_file`; an ambiguous name returns ranked candidates.
- `maxDepth` (default 10, max 30) bounds the search; `includeTests` (default false) lets the traversal pass through test-file symbols.

Returns ordered `hops` (each `{ name, filePath, startLine }`) and an aligned `edges[]` of `{ relType, confidence }`, so call hops and containment (`HAS_METHOD`) hops stay distinguishable. When no path exists it reports the **furthest** reachable node (where the chain breaks) and sets `truncated: true` if a traversal cap was hit first. Every result carries a `status`: `ok` / `no_path` / `ambiguous` / `not_found` / `error`.

Cross-repo (experimental): pass `repo: "@groupName"` to trace across a group's member repos — the path may cross **one** `ContractLink` boundary (reported as a `CONTRACT_LINK` hop with the bridged contract in `crossings[]`). Omit `to` entirely to follow `from`'s outgoing HTTP call to whatever provider endpoint it lands on. Groups are configured via `group_list` / `group_sync`.

## Resources Reference

Lightweight reads (~100-500 tokens) for navigation:

| Resource                                       | Content                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `gitnexus://repo/{name}/context`               | Stats, staleness check                    |
| `gitnexus://repo/{name}/clusters`              | All functional areas with cohesion scores |
| `gitnexus://repo/{name}/cluster/{clusterName}` | Area members                              |
| `gitnexus://repo/{name}/processes`             | All execution flows                       |
| `gitnexus://repo/{name}/process/{processName}` | Step-by-step trace                        |
| `gitnexus://repo/{name}/schema`                | Graph schema for Cypher                   |

## Graph Schema

**Nodes:** File, Folder, Function, Class, Interface, Method, CodeElement, Community, Process, Route, Tool, plus language-specific types (Struct, Enum, Trait, Impl, Namespace, Module, …) and BasicBlock (`--pdg` indexes only). The full node list lives in `gitnexus://repo/{name}/schema`.
**Edges (via CodeRelation.type):** CALLS, IMPORTS, EXTENDS, IMPLEMENTS, DEFINES, CONTAINS, MEMBER_OF, HAS_METHOD, HAS_PROPERTY, ACCESSES, METHOD_OVERRIDES, METHOD_IMPLEMENTS, STEP_IN_PROCESS, HANDLES_ROUTE, FETCHES, HANDLES_TOOL, ENTRY_POINT_OF, WRAPS, QUERIES, INJECTS, plus `--pdg`-only types (CFG, REACHING_DEF, TAINTED, SANITIZES, TAINT_PATH, CDG — zero rows on a default index).

Read `gitnexus://repo/{name}/schema` before writing Cypher — it is the authoritative schema for the indexed repo.

```cypher
MATCH (caller)-[:CodeRelation {type: 'CALLS'}]->(f:Function {name: "myFunc"})
RETURN caller.name, caller.filePath
```
